teile.einleitung: War crimes are serious breaches of the rules that apply even in war. These rules are called international humanitarian law. Above all, they are meant to protect civilians, the wounded and prisoners.
wichtigste: International humanitarian law applies even in war.
Article 8 of the Rome Statute lists the war crimes.
Starving civilians is a war crime.
Children under 15 must not be recruited into armed forces.
Every state party must prosecute or hand over people accused of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions.
In 2016 the International Criminal Court convicted al-Mahdi for destroying cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: Even in war, not everything is allowed. The **Geneva Conventions** of 1949 protect the wounded, prisoners and **civilians**. Switzerland is the **depositary state** of these conventions, meaning it keeps the originals. The **Rome Statute** of 1998 founded the **International Criminal Court** in The Hague. Its **Article 8** lists the war crimes in detail.

**Treachery**, also called **perfidy**, is forbidden. This means attacking by abusing the enemy's trust in protection, for example by pretending to be a civilian. Ordinary **ruses of war** such as camouflage are still allowed. **Starving** civilians is also a war crime, for example by blocking aid deliveries. It is equally forbidden to recruit **children under 15** into armed forces.

Particularly serious breaches of the Geneva Conventions are called **grave breaches**. They include, for example, wilful killing, torture or taking protected persons hostage. Every state party must **bring suspected offenders before its own courts or hand them over**. This applies regardless of their nationality. The aim is that offenders are safe nowhere.

**Cultural heritage** such as churches, mosques or monuments is also protected. In **2016** the International Criminal Court convicted **Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi**. In 2012 he had ordered the destruction of mausoleums and a mosque in **Timbuktu** in Mali. It was the Court's first case dealing only with the destruction of cultural heritage. Al-Mahdi was sentenced to 9 years in prison.

As early as the **American Civil War**, the US Army issued the **Lieber Code** in **1863**. With it, the lawyer **Francis Lieber** wrote down rules for the Union troops. They later influenced the **Hague Conventions**. After the First World War, the **Treaty of Versailles** of 1919 provided for charges against **Kaiser Wilhelm II**. However, the Netherlands, where he had fled, did not hand him over.

gewusst: The Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions have their origins in Switzerland.
The mausoleums of Timbuktu were rebuilt with the help of UNESCO after they were destroyed.

teile.einleitung: OPEC is the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Its members are countries that produce and sell a lot of oil. With its decisions, OPEC can influence the price of oil all over the world.
wichtigste: OPEC stands for “Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries”.
It was founded in Baghdad in September 1960.
Its founders were Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
From 1961 to 1965 it was based in Geneva, and since then in Vienna.
Since 2016 OPEC has worked as “OPEC+” together with other oil countries such as Russia.
A barrel of oil is about 159 litres.

abschnitte.text: OPEC was founded in **September 1960** in **Baghdad** in Iraq. The five founders were Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. They wanted to have more influence on the oil market together. At that time prices were set mainly by large Western oil companies. Later more countries joined, for example **Nigeria** in 1971.

From 1961 to 1965 OPEC was based in **Geneva**. However, Switzerland did not grant it diplomatic status at the time. So in 1965 the organisation moved to **Vienna** in Austria. Its headquarters is still there today. The oil ministers of the member countries meet regularly in Vienna.

The members agree on how much oil they produce. If they decide to produce **less**, oil becomes scarcer. If demand stays the same, the price then usually **rises**. Oil prices are given in US dollars per **barrel**. A barrel is a cask and holds about 159 litres.

Since **2016** the OPEC countries have coordinated with other producing countries. These include **Russia**, Kazakhstan and Mexico. This group is called **OPEC+**. Together they control a large part of the world's oil production. However, the members do not always agree.

In autumn 1973 the Arab oil states delivered less oil. The oil price rose sharply, and many countries feared shortages. In November and December 1973 Switzerland ordered three **car-free Sundays**. On these days people were not allowed to drive. Many people went for walks, rode bikes or even roller-skated on the empty roads.

gewusst: OPEC had its first headquarters in Geneva before it moved to Vienna.
The word “barrel” means a cask, or a large wooden container for liquids.

teile.einleitung: The Rome Statute is the founding treaty of the International Criminal Court in The Hague. This court can prosecute people who are responsible for the world's most serious crimes.
wichtigste: The statute was adopted at a conference in Rome in 1998.
120 countries voted in favour, 7 against and 21 abstained.
The Court has had jurisdiction since 1 July 2002.
Under the principle of complementarity, the states themselves are responsible first.
Switzerland ratified the statute in 2001.
In 2023 the Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin.

abschnitte.text: On **17 July 1998** a diplomatic conference in **Rome** adopted the statute. **120 countries** voted in favour, 7 against, including the USA and China, and 21 abstained. After the 60th ratification, the statute came into force on **1 July 2002**. The Court cannot prosecute acts committed before this date. Today 17 July is marked as the **Day of International Criminal Justice**.

The **International Criminal Court** sits in **The Hague** in the Netherlands. It prosecutes individual people, not states. It is responsible for **genocide**, **crimes against humanity**, **war crimes** and the crime of aggression. Under the principle of **complementarity**, the states are responsible first. The Court only steps in if a state is unwilling or unable to investigate genuinely.

Switzerland deposited its instrument of ratification on **12 October 2001**. This made it the 43rd state party, even before the statute came into force. Switzerland has long worked for **international law** and international criminal justice. Some large countries such as the USA, China and Russia have still not joined the statute.

In its first verdict in **2012**, the Congolese militia leader **Thomas Lubanga** was convicted. He had recruited **child soldiers** and made them fight, and he was sentenced to 14 years in prison. In **2009** the Court issued an arrest warrant for the Sudanese president **Omar al-Bashir** for crimes in **Darfur**. In **2023** an arrest warrant followed for **Vladimir Putin** for the unlawful **deportation of Ukrainian children** to Russia.

gewusst: Omar al-Bashir was the first serving head of state against whom the Court issued an arrest warrant.
The Court has no police of its own and depends on countries to arrest wanted people.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Rescue Chain (Rettungskette Schweiz) is a team that searches for and rescues buried people after severe earthquakes abroad. It is made up of several partners who bring together their knowledge and equipment.
wichtigste: The Swiss Rescue Chain was set up in 1981.
Its partners include the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA), REDOG, Rega and the army's rescue troops.
It is certified by the UN according to the INSARAG guidelines.
Its first mission took place in Yemen in 1982.
In February 2023 it helped after the earthquake in Turkey.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Rescue Chain was founded in **1981**. It is called a chain because several partners work together like links. They include the federal government's **Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit (SHA)**, the association **REDOG** with its search dogs, **Rega** and the **rescue troops** of the Swiss Army. The rescue troops specialise in recovering people from collapsed buildings and bring heavy equipment with them.

The Rescue Chain is certified by the UN according to the guidelines of **INSARAG**, the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group. It sets worldwide **standards** for rescue teams. In an emergency, certified teams work according to common rules and can therefore coordinate well with teams from other countries. After an earthquake, the Rescue Chain can set off within a few hours.

Its first mission took place in **1982** after an earthquake in **Yemen**. In **1985** the Rescue Chain helped after the severe earthquake in **Mexico City**. In 1988, after the **Spitak** earthquake, it travelled to **Armenia**, then part of the Soviet Union. In November 2019 it searched for buried people in **Albania**. After the earthquakes of February 2023 in the border region of Turkey and Syria, it was deployed in **Hatay** province in **Turkey**.

gewusst: Turkey has been a mission country of the Swiss Rescue Chain several times.
The Rescue Chain includes not only people but also specially trained search dogs.

teile.einleitung: In 2014 Switzerland held the chairmanship of the OSCE. It was the second time after 1996. The year was strongly shaped by the crisis in and around Ukraine.
wichtigste: The Chairperson-in-Office was Federal Councillor Didier Burkhalter.
In 2014 Burkhalter was both President of the Confederation and head of the FDFA.
Switzerland planned its chairmanship together with Serbia, which followed in 2015.
In March 2014 the OSCE deployed a civilian monitoring mission in Ukraine.
In December 2014 the meeting of the Ministerial Council took place in Basel.
The basis of the OSCE is the Helsinki Final Act of 1975.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland had already held the chair in **1996** under Federal Councillor Flavio Cotti. In 2014 it took it over for the **second time**. The Chairperson-in-Office was **Didier Burkhalter**. That year he was at the same time **President of the Confederation** and head of the FDFA. Switzerland and **Serbia**, which followed in 2015, planned their years in the chair together.

The OSCE has its headquarters in **Vienna**, where the Permanent Council also meets. It works in three areas: security, economics and the environment, and the **human dimension**. The latter includes human rights and democracy. Its roots lie in the **Helsinki Final Act** of 1975. This was signed by 35 countries, including Switzerland.

In 2014 Russia **annexed** Crimea, which means it took possession of it in breach of international law. Fighting broke out in the east of Ukraine. The OSCE became an important **forum for dialogue**, because Russia and Ukraine are both members. In March 2014 it deployed a **Special Monitoring Mission**. The unarmed civilian monitors reported on the situation in the country.

At the end of its year in the chair, Switzerland invited the members to the **Ministerial Council**. In December 2014 the foreign ministers of the OSCE countries met in **Basel**. There they discussed the situation in Europe. Afterwards Switzerland handed over the chair to Serbia. The Swiss chairmanship attracted international attention because of its mediation in the Ukraine crisis.

gewusst: In 2014 Didier Burkhalter held three roles at once: President of the Confederation, foreign minister and OSCE Chairperson-in-Office.
Switzerland and Serbia presented a joint work plan for their two years in the chair.

teile.einleitung: The Kyoto Protocol is an international treaty to protect the climate. It was agreed in 1997 in the Japanese city of Kyoto. For the first time, countries made a binding commitment to emit fewer greenhouse gases.
wichtigste: The aim of the Kyoto Protocol was to commit countries to reducing greenhouse gases.
The treaty was agreed in December 1997 at the climate conference in Kyoto.
It only came into force in February 2005.
From 2008 to 2012, industrialised countries were to cut their emissions by about 5 per cent on average compared with 1990.
The USA signed the treaty but never put it into force.
Switzerland committed itself to cutting its emissions by 8 per cent.
Its successor is the Paris Agreement of 2015.

abschnitte.text: The Kyoto Protocol is an additional treaty to the United Nations **Framework Convention on Climate Change** of 1992. That convention stated that global warming must be slowed down, but it contained no fixed figures. The Kyoto Protocol now set an exact **reduction commitment** for each industrialised country. This made climate protection a legal obligation for the first time.

abschnitte.titel: How it came about in Kyoto
abschnitte.text: In December 1997, experts and government representatives from more than 150 countries met in **Kyoto** in Japan. After long negotiations they agreed on the treaty on 11 December 1997. For it to take effect, enough countries had to ratify it, meaning have it confirmed by their own parliament. Only when Russia agreed in 2004 were enough countries on board, and the treaty came into force on **16 February 2005**.

The treaty covered six **greenhouse gases**, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. In the period from 2008 to 2012, industrialised countries were to cut their emissions by 5.2 per cent on average below the 1990 level. The European Union and Switzerland each promised minus 8 per cent. Developing countries such as China and India had no fixed targets, because at that time they emitted much less and were still meant to develop economically.

The protocol allowed so-called **flexible mechanisms**. A country that emitted less than allowed could sell its remaining rights to another country. This is called **emissions trading**. A country could also pay for climate projects in a poorer country, for example a solar power plant, and have the savings counted towards its own target.

Switzerland ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2003. To reach its target it relied on the **CO2 Act**, which has applied since 2000. Since 2008 there has been a CO2 levy on heating oil and natural gas, part of which is paid back to the population. Switzerland reached its target for 2008 to 2012, partly because it was allowed to count forests as CO2 stores and certificates from abroad.

Critics complained that big polluters such as the USA did not take part and that Canada pulled out again in 2011. In addition, worldwide emissions kept rising, mainly because China and other emerging economies grew strongly. In 2012 a second commitment period up to 2020 was agreed in Doha, but only a few countries took part. In 2015 came the **Paris Agreement**, in which almost all countries of the world set their own climate targets for the first time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that traps heat like the glass of a greenhouse, for example carbon dioxide.
A country officially confirms a treaty, usually through its parliament, and so makes it valid for itself.
A system in which rights to emit greenhouse gases can be bought and sold.
A yearly meeting of countries at which the protection of the climate is negotiated.

gewusst: More than seven years passed between the signing in Kyoto and the treaty coming into force.
Methane, one of the gases in the Kyoto Protocol, is also produced in the stomachs of cows.
The Kyoto climate conference was the third so-called Conference of the Parties, COP 3 for short.

teile.einleitung: A world order describes how power is distributed between the countries of the world. In a multipolar world order there are several great powers of roughly equal strength. Many experts believe the world is moving in this direction today.
wichtigste: Polarity describes the distribution of power in the international system.
Bipolar means two superpowers, like the USA and the Soviet Union in the Cold War.
Unipolar means a single superpower, like the USA after 1990.
Multipolar means several great powers share influence.
The Concert of Europe after 1815 is regarded as an example of a multipolar balance.
Experts argue about which order is the most stable.

abschnitte.text: In **political science**, people speak of poles when they mean centres of power. A pole is a country so strong that it helps shape world politics. If there are two such countries, the world is **bipolar**. If there is only one, it is **unipolar**. If there are several, it is **multipolar**.

After the **Congress of Vienna** in 1815, the great powers of Europe consulted one another in times of crisis. They included Great Britain, Russia, Austria, Prussia and later France. This system is called the **Concert of Europe** (the concert of the powers). No power was to dominate all the others. This contributed to a relatively long period of peace in Europe.

abschnitte.titel: The Cold War and the unipolar moment
abschnitte.text: In the **Cold War**, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other with their alliances. Most other countries aligned themselves with one of the two blocs. After the Eastern bloc collapsed, the USA was left as the only superpower. In 1990 the writer **Charles Krauthammer** called this the “unipolar moment”. He expected that this situation would not last for ever.

The political scientist **Kenneth Waltz** belonged to the school of neorealism. He argued that bipolar systems are more stable than multipolar ones. With only two great powers, he said, miscalculations are rarer. In a multipolar world, alliances are harder to keep track of. Other experts disagree and consider several centres of power to be more balanced.

Today, besides the USA, countries such as China are also gaining influence. New forums such as the **G20** show that more countries have a say. During the financial crisis of 2008, heads of state and government met there for the first time. In 1996 Samuel P. Huntington wrote about a “clash of civilisations” after the Cold War. His thesis was widely discussed and also criticised.

gewusst: The G20 had existed since 1999, but at first only as a meeting of finance ministers.
The word “pole” actually comes from physics and geography, as in the North Pole and the South Pole.

teile.einleitung: In July 1995, more than 8000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in the area around Srebrenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina. International courts have classified the crime as genocide. It is regarded as the worst war crime in Europe since the Second World War.
wichtigste: The massacre happened in July 1995, during the Bosnian War.
More than 8000 Bosniak men and boys were murdered.
Dutch UN soldiers were supposed to protect the safe area but could not prevent the attack.
In 2007 the International Court of Justice found that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide.
Ratko Mladić was sentenced to life imprisonment, partly because of Srebrenica.
The memorial and the cemetery of the victims are in Potočari.
Since 2024, 11 July has been an international UN day of remembrance.

abschnitte.text: After **Yugoslavia** broke apart, the **Bosnian War** took place from 1992 to 1995. In it, mainly Bosnian Serbs, Bosniaks and Croats fought each other. **Bosniaks** is the name for Bosnian Muslims. In 1993 the UN declared the town of **Srebrenica** in the east of the country a **safe area**. Many Bosniaks sought refuge there.

On 11 July 1995 **Bosnian Serb troops** took the enclave of Srebrenica. In the following days more than **8000 men and boys** were killed. The victims were buried in **mass graves**. Many could only be identified years later through **DNA analysis**. A lightly armed **Dutch battalion of UN peacekeepers** was stationed in the enclave. It could not prevent the attack.

The **Yugoslavia Tribunal** in The Hague prosecuted those responsible. The first to be found guilty of genocide, in 2001, was General **Radislav Krstić**. The army chief of the Bosnian Serbs, **Ratko Mladić**, was in hiding for years. He was arrested in 2011 and sentenced to **life imprisonment**, which was confirmed in 2021. In 2007 the **International Court of Justice** found that genocide had taken place in Srebrenica. Serbia was not found guilty of committing it, but it had breached its duty to prevent it.

In **Potočari** near Srebrenica are the central **memorial** and the cemetery of the victims. The UN troops' base used to be there. Every year on 11 July, newly identified victims are buried there. In 2024 the **UN General Assembly** declared 11 July an international day of remembrance. Serbia and Republika Srpska rejected the resolution.

gewusst: The Swiss lawyer Carla Del Ponte was chief prosecutor of the Yugoslavia Tribunal from 1999 to 2007.
Dutch courts later found the Dutch state partly responsible for the deaths of some of the victims.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland helps poorer countries so that fewer people there have to live in poverty. This is called development cooperation. Two federal bodies are mainly responsible: the SDC and SECO.
wichtigste: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) is part of the foreign ministry, the FDFA.
SECO is responsible for economic development cooperation.
Switzerland concentrates on four priority regions.
For 2025 to 2028 Parliament approved about 11 billion francs.
Of this, 1.5 billion francs are earmarked for Ukraine.
The UN recommends that rich countries spend 0.7 per cent of their gross national income.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation**, **SDC** for short, is part of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA). It runs many programmes in partner countries as well as humanitarian aid. The **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO)** belongs to the economics ministry. In partner countries it promotes, for example, **trade**, **jobs** and good **infrastructure**.

Since the 2021 to 2024 strategy, Switzerland has concentrated on four regions: **sub-Saharan Africa**, **North Africa and the Middle East**, **Asia** and **Eastern Europe**. The 2025 to 2028 strategy keeps them. The SDC withdrew its bilateral cooperation from **Latin America** by the end of 2024. SECO is still active in countries such as Colombia and Peru.

Switzerland has worked with **Nepal** in the Himalayas since the 1950s. It is one of the oldest partner countries of Swiss development cooperation. Swiss experts helped there, for example, to build suspension bridges in the mountains. Such bridges make it easier for many people to get to school, to market or to hospital.

For **International Cooperation 2025 to 2028**, Parliament approved framework credits totalling about **11 billion francs**. Of this, **1.5 billion francs** are reserved for **Ukraine**. The annual budget is decided separately each year. For decades the UN has recommended that rich countries spend **0.7 per cent** of their gross national income. According to the OECD, Switzerland was at about 0.56 per cent in 2022, partly because the costs of refugees may be counted.

Besides long-term cooperation, Switzerland provides **humanitarian aid** in disasters and wars. For this there is the **Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit**, SHA for short. It is part of the SDC. Its experts help, for example, with water supply, construction or medicine. Many Swiss aid organisations also work in poor countries.

gewusst: Switzerland has been working with Nepal for more than 70 years.
Only a few rich countries reach the UN target of 0.7 per cent.

teile.einleitung: A red carpet is rolled out for special guests. You see it at state visits, at film festivals and at award ceremonies such as the Oscars.
wichtigste: A red carpet shows that a guest is being specially honoured.
When a state guest arrives by plane, the carpet lies at the aircraft steps.
There is a famous red carpet at the Oscars in Los Angeles.
In Cannes the red carpet leads up a flight of steps.
The Zurich Film Festival has a green carpet.
The oldest known story with a red carpet comes from Greece.

abschnitte.text: Whoever is allowed to walk on a **red carpet** is a **guest of honour**. The carpet shows everyone that this person is especially important. In the past, red dyes were expensive and precious. That is why red was long regarded as the colour of kings and powerful people.

The oldest known story with a red carpet comes from ancient **Greece**. In the play **“Agamemnon”** by the poet Aeschylus, a red carpet is laid out for a king returning home. At first the king hesitates, because he does not want to be honoured like a god. The play is about 2500 years old.

When a **state guest** arrives by plane, the red carpet is laid right at the **aircraft steps**. The guest comes down and walks along the carpet to the hosts. Often a military band plays and a guard of honour stands ready. In Switzerland, too, the Federal Council welcomes state guests with such a ceremony.

Before the **Oscars ceremony** in **Los Angeles**, film stars walk along a long red carpet. At a **film premiere**, actors show themselves to the photographers there. At the **Cannes** Film Festival the carpet lies on the steps up to the festival palace, so the stars climb a **flight of steps**. The **Zurich Film Festival**, on the other hand, has a **green carpet**, because green is the festival's colour.

People also say **“to roll out the red carpet for someone”**. It means to **give someone a particularly warm welcome** and honour them greatly. There does not even have to be a carpet. People say it, for example, when a city goes to great lengths to attract a new company.

gewusst: At the Zurich Film Festival the stars walk not on a red but on a green carpet.
A red carpet already appeared in a Greek play about 2500 years ago.

teile.einleitung: Most-favoured-nation treatment is a basic principle of world trade. It says that a trade advantage a country grants to one partner must be granted to all partners. This way all members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) are meant to be treated equally.
wichtigste: If a WTO member lowers the customs duty for one country, this applies immediately to all members.
Most-favoured-nation treatment is set out in Article I of the GATT.
It applies unconditionally, meaning without anything in return.
Together with national treatment it forms the principle of non-discrimination.
Free trade areas and customs unions are a permitted exception.
Developing countries may receive lower customs duties.
Switzerland has been a full member of the GATT since 1966.

abschnitte.text: The term **most-favoured nation** sounds like a special privilege, but it actually means equal treatment. If a WTO member grants a country a lower **customs duty**, it must grant this advantage to all other members too. This must happen **immediately** and **unconditionally**. So the other members do not have to give anything in return. This prevents a country from treating its trading partners differently.

The **GATT** is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1947. Most-favoured-nation treatment appears right in **Article I**, which shows how important it is. **Article III** deals with **national treatment**: once imported goods have crossed the border, they must not be treated worse than domestic goods. Together, both rules form the **principle of non-discrimination**. Since 1995 the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, based in **Geneva**, has watched over these rules.

There are important exceptions. Under **Article XXIV** of the GATT, countries in **free trade areas** and **customs unions** may grant each other advantages without giving them to everyone. The condition is that essentially all trade between them becomes free. The **Enabling Clause** of 1979 allows rich countries to grant **developing countries** lower customs duties on a one-sided basis. Switzerland does this too with its **system of preferences**.

Switzerland joined the GATT provisionally in 1958 and definitively in **1966**. Since 1995 it has been a founding member of the **WTO**. As an exporting country, it benefits greatly from its goods being treated the same everywhere. In the USA, since 1998, most-favoured-nation treatment has mostly been called **“Normal Trade Relations”** in legal language. Congress chose this name because “most-favoured nation” wrongly sounded like a special privilege.

gewusst: Most-favoured-nation treatment is so important that it comes right at the start of the GATT, in Article I.
The World Trade Organization is based in Geneva, right on Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: 2022 was the first year of Russia's full-scale attack on Ukraine. During these months many events took place that shaped the further course of the war and politics in Europe.
wichtigste: On 28 February 2022 the Federal Council adopted the EU sanctions against Russia.
In March 2022 Russian troops occupied the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant.
In April 2022 the Russian flagship Moskva sank.
In June 2022 Ukraine became a candidate for EU membership.
In July 2022 the Ukraine Recovery Conference took place in Lugano.
In November 2022 Ukraine recaptured the city of Kherson.

abschnitte.text: In **March 2022** Russian troops occupied the **Zaporizhzhia** nuclear power plant, the largest in Europe. It has been under Russian control ever since, and the **International Atomic Energy Agency** has observers on site. In **April 2022** the missile cruiser **Moskva**, the flagship of the Russian **Black Sea Fleet**, sank. According to Ukraine, it was hit by anti-ship missiles.

In **June 2022** the European Council granted Ukraine and Moldova the status of **candidate countries** for the EU. At the end of 2023 the EU decided to open accession negotiations. In **July 2022** the **UN and Turkey** brokered a **grain deal** in Istanbul. It allowed grain exports across the Black Sea until Russia pulled out in July 2023.

On **28 February 2022**, four days after the war began, the **Federal Council** adopted the EU's sanctions. It considers this compatible with neutrality, because Switzerland does not support any party to the war militarily. In July 2022 the **Ukraine Recovery Conference** took place in **Lugano**, hosted jointly by Switzerland and Ukraine. The participants adopted principles for a transparent **reconstruction**.

At the end of September 2022, after **sham referendums**, Russia declared the regions of **Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson** annexed. This annexation **breaks international law**, and the UN General Assembly condemned it by a large majority. In **November 2022**, after a Ukrainian counter-offensive, Russian troops withdrew across the **Dnipro** river. Ukraine thus recaptured **Kherson**, the only regional capital Russia had taken in 2022.

gewusst: The Moskva was one of the biggest losses of a warship since the Second World War.
The conference in Lugano was the first to bear the name Ukraine Recovery Conference; it was later continued in other cities.

teile.einleitung: The Palais des Nations is a huge building in Geneva where many international conferences take place. It was built for the League of Nations and is now the European headquarters of the United Nations. Here diplomats from all over the world negotiate on peace, human rights and much more.
wichtigste: The Palais des Nations stands in Geneva in Ariana Park.
It was built between 1929 and 1936 for the League of Nations.
Since 1946 it has housed the United Nations Office at Geneva.
After New York, Geneva is the UN's second most important location.
Thousands of meetings and conferences take place here every year.
In front of the building stands the giant wooden sculpture “Broken Chair”.
Visitors can see the Palais on a guided tour.

abschnitte.text: The Palais des Nations lies near the shore of Lake Geneva in Ariana Park. The large park used to belong to a Geneva family, who gave it to the city. **Peacocks** roam freely in the park. In front of the entrance is the Place des Nations with the flags of the member states.

After the First World War, the **League of Nations** was founded in 1920 to keep the peace, and Geneva became its seat. The Palais des Nations was built for it from 1929 and was moved into in 1936. The League of Nations could not prevent the Second World War and was dissolved in 1946. After that the **United Nations** took over the building.

The Palais is about 600 metres long and is one of the largest building complexes in Europe. It has dozens of conference rooms, many offices and a large library. The biggest room is the **Assembly Hall**, where large meetings are held. The Human Rights Room is also famous; the Spanish artist Miquel Barceló decorated its ceiling with colourful stalactites.

The UN **Human Rights Council**, for example, meets in the Palais. There are conferences on disarmament, health, trade and refugees. Peace talks between parties to a conflict often take place here too. Many other organisations are based nearby, such as the World Health Organization and the Red Cross.

On the Place des Nations stands a twelve-metre-high wooden sculpture of a chair with a broken leg. The artist Daniel Berset created it in 1997. The **Broken Chair** is a reminder of the victims of landmines and cluster bombs. Today it is a well-known landmark of Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The forerunner of the UN, which existed from 1920 to 1946 and was based in Geneva.
A person who represents a country towards other countries or organisations.
A large meeting at which a topic is discussed.
An explosive charge hidden in the ground that still injures people even after wars.

gewusst: Interpreters work in the Palais des Nations, translating speeches simultaneously into the six official languages of the UN.
Switzerland provided the land for the Palais, even though it only became a UN member itself in 2002.

teile.einleitung: The Nordic cross is a cross on a flag that is shifted towards the flagpole. It is found on the flags of the countries of Northern Europe. The oldest of these flags is the Danish one.
wichtigste: In the Nordic cross, the crossing point is closer to the flagpole.
Five independent countries have a Nordic cross on their flag.
They are Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland.
The Danish flag was the model for the others.
The Faroe Islands also have a flag with a Nordic cross.
All these countries are in Northern Europe.

abschnitte.text: In the **Nordic cross**, the two bars do not cross in the middle of the flag. The crossing point is shifted towards the **flagpole**. The horizontal bar runs across the whole width of the flag. The Swiss cross is different: it stands in the middle and does not touch the edge. The name comes from the fact that all these countries are in the north of Europe.

The flag of **Denmark** shows a white cross on a red background. It is the oldest flag with a Nordic cross. The other Nordic countries took it as their **model**. The Danes call their flag the Dannebrog. It is one of the oldest national flags in the world.

**Sweden** has a yellow cross on a blue background. **Finland** shows a blue cross on white. **Norway** has a red flag with a blue cross edged in white. **Iceland** has exactly the reverse: a blue flag with a red cross edged in white. Together with Denmark, these are five independent countries.

The **Faroe Islands** are islands in the North Atlantic and belong to Denmark. Even so, they have their own flag. It is white with a red cross edged in blue. Some other islands and regions in the north also use a Nordic cross. This shows at first glance that they belong to the Nordic world.

gewusst: The flags of Norway and Iceland have the same colours, just swapped round.
The Danish flag is regarded as one of the oldest national flags still in use.

teile.einleitung: In the Council of the European Union, the presidency passes from one member state to the next every six months. This is called the rotating Council presidency.
wichtigste: A Council presidency lasts six months and changes on 1 January and 1 July.
Since 2007 three presidency countries at a time have worked together as a “trio”.
The presidency country chairs meetings and brokers compromises.
The Foreign Affairs Council is chaired by the High Representative, not by the presidency country.
The European Council has its own permanent president.
In 2026 Cyprus and then Ireland held the presidency.

abschnitte.text: In the **Council of the EU**, the ministers of the member states meet. One country at a time takes over the presidency for **six months**. The handover takes place on **1 January** and **1 July**. This way every member country, large or small, gets its turn at some point. Switzerland is not an EU member and therefore never holds the presidency.

The presidency country **plans and chairs** the meetings of the Council and its working groups. It is meant to act as an **“honest broker”** between the countries and find **compromises**. It negotiates **on behalf of the Council** with the **European Parliament** and the Commission, for example in the so-called **trilogues**. These are three-way talks about new laws.

Since **2007**, **three consecutive** presidency countries have worked closely together. This **trio** sets a joint programme for **18 months**. This way the work is planned better beyond the short half-years. For example, Belgium in the first half of 2024 was followed by **Hungary** in the second half, then Poland and Denmark in 2025. In the first half of 2026 **Cyprus** held the presidency, and in the second half **Ireland**.

Not everything is chaired by the presidency country. Since the **Treaty of Lisbon**, the Union's **High Representative** for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy has chaired the **Foreign Affairs Council**. The **European Council** of heads of state and government has its own **permanent president**. He or she is elected for **two and a half years** and can be re-elected once.

gewusst: The Council of the EU and the European Council are two different institutions, even though their names sound similar.
After Ireland, Lithuania and Greece follow as presidency countries in 2027.

t198cqny.t: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea governs who owns which part of the sea and who may use it. It is also called the “constitution of the oceans”. It applies to coastal states and also to countries without a coast, such as Switzerland.
wichtigste: The convention was signed in Montego Bay in Jamaica in 1982.
It only came into force in 1994.
The exclusive economic zone extends at most 200 nautical miles.
The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is based in Hamburg.
The mineral resources of the deep seabed are regarded as the common heritage of mankind.
Landlocked countries such as Switzerland have a right of access to the sea.

abschnitte.text: After almost ten years of negotiations, the convention was signed on 10 December **1982**. The signing took place in **Montego Bay** in **Jamaica**. That is why it is sometimes called the Montego Bay Convention. It only came into force in **1994**, after enough countries had ratified it. To ratify means that a country officially confirms the treaty and must then keep to it.

The convention divides the sea into **zones**. Directly off the coast lies the **territorial sea**, which extends up to 12 nautical miles. Further out lies the **exclusive economic zone**, which extends at most **200 nautical miles**. There only the coastal state may fish and extract raw materials such as oil. Foreign ships, however, may sail through it freely. Beyond that begin the **high seas**, which are open to all countries.

On the deep seabed of the high seas there are mineral resources, for example nodules containing metals. This seabed does not belong to any single country. The convention describes the resources there as the **common heritage of mankind**. An **international authority** is to regulate their use for the benefit of all people. The United States has never ratified the convention, mainly because of these rules (as of 2026), but it follows many of the rules as customary law.

The Convention on the Law of the Sea created the **International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea**. It is based in **Hamburg**. The court decides disputes about the law of the sea, for example about borders at sea or detained ships. The judges come from many different countries.

Switzerland has no coast. Even so, the convention is important for it. Countries without a coast, so-called **landlocked countries**, have the right to reach the sea through neighbouring countries. Their ships may use the high seas just like ships from coastal states. There are even ocean-going ships under the **Swiss flag**. Their home port is **Basel**, because the North Sea can be reached via the Rhine.

gewusst: A nautical mile is 1852 metres long, so 200 nautical miles are about 370 kilometres.
Although Switzerland has no coast, Basel is a home port for ocean-going ships.

teile.einleitung: The Lok Sabha is the lower house of the Indian Parliament. It is elected directly by the people. Because India has so many voters, the election to the Lok Sabha is regarded as the largest democratic election in the world.
wichtigste: The name Lok Sabha means “House of the People”.
The second chamber is called the Rajya Sabha, “Council of States”.
543 members are elected by the people in constituencies.
Members are elected for five years, and you can vote from the age of 18.
You can stand for the Lok Sabha from the age of 25.
The 2024 election lasted about six weeks.
The Lok Sabha meets in New Delhi.

abschnitte.text: The Indian Parliament has two chambers, similar to the Swiss Parliament. The **Lok Sabha** is the **lower house**. “Lok” means people, “Sabha” means assembly or house. The second chamber is the **Rajya Sabha**, the **upper house**. It represents India's states, just as the Council of States in Switzerland represents the cantons.

India is divided into **543 constituencies**. In each constituency exactly one member of the Lok Sabha is elected. Whoever gets the most votes wins the seat. You can vote from the age of **18**. Anyone who wants to be elected must be at least **25 years** old. The Lok Sabha is elected for **five years**, unless it is dissolved earlier.

The last election took place in 2024. It lasted from 19 April to 1 June, about **six weeks**. Voting took place in **seven phases**, one after another in different parts of the country. The reason is the huge number of almost one billion voters. This way, election workers and security forces can be deployed step by step all over the country. Votes are usually cast on **electronic voting machines**.

The Lok Sabha passes **laws** together with the Rajya Sabha. It also decides on the **national budget**, in other words what the state spends money on. The **prime minister** needs the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha. If the government loses this majority, it can be brought down. The sittings are chaired by a **Speaker**, the president of the chamber.

The Indian Parliament is based in the capital, **New Delhi**. Since 2023 it has met in a **new parliament building**. The old, round building dates from the time when India was a British colony. India has been independent since 1947. The first Lok Sabha was elected at the beginning of the 1950s.

gewusst: Because of its huge number of voters, India is regarded as the largest democracy in the world.
For the election, polling stations are set up even in very remote places so that everyone can vote.

teile.einleitung: After Russia's full-scale attack on Ukraine in February 2022, many countries imposed sanctions on Russia. Sanctions are punitive measures used to put pressure on a country.
wichtigste: On 24 February 2022 Russia's full-scale attack on Ukraine began.
On 28 February 2022 Switzerland adopted the EU's sanctions.
In Switzerland, SECO implements the sanctions.
Many Russian banks were excluded from SWIFT.
At the end of 2022 the G7 set a price cap of 60 dollars per barrel of crude oil.
Adopting the sanctions sparked a debate about neutrality.

abschnitte.text: **Sanctions** are measures with which countries put pressure on another country without going to war. After the attack of **24 February 2022**, the EU, the USA and other countries adopted numerous sanctions against Russia. They concern trade, banks and individual people. The aim is to make it harder for Russia to finance the war.

Many Russian banks were excluded from **SWIFT**. Through this system, banks worldwide exchange messages for payments. At the end of 2022 the **G7** set a **price cap** of **60 dollars** per barrel for Russian crude oil transported by ship. The export of **dual-use goods** is also banned; these are goods that can be used for both civilian and military purposes, for example certain electronics. The accounts and yachts of many **oligarchs**, very rich and influential business people, were frozen.

On **28 February 2022** the **Federal Council** decided to adopt the **EU's sanctions**. Since then Switzerland has also adopted most of the further sanctions packages. The President of the Confederation at that time was **Ignazio Cassis**, head of the FDFA. The **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO)** is responsible for implementation. Companies and banks must report frozen assets to it, for example.

Switzerland is a **neutral state**. That is why adopting the sanctions was hotly debated. The Federal Council explains that the **law of neutrality** mainly concerns military matters, such as not taking part in wars. Economic measures, it says, are not covered by it, although they do affect **neutrality policy**. Critics, on the other hand, believe that Switzerland is giving up part of its neutrality.

gewusst: After the annexation of Crimea in 2014, Switzerland had not yet adopted the EU sanctions; it had only prevented them from being circumvented through Switzerland.
In 2025 the EU lowered its price cap on Russian oil further.

teile.einleitung: A qualified majority is a majority that has to meet stricter conditions than a simple majority. It is especially important in the Council of the European Union, where it is calculated using the double majority procedure.
wichtigste: A simple majority means more yes than no votes. A qualified majority requires more.
In the Council of the EU, at least 55% of the countries, representing 65% of the population, must agree.
With 27 member states, that is at least 15 countries.
A blocking minority needs at least four countries.
The double majority comes from the Treaty of Lisbon and has applied since 2014.
In foreign and security policy the Council usually decides unanimously.

abschnitte.text: With a **simple majority**, it is enough for more yes votes than no votes to be counted. A **qualified majority** sets stricter conditions, for example two thirds of the votes. Switzerland has similar rules: a **change to the constitution** needs a **majority of the people** and a **majority of the cantons**. Under the **expenditure brake**, a majority of all members of both chambers of Parliament must agree, not just of those present.

abschnitte.titel: The double majority in the Council of the EU
abschnitte.text: Since **2014** the **double majority** has applied in the **Council of the EU**. It was introduced with the **Treaty of Lisbon**. At least **55% of the member states** must agree, and they must represent at least **65% of the EU population**. With 27 countries, that is **at least 15**. If the Council is not deciding on a proposal from the Commission, a **reinforced** majority of 72% of the countries applies.

A **blocking minority** can prevent a decision. It must consist of at least **four countries**. This way a few large countries cannot block a decision on their own. The threshold for countries protects the **small members**, while the population threshold takes into account how many **people** stand behind a decision. With a qualified majority, an **abstention** counts in practice like a **no**, because only votes in favour are counted.

Not everything is decided by qualified majority. In the **Common Foreign and Security Policy**, **unanimity** usually applies, as it does for taxes and new members. With the **passerelle clause**, the European Council can decide unanimously that decisions in a certain area will in future be taken by qualified majority. No new treaty is then needed for this.

gewusst: With unanimity, an abstention does not prevent a decision, but with a qualified majority it acts like a no.
Passerelle is the French word for “bridge”.

teile.einleitung: Media such as newspapers, radio, television and social networks report on what is happening in politics. They influence what people think about and how they vote. At the same time they keep a check on those in power, which makes them very important for a democracy like Switzerland.
wichtigste: The media are often called the “Fourth Estate” because they keep a check on government, parliament and the courts.
According to agenda-setting theory, the media decide which topics the public thinks about.
With framing, the media place a topic in a particular frame of interpretation through selection and emphasis.
The spiral of silence theory says that people tend to keep quiet about their opinion if they think they are in the minority.
The term “filter bubble” was coined by Eli Pariser in 2011.
Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship.
The Swiss Press Council judges complaints about breaches of the journalists' code.

abschnitte.text: In a democracy, power is divided between three branches: parliament, government and the courts. The media are often called the **Fourth Estate** because they watch over and keep a check on these three. Journalists uncover abuses, waste or bribery, for example. Without free media, citizens could hardly know what the authorities are doing. In Switzerland in particular, with its many **popular votes**, people need good information to be able to decide.

In 1972 the researchers Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw showed with their **agenda-setting** theory that the media decide what we think about. What often appears on the front page is seen by many people as especially important. **Framing** is about how a topic is presented. Whether you speak of “tax relief” or “loss of revenue”, for example, stirs up very different feelings. So the same news can have a different effect depending on its frame.

abschnitte.titel: Spiral of silence and filter bubble
abschnitte.text: In 1974 the German researcher Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann described the **spiral of silence**. Anyone who believes their opinion is in the minority is more likely to keep quiet, and so the other opinion seems even stronger. On the internet there is also the **filter bubble**, a term Eli Pariser made famous in 2011 with his book of the same name. Algorithms of search engines and social networks mostly show us what fits our previous clicks. As a result, we see other opinions less often.

Article 17 of the **Federal Constitution** guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship. So the state may not dictate what newspapers or broadcasters report. The **SRG SSR** offers radio and television programmes in all four national languages and is mainly funded by a fee paid by households and businesses. In 2018 the No Billag initiative wanted to abolish these fees, but it was clearly rejected, with about 72 per cent voting no.

Journalists in Switzerland follow a **journalists' code** with duties and rights. This includes reporting truthfully, checking facts and respecting people's privacy. Anyone who thinks a report breaks these rules can complain to the **Swiss Press Council**. The Press Council judges the case and publishes its opinion, but it does not impose penalties.

Always check who is behind a news item and whether reliable sources report the same thing. False reports, also called **fake news**, often spread especially quickly on social networks. On important topics, read reports from different media to get to know several points of view. Also pay attention to whether a text is a news report or a comment giving a personal opinion.

begriffe.erklaerung: When the state forbids or controls what may be published.
The way a topic is presented so that people understand it in a particular way.
A set of calculation instructions that a computer program uses, for example, to choose which posts you see.
A body that checks whether the media are following the rules of good journalism.

gewusst: The Swiss Press Council was founded in 1977 and is supported by journalists' associations and publishers.
The SRG broadcasts programmes in German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The term “Fourth Estate” is unofficial, because the constitution only has three branches of power.

t1avp14i.t: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development

teile.einleitung: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development is known as UNCTAD for short. It works to make sure that poorer countries also benefit from world trade. It is based in Geneva.
wichtigste: The first UNCTAD conference took place in Geneva in 1964.
The first Secretary-General was the Argentinian Raúl Prebisch.
The Group of 77 developing countries was formed there in 1964.
In 1968 the Generalised System of Preferences was agreed.
UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report every year.
Together with the WTO it runs the International Trade Centre in Geneva.
Since 2021 Rebeca Grynspan has led UNCTAD as the first woman in the role (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: The first **UNCTAD conference** met in **Geneva** in **1964**. It led to a permanent body of the **UN General Assembly**. Many countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America had just become independent at that time. They wanted the rules of world trade to benefit them as well. UNCTAD is still based in Geneva today.

The first Secretary-General was the Argentinian **Raúl Prebisch**, from 1964 to 1969. Together with Hans Singer he put forward the **Prebisch-Singer thesis**. It says that in the long run the prices of **raw materials** fall compared with those of **manufactured goods**. Countries that mainly sell raw materials therefore fall behind. This is why UNCTAD called for industrialisation and trade advantages for developing countries.

At the first conference, **77 developing countries** signed a joint declaration. This is how the **Group of 77**, or G77 for short, came about. Today more than 130 countries belong to it, but the name has stayed. Together the countries carry more weight at the UN.

abschnitte.titel: Lower customs duties for poorer countries
abschnitte.text: At the conference in **New Delhi** in **1968**, the **Generalised System of Preferences** was agreed. Under it, industrialised countries grant developing countries **lower customs duties** on a one-sided basis. This makes it easier for them to sell their goods. **Switzerland** also uses such a system.

Every year UNCTAD publishes the **World Investment Report**. It shows how much money flows into other countries worldwide as **direct investment**. Together with the **WTO**, UNCTAD runs the **International Trade Centre** (ITC) in Geneva. It helps small and medium-sized firms in developing countries to export. Since **2021** UNCTAD has been led by **Rebeca Grynspan** from Costa Rica (as of 2025).

gewusst: Geneva is an important place for world trade, because UNCTAD, the WTO and the International Trade Centre are all based there.
The World Trade Report is published not by UNCTAD but by the WTO.

teile.einleitung: Many poor countries have such high debts that they have hardly any money left for schools or hospitals. With debt relief, the lenders give up all or part of the repayment.
wichtigste: With debt relief, creditors give up all or part of the repayment.
In 1996 the IMF and the World Bank launched the HIPC Initiative for heavily indebted poor countries.
At the G8 summit in Cologne in 1999 the initiative was extended.
The campaign “Erlassjahr 2000” (Jubilee 2000) drew on the Bible.
In the Paris Club, creditor countries negotiate debt rescheduling; Switzerland takes part too.
About 37 countries have completed the HIPC Initiative.

abschnitte.text: Countries often borrow money from other countries, from banks or from international organisations. Whoever lends money is called a **creditor**. If repayment becomes too hard, there may be **debt relief**: the creditors give up part of what they are owed. The country can then use the money saved for **schools** or **hospitals**, for example.

The **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** launched the **HIPC Initiative** in **1996**. HIPC stands for **Heavily Indebted Poor Countries**. In **1999**, at the **G8 summit in Cologne**, the industrialised countries decided to extend and speed up the relief. In return the countries had to carry out **reforms**. About **37 countries**, most of them in Africa, have reached the completion point, one of the last being **Somalia**.

A lot of pressure came from campaigns such as **“Erlassjahr 2000”**, known in English as Jubilee 2000, in which churches also took part. The name comes from the **Bible**: the Old Testament describes a **jubilee year** in which debts are cancelled. At the turn of the millennium, the campaign called for a fresh start for poor countries. Millions of people around the world signed in support.

In the **Paris Club**, creditor countries have negotiated payment relief with debtor countries since **1956**. It meets in France, and **Switzerland** is also a member. Debt relief is not without controversy: supporters see it as an opportunity for poor countries. Critics fear that some countries will then run up too much debt again.

gewusst: The Paris Club has no founding charter; it grew in 1956 out of a meeting about Argentina's debts.

teile.einleitung: The Copenhagen criteria set out the conditions a country must meet to join the EU. The European Council agreed them in Copenhagen in June 1993. They still apply today.
wichtigste: The criteria were laid down in Copenhagen in 1993.
Politically, democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the protection of minorities are required.
Economically, a functioning market economy is required.
A country that wants to join must adopt the acquis communautaire.
The EU itself must also be able to take in new members.
The accession procedure is set out in Article 49 of the EU Treaty.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the Cold War, many countries in **Central and Eastern Europe** wanted to join the EU. In **June 1993** the **European Council** decided in **Copenhagen** which conditions they had to meet. Since then these rules have been called the **Copenhagen criteria**. They apply to all countries that want to become members today.

A candidate country needs **stable institutions**. They must guarantee **democracy**, the **rule of law** and **human rights**. The **protection of minorities** is also named explicitly. These values also appear in **Article 2** of the EU Treaty, together with human dignity. Respecting them is a condition for applying.

The country needs a **functioning market economy**. Its companies must be able to cope with **competitive pressure** in the single market. In the single market there are no customs duties between members. So the economy must be strong enough to keep up with the competition.

A candidate country must adopt the **acquis communautaire**. This is the entire body of EU law: treaties, laws, court rulings and agreements. The **accession negotiations** are divided into **chapters**, for example on agriculture or the environment. In **1995** the European Council in **Madrid** also stressed that candidates need an administration able to apply EU law effectively.

abschnitte.titel: The EU must be ready too
abschnitte.text: The Copenhagen Council named one more condition for the EU itself. It must be able to **take in new members** without losing momentum. This **capacity to absorb** new members is often called the fourth criterion. The procedure is governed by **Article 49** of the EU Treaty. The Council must decide **unanimously**, and the European Parliament must give its consent.

gewusst: Under Article 49, only a European state can apply for membership.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU; it organises its relations through bilateral agreements.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Army protects the country and its population. It is a militia army: most soldiers have a normal job and do their service alongside it. The army also helps in disasters at home.
wichtigste: According to the Federal Constitution, the army defends the country and its population.
In disasters and major emergencies it supports the civilian authorities.
The army is organised on the militia principle.
Compulsory military service applies to Swiss men; women serve voluntarily.
Basic military training lasts 18 weeks for most recruits.
Civilian service has existed since 1996.

abschnitte.text: The army's tasks are set out in **Article 58** of the **Federal Constitution**. The army **defends** the country and its population and helps to preserve peace. It **supports** the civilian authorities when their own resources are not enough. This is the case, for example, with **floods**, **avalanches** or major events. The responsible ministry is the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS).

The Swiss Army is organised on the **militia principle**. This means that most of its members are citizens who do **military service** alongside their jobs. Only a small number work as professional soldiers. The Federal Constitution requires every **Swiss man** to do military service. **Women** can serve voluntarily.

Training begins with **basic military training** (Rekrutenschule, RS for short). For most recruits it lasts **18 weeks**, and longer for some roles. After that come refresher courses. Since **1996** there has been **civilian service**. Anyone who cannot reconcile military service with their conscience works instead, for example, in hospitals, care homes or nature conservation.

In normal times the Swiss Army has no **general**. A general is only appointed in times of great threat, for example in the event of war. He is elected by the **United Federal Assembly**, meaning the National Council and the Council of States together. The best-known general is Henri Guisan, who led the army in the Second World War.

In Switzerland the people can even vote on the army. In **1989** an initiative to **abolish the army** went to the polls. Voters **rejected it**, with about 64 per cent voting no. The high yes vote of about 36 per cent surprised many people at the time. Since then there have been further votes on the army, for example on fighter jets.

gewusst: In peacetime Switzerland has no general, only a Chief of the Armed Forces.
Many members of the army keep their personal equipment at home.

teile.einleitung: At the San Francisco Conference in 1945, the Charter of the United Nations was drawn up. Representatives of 50 countries negotiated for about two months. This founded the UN.
wichtigste: The conference began on 25 April 1945.
Representatives of 50 countries took part.
Poland was absent but still became a founding member.
The UN was prepared in 1944 at Dumbarton Oaks and in 1945 at Yalta.
President Roosevelt died shortly before the conference began.
The plenary sessions were held in the San Francisco opera house.
China was the first country to sign the Charter.

abschnitte.text: Even during the **Second World War**, the Allies were planning a new world organisation. In **1944** the USA, Great Britain, the Soviet Union and China drew up its basic structure at **Dumbarton Oaks** near Washington. In **February 1945** the “Big Three”, **Roosevelt**, **Churchill** and **Stalin**, met at **Yalta** in Crimea. There they decided to hold the founding conference in San Francisco in April.

US President **Franklin D. Roosevelt** had pushed hard for the founding of the UN. However, he died on **12 April 1945**, shortly before the conference began. His successor **Harry S. Truman** carried the project forward. The conference began as planned on **25 April 1945**. In the Pacific, the war was still going on at that time.

The official name of the meeting was the **“United Nations Conference on International Organization”**, or **UNCIO** for short. Representatives of **50 countries** negotiated for about two months. The large plenary sessions were held in the **War Memorial Opera House**, the city's opera house. Many other meetings took place in committees.

At the end, the **UN Charter** was signed. **China** was allowed to sign first. It had been the first country to be attacked by an Axis power, namely by Japan in **1937**. **Poland** had not been invited because of a dispute over its government. It signed in October 1945 and counts as one of the **51 founding members**.

**Switzerland** was not present in San Francisco. It stayed outside the UN for a long time, partly because of its **neutrality**. Even so, **Geneva** became an important UN location in Europe. Switzerland only joined the UN after a **popular vote in 2002**. Today almost every country in the world belongs to the UN.

gewusst: The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, which is why this day is United Nations Day.
In 2002 Switzerland became the 190th member of the UN.

teile.einleitung: Mediation means helping to settle a dispute. A neutral person helps the people in conflict to find a solution themselves. In world politics Switzerland is known for its mediation.
wichtigste: In mediation, a neutral third party helps the sides find a solution themselves.
All parties to the conflict must agree to the mediation.
As a neutral country, Switzerland offers its “good offices”.
In 2009 Armenia and Turkey signed protocols in Zurich that Switzerland had mediated.
On the Bürgenstock, talks were held about the Nuba Mountains in 2002 and about Cyprus in 2004.
Within the FDFA, the Peace and Human Rights Division is responsible for mediation.

abschnitte.text: In **mediation**, a neutral person, the **mediator**, supports the talks between two sides. The mediator does not decide who is right. The **parties to the conflict** must find and accept the solution themselves. What matters is that everyone involved agrees. Nobody can be forced into mediation. Many schools also have peer mediators who work in this way.

Switzerland is **neutral** and does not belong to any military alliance. That is why both sides of a conflict often trust it. It offers its **good offices**: it provides places for negotiations or mediates itself. Many international organisations are based in **Geneva**, and peace talks often take place there. In the **FDFA**, the foreign ministry, the **Peace and Human Rights Division** is responsible for promoting peace.

The **Bürgenstock**, high above Lake Lucerne, has several times been the setting for important talks. In January 2002 Switzerland and the USA made talks about the **Nuba Mountains** in Sudan possible there. A **ceasefire** was agreed. In March 2004 the reunification of the island of **Cyprus** was negotiated on the Bürgenstock. The UN plan later failed in a referendum on the island.

On 10 October 2009 **Armenia** and **Turkey** signed protocols in **Zurich** to improve their relations. Switzerland had accompanied the talks. In 2011 it mediated between **Russia** and **Georgia**, so that Russia was able to join the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2012. In **Mozambique**, the Swiss diplomat **Mirko Manzoni** helped with the talks between the government and the opposition. A peace agreement was signed there in 2019.

gewusst: Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran as a so-called protecting power.
The word mediation comes from the Latin word for “middle”: the mediator stands in the middle between the parties.

teile.einleitung: A non-governmental organisation, NGO for short, is an organisation that works independently of governments. It works, for example, for the environment, for human rights or for people in need. Well-known NGOs are Greenpeace, Amnesty International and Doctors Without Borders.
wichtigste: NGO is the abbreviation for “Non-Governmental Organization”.
An NGO works independently of governments and does not aim to make a profit.
NGOs are usually funded by donations and membership fees.
Many NGOs help in disasters, protect the environment or work for human rights.
The term comes from the Charter of the United Nations of 1945.
Many large NGOs are based in Switzerland, for example the WWF in Gland.
NGOs can be granted consultative status at the UN.

abschnitte.text: An NGO is a group of people working together towards a goal. It does not belong to the state and is not controlled by a government. Unlike a company, it does not want to make a profit; it is **non-profit**. In Switzerland, NGOs are often organised as an **association** or a foundation.

**Greenpeace** was founded in Canada in 1971 and campaigns for environmental protection. Since 1961 Amnesty International has worked for people who are persecuted because of their opinions. Doctors Without Borders sends doctors to war and disaster zones. The WWF protects animals and habitats and has its international headquarters in Gland in the canton of Vaud.

Most NGOs live on **donations**, membership fees and sometimes also government funding for particular projects. Many people help as volunteers. NGOs gather information, draw attention to problems and organise help on the ground. Some also run campaigns to influence politics and companies.

The term NGO appears for the first time in the Charter of the United Nations of 1945. Today thousands of NGOs have **consultative status** with the UN Economic and Social Council. This allows them to take part in meetings and contribute their views. In Geneva in particular, many NGOs work closely with international organisations.

There are hundreds of aid organisations in Switzerland, for example Caritas, Helvetas, Swissaid or Pro Juventute. The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva is a special organisation with its own mandate under international law. Anyone donating to a Swiss aid organisation can look out for the **Zewo** quality seal. It shows that the money is handled carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that does not belong to the state and works for a shared goal.
Doing something that benefits the public without making a profit.
Money or things that you give away voluntarily in order to help.
People who help without being paid.

gewusst: There are millions of NGOs worldwide, from small village clubs to huge international organisations.
Several NGOs have received the Nobel Peace Prize, for example Amnesty International in 1977 and Doctors Without Borders in 1999.

teile.einleitung: Shuttle diplomacy is a way of mediating between parties in a dispute who do not talk to each other directly. A mediator travels back and forth between the parties, carrying proposals and replies.
wichtigste: In shuttle diplomacy, the parties to the conflict do not meet directly.
A mediator shuttles back and forth between the sides.
The term became known through US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger.
Kissinger mediated in the Middle East after the Yom Kippur War of 1973.
In 1974 his work led to disengagement agreements.
In proximity talks, the parties are in the same place but in separate rooms.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes parties to a conflict do not want to sit down at the same table. Often they do not **recognise** each other or do not want to be seen together. Then a **mediator** can help. He travels from one side to the other, carrying **proposals and replies**. In doing so he can also carefully explain or soften demands before they reach the other side.

The term **shuttle diplomacy** became known through US Secretary of State **Henry Kissinger**. After the **Yom Kippur War** of October 1973, Israeli, Egyptian and Syrian troops faced each other at close quarters. Kissinger repeatedly flew back and forth between **Cairo, Jerusalem and Damascus**, often several times a day. Only the **aeroplane** made such rapid journeys possible.

In 1974 **disengagement agreements** were reached: between Israel and Egypt in the **Sinai** and between Israel and Syria on the **Golan Heights**. The armies were separated by **buffer zones**. This reduced the danger of fighting flaring up again. However, it was not yet a final peace.

One form of shuttle diplomacy over short distances is **proximity talks**. The delegations are in the same place but sit in **different rooms**. The mediator moves back and forth between them. **Switzerland** also often offers its **good offices** and provides places such as Geneva for such talks.

gewusst: The English word “shuttle” describes a service that runs back and forth, such as a bus that constantly goes to and fro.
Kissinger flew thousands of kilometres during his mediation.

teile.einleitung: Martin Luther King was an American minister and the best-known leader of the civil rights movement. He fought without violence for Black people in the USA to have the same rights as white people. His speech “I Have a Dream” is world-famous.
wichtigste: Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta in 1929.
In 1963 he gave the speech “I Have a Dream” in front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington.
His model for non-violent resistance was Mahatma Gandhi.
In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned racial segregation in public places.
In 1965 he marched from Selma to Montgomery for the right to vote.
In 1968 he was murdered in Memphis.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther King was born on 15 January 1929 in **Atlanta** in the state of Georgia. His father was a minister, and Martin also became a **Baptist minister**. At that time there was **racial segregation** in the southern states of the USA. Black people were not allowed to use the same schools, restaurants or bus seats as white people. King wanted to end this injustice.

King's great role model was **Mahatma Gandhi**, who had led India to independence without violence. In 1959 King travelled to India to learn more about him. He relied on **non-violent** methods such as boycotts, marches and sit-ins. He became known in 1955 during the **Montgomery bus boycott**. It began after Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat to a white man.

On 28 August 1963, during the **March on Washington**, King gave his famous speech **“I Have a Dream”**. He stood in front of the **Lincoln Memorial**, the monument to Abraham Lincoln. The place was well chosen, because Lincoln stands for the end of slavery. In the speech King dreamed of a country in which all people are treated equally. In 1964, at the age of 35, he received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

The civil rights movement achieved important laws. The **Civil Rights Act** of 1964 banned discrimination in restaurants, hotels and at work. But many Black people were still prevented by tricks from registering as voters. So in 1965 King led the **march from Selma to Montgomery**. After that Congress passed the **Voting Rights Act**, which protected the right to vote.

On 4 April 1968 Martin Luther King was shot dead in **Memphis**. He was there to support striking refuse workers. His death caused great grief. Since 1986 **Martin Luther King Day** has been a public holiday in the USA. It falls on the third Monday in January, close to his birthday.

gewusst: Martin Luther King and his father were named after the German reformer Martin Luther.
When he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, he was the youngest winner up to that time.

teile.einleitung: The Ramsar Convention is an international treaty to protect wetlands such as bogs, marshes and floodplains. It is one of the oldest environmental agreements in the world and has its secretariat in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The convention was adopted on 2 February 1971 in Ramsar in Iran.
It came into force in 1975.
Originally it was mainly about protecting waterbirds and wading birds.
The secretariat is in Gland in the canton of Vaud.
Every year on 2 February is World Wetlands Day.
Switzerland has 11 Ramsar sites (as of 2025); the oldest is the Fanel.

abschnitte.text: **Wetlands** are places where the ground is wet or covered with water, for example **bogs, marshes, floodplains** and shallow lake shores. Especially many animals and plants live there. **Waterbirds** rest here on their long journeys. Wetlands also store water and can lessen floods. Many were drained in the past to create fields.

The convention was adopted on **2 February 1971** in the town of **Ramsar**. It lies on the **Caspian Sea** in the north of **Iran**. The treaty came into force in **1975**. Its full name is the **“Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat”**. Today the convention protects wetlands as whole habitats. Well over 150 countries take part.

Each state party reports sites that are **internationally important**. They are added to the **Ramsar List**, and the country commits itself to protecting them and using them wisely. There are several thousand such sites worldwide. The convention's **secretariat** is in **Gland** on **Lake Geneva** in the canton of Vaud. The **International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)** is also based there.

Switzerland has **11 Ramsar sites** (as of 2025). The oldest is the **Fanel** on **Lake Neuchâtel**. In **1976** it was the first Swiss site to be added, and it is an important resting place for **waterbirds**. The **Bolle di Magadino** in **Ticino**, where the River Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore, are also well known.

gewusst: World Wetlands Day on 2 February marks the day of signing and has been celebrated since 1997.
A list of particularly threatened Ramsar sites is called the “Montreux Record”, named after a conference in Montreux.

teile.einleitung: A national flag is the flag that stands for a whole country. Every country has its own flag with particular colours and symbols. You see them on public holidays, at sports events and on official buildings.
wichtigste: A national flag is a symbol of a country.
The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background.
The four arms of the Swiss cross are the same length.
On 1 August especially many flags are hung out in Switzerland.
A flag at half-mast shows mourning.
Switzerland has 26 cantons, and each has its own flag.

abschnitte.text: A **national flag** shows at a glance which country something belongs to. Every flag has its own colours and symbols, for example stripes, stars or crosses. The colours often have a meaning from history. Flags hang on government buildings, embassies and schools. Many people are proud of their country's flag.

The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. The **Swiss cross** has four arms of equal length. Each arm is a little longer than it is wide. The Swiss flag is **square**, meaning it is as high as it is wide. Only a few countries have a square flag.

**1 August** is the Swiss national day. On that day many people decorate their houses and balconies with Swiss flags. You also see many flags at sports events. When someone wins a medal at the Olympic Games, the flag of their country is raised. For gold, the national anthem is also played.

A flag is raised on a **flagpole** with a rope. Many town halls and schools have such a pole. When the flag hangs only halfway up, this is called **half-mast**.
