It is a way of showing mourning, for example when an important person has died. Ships carry flags too: the flag at the stern of a ship shows which country it comes from.

Switzerland is made up of **26 cantons**. Each canton has its own coat of arms and its own flag. The canton of Bern, for example, shows a bear, and Uri a bull's head. At celebrations the Swiss flag, the cantonal flag and the municipal flag often hang side by side. This shows that people belong to their municipality, their canton and the Confederation.

gewusst: Switzerland has ocean-going ships too, even though it has no sea. They sail under the Swiss flag.
Besides Switzerland, Vatican City also has a square flag.

teile.einleitung: The North Atlantic Alliance, better known as NATO, is a military defence alliance. The member countries promise to help one another if one of them is attacked. Unlike the EU, which is an economic and political union, NATO is about security and defence.
wichtigste: NATO was founded on 4 April 1949 in Washington.
NATO stands for “North Atlantic Treaty Organization”.
NATO is a military defence alliance, the EU an economic and political union.
The most important principle is Article 5: an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
NATO's headquarters is in Brussels in Belgium.
Since 2024 NATO has had 32 members; the most recent to join was Sweden.
Neutral Switzerland is not a member, but it takes part in the Partnership for Peace.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, many Western countries feared the power of the Soviet Union. So on 4 April 1949 twelve countries signed the **North Atlantic Treaty** in Washington. The founders included the USA, Canada, Great Britain, France and other European countries. As a counterpart, the Eastern bloc founded the Warsaw Pact in 1955.

The heart of NATO is **Article 5** of the treaty. It says that an armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all. Each country then decides for itself how it will help. Collective defence has so far been invoked only once, after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 in the USA.

After the end of the Cold War, many countries from Eastern Europe joined, for example Poland and Hungary in 1999. After Russia attacked Ukraine, Finland became a member in 2023 and Sweden in 2024. This means NATO has 32 member countries. The USA is by far the strongest member.

Many countries are in both the EU and NATO, but not all. The **EU** deals mainly with the economy, trade and common rules. **NATO**, on the other hand, is responsible for joint defence. The USA, Canada and Norway, for example, are in NATO but not in the EU.

Because of its **neutrality**, Switzerland cannot join NATO. But since 1996 it has taken part in the **Partnership for Peace**. In it, Switzerland cooperates, for example, in training, disaster relief and peacebuilding. Swiss soldiers are deployed in Kosovo, for example, where the KFOR peacekeeping force is led by NATO.

begriffe.erklaerung: Countries that promise to help one another if attacked.
The moment when the members must stand by a partner that has been attacked.
The period from about 1947 to 1991 in which East and West were hostile to each other without fighting a war directly.
The central place from which an organisation is run.

gewusst: NATO does not have a large army of its own; the soldiers come from the armies of the member countries.
Iceland is a NATO member, even though it has no army of its own.

t1hchu3g.t: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe

teile.einleitung: The OSCE is the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. In it, countries talk about security, human rights and cooperation. It is the largest regional security organisation in the world.
wichtigste: The OSCE has 57 participating states (as of 2025).
It grew out of the CSCE, the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
In 1975 the CSCE Final Act was signed in Helsinki.
It has been called the OSCE since 1995.
Its secretariat is in Vienna.
From North America, the USA and Canada belong to it.
Switzerland held the chair in 1996 and 2014.

abschnitte.titel: From the CSCE to the OSCE
abschnitte.text: During the Cold War, countries from East and West met at the **CSCE**, the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. In 1975 they signed the **Helsinki Final Act**. It contained important principles, such as the inviolability of borders and respect for human rights. In November 1990 the **Charter of Paris** followed. It declared that the era of confrontation and division in Europe had ended.

The **Budapest** summit in December 1994 decided on a change of name. Since 1 January **1995** the CSCE has been called the **OSCE**. In this way the conference became an organisation with permanent structures. The **secretariat** and the Permanent Council are based in **Vienna**. The representatives of the countries meet there regularly.

The OSCE has **57 participating states** (as of 2025). They stretch from North America across Europe to Central Asia. From North America, the **USA** and **Canada** belong to it, but not Mexico. Russia and Ukraine are also members. That is why the OSCE is a place where even countries in conflict can talk to each other.

The OSCE sends **election observers** to many countries, for example. They check whether elections are free and fair. It also helps in conflicts and works for human rights. Switzerland held the chair in **1996** and again in **2014**, at that time with President of the Confederation Didier Burkhalter. In this way Switzerland, as a neutral country, plays an important role as a mediator.

gewusst: The OSCE stretches across three continents, from North America to Central Asia.
Switzerland also signed the Helsinki Final Act in 1975.

teile.einleitung: The eastward enlargement of NATO means the admission of countries in Central and Eastern Europe into NATO after the end of the Cold War. Many of these countries used to belong to the Eastern bloc or even to the Soviet Union. The enlargement took place in several rounds.
wichtigste: In 1990, with German reunification, the territory of the GDR also became part of NATO.
In 1999 Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary joined.
In 2004 seven countries joined at once, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
In 2009 Albania and Croatia followed.
In 2017 Montenegro joined as the 29th member, and in 2020 North Macedonia as the 30th.
In 2008 NATO held out the prospect of future membership to Ukraine and Georgia.

abschnitte.text: On **3 October 1990** the two German states were reunited. This meant that the whole of united Germany belonged to NATO. So the territory of the former **GDR** (East Germany) also became part of the alliance. The GDR had previously been a member of the Warsaw Pact. The **Warsaw Pact** was the military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies.

On **12 March 1999**, **Poland**, the **Czech Republic** and **Hungary** became members of NATO. All three had previously been in the Warsaw Pact. This marked the start of the actual eastward enlargement. After the end of Soviet rule, these countries wanted to bind themselves firmly to the West. They later also joined the European Union.

In March 2004 seven countries joined at the same time. This was the **largest enlargement** in NATO's history. It included the three Baltic states, **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania**. They had once even been part of the Soviet Union. Other countries of Central and Eastern Europe also joined in this round.

In April 2009 **Albania** and **Croatia** became members together. On 5 June 2017 **Montenegro** followed as the 29th member. In 2020 **North Macedonia** joined as the 30th member. Before that, the country had to settle a long **dispute over its name** with Greece.

At the **Bucharest** summit in 2008, NATO declared that Ukraine and Georgia would become members. However, it did not set a timetable. Russia sees the eastward enlargement as a threat and criticises it sharply. The new members, on the other hand, stress that they wanted to decide freely about their alliances. This question is still much debated today.

gewusst: The three Baltic states were the first former parts of the Soviet Union to become NATO members.
New members can only be admitted if all existing members agree.

teile.einleitung: The Schuman Declaration is a famous speech of 9 May 1950. In it, the French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed that France's and Germany's coal and steel be managed jointly. This was the first step towards today's European Union.
wichtigste: Robert Schuman read out the declaration in Paris on 9 May 1950.
He spoke to the press in the Clock Room of the foreign ministry at the Quai d'Orsay.
The declaration called the coal and steel community the first stage of a European federation.
Schuman was a Christian Democrat.
He was French prime minister from 1947 to 1948.
In 1958 he received the Charlemagne Prize of the city of Aachen.

abschnitte.titel: A speech in the Clock Room
abschnitte.text: On 9 May 1950 Robert Schuman invited journalists to the French **foreign ministry** at the **Quai d'Orsay** in Paris. In the magnificent **Clock Room**, the Salon de l'Horloge in French, he read out his declaration. Only five years after the Second World War, he proposed that France and Germany should work together. Today 9 May is celebrated in the EU as **Europe Day**.

Schuman proposed placing the production of **coal** and **steel** under a joint authority. At that time these raw materials were needed for factories, but also for weapons. If they are managed jointly, a new war is hardly possible. The declaration called this community the **first stage** of a European **federation**. A federation is a union of states that manage many things together.

Robert Schuman was born in Luxembourg in 1886 and became a French politician. He was a **Christian Democrat**, a member of the party Mouvement républicain populaire (MRP). From November 1947 to July 1948 he was **prime minister** of France. After that he was foreign minister until early 1953. Like Konrad Adenauer and Alcide De Gasperi, he is counted among the founding fathers of Europe.

In 1958 Schuman received the **Charlemagne Prize** of the city of Aachen. This prize honours people who have made an outstanding contribution to uniting Europe. Schuman was a deeply religious Catholic. The Catholic Church is therefore considering his **beatification**. In 2021 Pope Francis granted him the title **Venerable Servant of God**. For beatification, a recognised miracle is still needed.

gewusst: In 1951 the proposal led to the European Coal and Steel Community, also known as the Montan Union.
Robert Schuman is often called the “father of Europe”.

teile.einleitung: In world politics, sanctions are punitive measures against a country, for example bans on trade. With them, other countries want to make a country change its behaviour, such as ending a war or respecting human rights. Sanctions are a tool somewhere between mere words and military force.
wichtigste: Sanctions are punitive measures against a country, a company or particular people.
Examples are trade bans, arms embargoes, entry bans and freezing assets.
The UN Security Council can decide on sanctions that are binding for all UN members.
The EU and individual countries such as the USA also impose their own sanctions.
Switzerland implements sanctions through the Embargo Act.
In 2022 Switzerland adopted the EU's sanctions against Russia.
Whether sanctions work is often disputed.

abschnitte.text: A **sanction** is a penalty or a means of pressure. In world politics, countries impose sanctions when another country breaks rules, for example by starting a war. The aim is to persuade that country to change its behaviour. Sanctions are peaceful means, without weapons.

With an **embargo**, trade in certain goods is banned, for example in weapons or oil. With financial sanctions, the money of people or companies in banks is **frozen**, so that they can no longer access it. Entry bans prevent certain politicians from travelling to other countries. Targeted sanctions are aimed only at those responsible and are meant to spare the ordinary population.

The **UN Security Council** can decide on sanctions that all UN members must respect. But this is difficult, because each of the five permanent members has a veto. That is why the EU, the USA and other countries also decide on their own sanctions. Well-known examples are sanctions against North Korea, Iran and Russia.

Switzerland implements UN sanctions; as a UN member it has been obliged to do so since 2002. The basis for this is the **Embargo Act**, and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) is responsible for implementation. After Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, Switzerland also adopted the EU's sanctions. This sparked a debate about how this fits with neutrality.

Whether sanctions achieve their aim is disputed. A well-known example is the sanctions against South Africa, which are said to have contributed to the end of **apartheid** around 1990. In other cases it is mainly ordinary people who suffer, while the government stays in power. Some countries also get round sanctions by trading through other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ban on delivering certain goods to a country or buying them from it.
Blocking money in bank accounts so that the owner can no longer use it.
The right to prevent a decision with a single vote.
The former policy in South Africa that separated people by the colour of their skin and discriminated against them.

gewusst: As early as ancient Greece, around 432 BC, Athens imposed a trade ban on the city of Megara.
Because of sanctions, large yachts belonging to rich business people were also held in harbours.

teile.einleitung: Liechtenstein is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria. It is closely linked to Switzerland: people pay in francs there and speak German. At the head of the country is a prince.
wichtigste: Liechtenstein borders only Switzerland and Austria.
The Rhine forms the border with the canton of St Gallen.
People pay in Swiss francs and speak German.
The country is only about 160 square kilometres in size and has 11 municipalities.
The capital is Vaduz, and the highest mountain is the Grauspitz at 2599 metres.
The parliament, the Landtag, has 25 members.

abschnitte.text: Liechtenstein lies in the **Rhine Valley**. In the west it borders Switzerland, in the east Austria. The **Rhine** forms the border with the canton of **St Gallen**. In the south it borders the canton of the **Grisons**. At about **160 square kilometres** it is one of the smallest countries in the world, even smaller than the canton of Zug. The highest mountain is the **Grauspitz** at 2599 metres.

Liechtenstein is a **monarchy**: its head of state is a **prince**. At the same time there is a parliament, the **Landtag**, with 25 members. Of these, 15 come from the **Oberland** (upper country) and 10 from the **Unterland** (lower country). As in Switzerland, the people can also vote on some questions. Above the capital **Vaduz** stands **Vaduz Castle**, the home of the princely family.

Liechtenstein has only **11 municipalities**. They include **Vaduz**, where the government and parliament have their seat, as well as **Schaan** and **Balzers**. The official language is **German**. In everyday life people speak an Alemannic dialect that sounds similar to the one in the St Gallen Rhine Valley.

Liechtenstein has no currency of its own. For more than 100 years people there have paid in **Swiss francs**. Since a **customs treaty** of 1923 there has also been no customs border between the two countries. The border with Switzerland is open, and you hardly notice when you cross it. Unlike Switzerland, Liechtenstein is a member of the **European Economic Area (EEA)**. It joined the UN as early as 1990.

The flag of Liechtenstein has two horizontal stripes: **blue** at the top and **red** at the bottom. In the top left there is a golden **crown**. It stands for the bond between the people and the princely house. The crown was added in 1937, because before that the flag looked exactly the same as that of Haiti.

gewusst: Liechtenstein is a doubly landlocked country: its neighbours Switzerland and Austria have no sea either.
At the 1936 Olympic Games it was noticed that Liechtenstein and Haiti had almost the same flag.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes two countries stop talking to each other and close their embassies. Then a third country can help: it becomes a protecting power and represents the interests of one country towards the other. Switzerland takes on this task especially often.
wichtigste: A protecting power is a country that represents another country in a third country.
It is needed when a country no longer has an embassy in the other.
The protecting power passes on messages between the countries, for example.
The task is called a protecting power mandate.
Both countries concerned must agree.
Switzerland is often chosen because it is neutral.

abschnitte.text: Normally a country has an **embassy** in another country. It helps its own citizens and keeps in contact with the government. If two countries break off their **diplomatic relations**, this link is missing. Then a **protecting power** takes over important tasks of the missing embassy. It passes on messages and letters, for example, so that the countries can still stay in contact.

A **mandate** is a task someone is given. With a **protecting power mandate**, a country is given the task of representing another. This needs the consent of **both** countries concerned: the country being represented and the country where the protecting power works. The protecting power's embassy often has its own sections just for this task.

Switzerland is **neutral** and does not take sides in conflicts. That is why both sides often trust it. In the **Second World War**, Switzerland held an especially large number of protecting power mandates. At that time it represented many countries that were at war with each other. This allowed them to exchange messages anyway, for example about prisoners of war.

From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland represented the **USA in Cuba**, until the two countries reopened embassies. Since 1980 it has represented the interests of the USA in Iran. After the war of 2008, Switzerland has represented **Russia and Georgia** in each other's country since 2009. Between **Saudi Arabia and Iran** it was also a protecting power for both sides after their break in 2016, until the two countries restored relations in 2023.

gewusst: Protecting power mandates are part of Switzerland's “good offices”, with which it mediates in conflicts.
Switzerland took on the mandate for the USA in Iran back in 1980 and has carried it on ever since.

teile.einleitung: The Millennium Development Goals were eight UN goals against poverty, hunger and disease. They were agreed in 2000 and were to be reached by 2015. After that they were replaced by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
wichtigste: There were eight Millennium Development Goals.
189 countries adopted the Millennium Declaration in September 2000.
The goals were to be reached by 2015, compared with 1990.
Goal 1 aimed to halve the proportion of people in extreme poverty.
Goal 2 called for primary education for all children.
Goal 8 was aimed mainly at the rich countries.
In 2015 they were replaced by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

abschnitte.text: In September 2000, heads of state and government met at the UN **Millennium Summit** in **New York**. On 9 September, 189 member states adopted the **Millennium Declaration**. The **eight Millennium Development Goals** were drawn from it. They were to be reached by **2015**. The year of comparison was usually **1990**.

**Goal 1** aimed to halve extreme poverty and hunger. **Goal 2** called for all girls and boys to be able to complete **primary school**. Goal 3 promoted equality between women and men. **Goal 4** called for cutting the death rate of children under five by **two thirds**. Goal 5 concerned the health of mothers. **Goal 6** was aimed at **HIV/AIDS**, malaria and other serious diseases. Goal 7 concerned protecting the environment, and **Goal 8** a global partnership.

abschnitte.titel: The task of the rich countries
abschnitte.text: Most of the goals concerned mainly the **developing countries**. **Goal 8**, however, was aimed at the **rich countries**. They were to give more development aid, create fairer trade rules and cancel the **debts** of poor countries. Switzerland also supported the goals, mainly through the **SDC**, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation.

According to the UN report of 2015, the number of people in extreme poverty fell from about **1.9 billion** to about **836 million**. A large part of the progress came from **China** and **India**. The number of deaths among children under five fell by about half. So the target of two thirds was not quite reached. In addition, much of the progress was unevenly spread.

In 2015 the **17 Sustainable Development Goals** replaced the Millennium Goals. They are part of the **2030 Agenda** and are to be reached by 2030. Unlike the Millennium Goals, they apply to all countries, including the rich ones. Besides poverty and education, they also deal with climate, energy and cities.

gewusst: The Millennium Goals got their name because they were agreed at the turn of the millennium in 2000.
Between 1990 and 2015 the number of people in extreme poverty fell by more than half.

teile.einleitung: A national anthem is a solemn song that stands for a country. It is played at celebrations, official occasions and sports events. The anthem of Switzerland is called the Swiss Psalm.
wichtigste: Every country has its own national anthem.
The Swiss anthem is called the Swiss Psalm.
In German it begins with “Trittst im Morgenrot daher” (“When you come in the red of morning”).
The text exists in all four national languages.
Before international matches, the anthems of both teams are played.
When the anthem is played, people usually stand up and keep quiet.

abschnitte.text: A **national anthem** is a song that solemnly represents a country. Like the flag, it is a **symbol** of the whole country. You hear it at state visits, on public holidays and at medal ceremonies. Some anthems are very old, others were chosen only recently. Their words often tell of homeland, freedom or nature.

The Swiss anthem is called the **Swiss Psalm**. A psalm is a solemn song, often with a prayer. In German the first line is “Trittst im Morgenrot daher”, which means “When you come in the red of morning”. It is followed by the words “Seh' ich dich im Strahlenmeer” (“I see you in a sea of rays”). The song was written in the 19th century.

Switzerland has four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. The Swiss Psalm exists in all four languages. This way every region can sing the anthem in its own language. On 1 August the Swiss Psalm is sung at many celebrations. But many people only know the first verse by heart.

Before an international **football match**, the anthems of both teams are played. The players stand in a line. Some sing along loudly, others listen quietly. At the Olympic Games, too, the anthem is played when someone wins gold. Out of **respect**, people stand up and keep quiet, even for another country's anthem.

gewusst: The Swiss Psalm is very solemn and sounds almost like a hymn sung in church.
When a gold medal is won at the Olympic Games, the anthem of the winner's country is played.

teile.einleitung: A crown is a precious ornament worn on the head. It shows that someone rules a country, for example a king or a queen. Crowns are usually made of gold and decorated with precious stones.
wichtigste: A king or queen wears the crown on their head.
Crowns are usually made of gold or silver.
Precious stones such as diamonds, rubies and sapphires sparkle on crowns.
A crown is usually a ring with points or arches.
The crown is a sign of power.
The British Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London.

abschnitte.text: A **crown** is an ornament that you put on your **head**. Usually it is a **band**, in other words a ring, with **points** or **arches**. That way it fits nicely on the head. Some crowns are closed at the top, others are open. There is often soft fabric inside so that it sits more comfortably.

Crowns are usually made of **gold** or **silver**. These metals shine beautifully and are valuable. On top of that come **precious stones** such as **diamonds**, **rubies** and **sapphires**. Pearls are often seen too. That is why crowns are among the most valuable objects in the world.

The crown is a **sign of power**. Whoever wears it is a **king**, **queen** or **emperor**. At a **coronation**, the crown is ceremonially placed on the head of a new ruler. In everyday life, however, kings hardly ever wear their crown. It is only used at special celebrations.

In **Great Britain** there are the famous **Crown Jewels**. They include crowns, sceptres and other treasures. They are kept under close guard in the **Tower of London**, an old castle on the **Thames**. Visitors can see them there. King **Charles III** was crowned with one of these crowns in May 2023.

**Switzerland** has no king and no crown. It is a **republic** in which the people have a say. Here you only see crowns in a **museum** or at carnival time. On **Epiphany** (Three Kings' Day) in January, though, there is the **Three Kings' cake**. Whoever finds the hidden little figure may wear a paper crown and is king for a day.

gewusst: In Denmark, Norway and Sweden the money is called the “krone” or “krona”, which means crown.
The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire dates from the Middle Ages and is now kept in Vienna.

teile.einleitung: The OSCE is the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. Switzerland plays an important role in it and has held the chair several times. Many Swiss diplomats have also worked for the OSCE.
wichtigste: In 1996 Federal Councillor Flavio Cotti held the OSCE chair.
In 1996 the OSCE organised the first post-war elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The chair is held by the foreign minister of the country holding the chairmanship.
The previous, current and future chairs form the Troika.
In 2014 Heidi Tagliavini represented the OSCE in the Contact Group on Ukraine.
Thomas Greminger was OSCE Secretary General from 2017 to 2020.
In 2026 Switzerland holds the chair again, with Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis.

abschnitte.text: The OSCE chair changes every year. It is held by the **foreign minister** of the country holding the chairmanship. In Switzerland this is the head of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, the **FDFA** for short. So that the work continues smoothly, there is the **Troika**. It consists of the previous, the current and the future chair.

In 1996 Federal Councillor **Flavio Cotti** held the OSCE chair. After the **Dayton Agreement** of 1995, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was over. The OSCE was given the task of preparing elections there. In September 1996 the first post-war elections took place. This was a big task for Switzerland as the chairing country.

In 2014 the **Trilateral Contact Group** on Ukraine was set up. It included representatives of Ukraine, Russia and the OSCE. The Swiss diplomat **Heidi Tagliavini** represented the OSCE chair there. In September 2014 the **Minsk Protocol** was signed. It provided for a ceasefire and monitoring by the OSCE and was supplemented by another agreement in 2015.

The Swiss diplomat **Thomas Greminger** was **Secretary General** of the OSCE from 2017 to 2020. He headed the secretariat in Vienna. Before that he had been Switzerland's ambassador to the OSCE. In 2026 Switzerland took over the chair again. The Chairperson-in-Office is Federal Councillor **Ignazio Cassis**.

gewusst: Switzerland held the OSCE chair in 1996 and 2014, and in 2026 for the third time.
The OSCE chairmanship always lasts only one year.

teile.einleitung: The New Silk Road is a large infrastructure programme of China. With it, China finances and builds roads, railways, ports and power stations in many countries. The project is huge and opinions on it differ.
wichtigste: Xi Jinping announced the initiative in 2013.
In English it is called the Belt and Road Initiative, BRI for short.
“Belt” stands for land routes, “Road” for sea routes.
Xi first presented the land route in Kazakhstan.
Italy joined in 2019 as the only G7 country and withdrew at the end of 2023.
Switzerland is a founding member of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

abschnitte.text: In the past there were trade routes between China and the West on which silk, among other goods, was traded. In 1877 the German geographer **Ferdinand von Richthofen** coined the term “Silk Road” for them. Traders travelled in caravans through the deserts and mountains of Asia. The Chinese initiative deliberately links back to this image. It is meant to show that China wants to be a centre of world trade again.

In **2013** **Xi Jinping** presented the initiative. He introduced the land route, the “Silk Road Economic Belt”, at a university in Astana in **Kazakhstan**. After that came a route across the sea. In English the project is called the **Belt and Road Initiative**. The “Belt” stands for the land routes, the “Road” for the sea routes.

One important project is the **China-Pakistan Economic Corridor**. It links the province of Xinjiang by roads, pipelines and power stations with the port of **Gwadar** on the Arabian Sea. This gives China a route to the Indian Ocean. In Sri Lanka, the port of **Hambantota** was leased to a Chinese company for 99 years in 2017. Sri Lanka could hardly repay the loans for the port.

Supporters say the project brings badly needed infrastructure to many poor countries. Critics speak of a **debt trap**: countries take on too many loans and become dependent as a result. Whether this is a deliberate strategy by China is disputed among experts. In 2019 **Italy** signed a memorandum of understanding as the only G7 country. At the end of 2023 Italy did not renew the agreement.

On China's initiative, the **Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank**, AIIB for short, was founded in 2015. It is based in Beijing and finances infrastructure in Asia. Switzerland is one of its **founding members**. It joined even though the USA was sceptical. Many European countries are also members.

gewusst: The term “Silk Road” is only about 150 years old, even though the trade routes are much older.
The port of Hambantota in Sri Lanka was leased for 99 years.

t1n38m0p.t: Member states of the United Nations

teile.einleitung: The United Nations (UN) has 193 member states. Almost every country in the world belongs to it. Switzerland has been a member since 2002, the first country to join as a result of a popular vote.
wichtigste: The UN has 193 member states.
The most recent member is South Sudan, since 2011.
Vatican City is not a member, only an observer.
Liechtenstein has been a member since 1990, Austria since 1955.
Switzerland joined in 2002 after a popular vote.
In the General Assembly each country has one vote.
Most members come from Africa.

abschnitte.text: The UN was founded in 1945, with 51 members at the time. According to the **UN Charter**, **peace-loving states** can become members. For a country to join, the **Security Council** and the **General Assembly** must agree. Today the UN has **193 members**. Most of them come from **Africa**: all 54 African countries belong to it.

In the **General Assembly**, each member country has exactly **one vote**. It makes no difference whether a country is large or small. So Switzerland counts just as much as China. Things are different in the **Security Council**: there, five permanent members have a right of veto. With it, each of them can block decisions on its own.

**Austria** became fully independent again in 1955 and joined the UN in the same year. In 1973 the two German states, **West and East Germany**, became members at the same time. **Liechtenstein** joined as early as **1990**, twelve years before Switzerland. Small states such as San Marino and Monaco are full members too. **Vatican City**, on the other hand, is only an **observer**, as is Palestine.

Switzerland had worked with the UN for a long time, and an important UN office is in **Geneva**. But it only became a member late. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected joining. On **3 March 2002** the **people and the cantons** said yes. Switzerland was the first country to join as a result of a **popular vote**. In September 2002 it became the 190th member.

The most recent member is **South Sudan**. It became a separate country in 2011 and shortly afterwards the **193rd member**. There was a special case with **Indonesia**: in January 1965 it announced it was leaving in protest. In 1966, however, it resumed its participation. The UN treated this only as a temporary interruption.

gewusst: In front of the UN headquarters in New York fly the flags of all the member states.
Shortly after Switzerland, East Timor also joined the UN in 2002.

teile.einleitung: The Neutrality Initiative was a federal popular initiative. It wanted to write Switzerland's neutrality into the Federal Constitution in detail and in strict terms. On 27 September 2026 voters clearly rejected it.
wichtigste: In March 2022 Christoph Blocher announced an initiative for “integral neutrality”.
The organisation Pro Schweiz launched the initiative in November 2022.
In April 2024 it was submitted with almost 130,000 valid signatures.
It wanted to add a new Article 54a to the Federal Constitution.
The Federal Council recommended rejecting it, without a counter-proposal.
On 27 September 2026 about 70 per cent said no.

abschnitte.text: After Russia attacked Ukraine, Switzerland adopted the EU's **sanctions** against Russia in 2022. Sanctions are punitive measures, for example bans on trade. For some people this was a break with neutrality. In March 2022 former Federal Councillor **Christoph Blocher** announced an initiative for “integral neutrality”. In November 2022 the organisation **Pro Schweiz** launched the initiative.

A **popular initiative** needs 100,000 valid signatures. On 11 April 2024 the signatures were submitted in Bern. The **Federal Chancellery** counted almost 130,000 valid signatures. In May 2024 it declared that the initiative had been formally successful. The committee was made up mainly of SVP politicians.

The initiative wanted to write a new **Article 54a** into the Federal Constitution. It was to say that Switzerland is neutral and that its neutrality is **perpetual and armed**. Joining military or defence alliances would have been forbidden. Cooperation would only have been allowed in the event of a direct attack on Switzerland. Non-military sanctions against countries at war would have been banned, except for those based on UN obligations.

In its dispatch of November 2024, the **Federal Council** recommended rejection. It did not make a counter-proposal. It feared that a rigid rule would take away the **flexibility** of neutrality policy. The supporters, on the other hand, believed that only a clear rule could protect neutrality. So both sides wanted to preserve neutrality, but in different ways.

On **27 September 2026** the people voted on the initiative. It was clearly rejected, with 70.15 per cent voting no. The **cantons** also mostly said no. A change to the constitution needs a yes from both the people and the cantons. So neutrality remains set out in the constitution as before.

gewusst: The formula “perpetual and armed” has described Swiss neutrality for a long time.
A popular initiative always needs a double yes: from a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

teile.einleitung: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty to protect the ozone layer. It bans substances such as CFCs that destroy ozone. It is regarded as one of the most successful environmental agreements in the world.
wichtigste: The Montreal Protocol was signed on 16 September 1987.
It came into force on 1 January 1989.
It mainly regulates CFCs, which used to be found in spray cans and fridges.
The ozone layer protects us from the sun's UV radiation.
The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica in the 1980s.
By 2009 all UN member states had ratified the protocol.
Ozone has been measured in Arosa since 1926.

abschnitte.text: **Ozone** is a gas made of three oxygen particles. About 90 per cent of ozone is in the **stratosphere**, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground. This **ozone layer** acts like a filter. It holds back a large part of the sun's **UV radiation**. Too much UV radiation causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer.

Certain substances destroy ozone, above all **CFCs**, **chlorofluorocarbons**. They used to be found in spray cans, fridges and foams. In 1985 British researchers reported a strong thinning of the ozone layer over **Antarctica**. It is called the **ozone hole**. It appears there every year in the southern hemisphere's spring. The researchers **Paul Crutzen**, **Mario Molina** and **Sherwood Rowland** had explained how ozone is broken down, and for this they received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1995.

The **Montreal Protocol** was signed on **16 September 1987** in Montreal in Canada. It came into force on **1 January 1989** and was later tightened several times. The production of CFCs was banned step by step. By 2009 all UN member states had ratified the protocol, the last being East Timor. No UN treaty had managed this before. Today 16 September is the **International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer**.

**Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)** were often used to replace CFCs. They do not harm ozone, but they are very powerful **greenhouse gases**. That is why the protocol was extended in 2016 with the **Kigali Amendment**. It restricts these substances too. In this way the Montreal Protocol also helps the climate today.

In **Arosa** in the Grisons, the researcher **Paul Götz** began measuring ozone in 1926. Measurements have been taken there ever since, for longer than anywhere else in the world. Today **MeteoSwiss** continues this longest ozone measurement series in the world. The measurements show how the ozone layer has changed over decades. Experts expect the ozone layer to recover over the coming decades thanks to the protocol.

gewusst: The Montreal Protocol was the first UN treaty to be ratified by truly every member state.
The ozone measurement series from Arosa is the longest in the whole world.

teile.einleitung: The Khmer Rouge Tribunal was a special court in Cambodia. It was meant to hold the leading figures responsible for the serious crimes of the Khmer Rouge between 1975 and 1979 to account.
wichtigste: The Khmer Rouge ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979.
Under their rule about 1.5 to 2 million people died.
The tribunal was made up of Cambodian and international judges.
It was based in Phnom Penh and began its work in 2006.
The first to be convicted was Kaing Guek Eav, known as “Duch”.
Pol Pot died in 1998 and never stood trial.

abschnitte.titel: The rule of the Khmer Rouge
abschnitte.text: The **Khmer Rouge** were a communist movement. In April 1975 they took the capital **Phnom Penh**. They forced the city's inhabitants into the countryside and suppressed all resistance. Through executions, **forced labour**, hunger and disease, about **1.5 to 2 million people** died, roughly a fifth to a quarter of the population. At the beginning of 1979 the Khmer Rouge were overthrown by Vietnamese troops.

The tribunal's official name was the **Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia**. It was based on an agreement between Cambodia and the **UN**. **Cambodian and international judges** sat on it together. A verdict required a majority that included at least one international judge. The court sat on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, so many survivors could follow the trials themselves.

The first to be convicted was **Kaing Guek Eav**, known as **“Duch”**. He had run the **Tuol Sleng** prison, also called S-21. It was in a former school. On appeal, Duch was sentenced to **life imprisonment**. In 2018 **Nuon Chea** and **Khieu Samphan** were convicted of **genocide** against the Vietnamese minority, and Nuon Chea also of genocide against the Muslim **Cham**. Both were sentenced to life imprisonment.

The leader **Pol Pot** never stood trial. He died in **1998** on the border with Thailand, and the tribunal only began its work in **2006**. Other defendants also died during the long proceedings. In **2022** the tribunal concluded its trials. Critics complained that only a few people were convicted. Others stress that the trials were important for remembrance.

gewusst: The former Tuol Sleng prison is now a museum in memory of the victims.
More than 25 years passed between the fall of the Khmer Rouge and the start of the tribunal.

teile.einleitung: A president is at the head of a state, an organisation or an assembly. In many republics the president is the head of state; in Switzerland the post changes every year.
wichtigste: In many republics a president is the head of state.
The word comes from the Latin “praesidere”, “to preside”.
In Switzerland, Parliament elects a member of the Federal Council as President of the Confederation every year.
In 2026 Guy Parmelin is President of the Swiss Confederation.
George Washington was the first President of the USA, from 1789.
Barack Obama was the first Black President of the USA.
Since January 2025 Donald Trump has been President of the USA again.

abschnitte.text: The word **president** comes from the Latin **“praesidere”**, which means “to preside”. In a **republic** there is no king. At the head of the state there is often a president. In some countries the president has a lot of power and also leads the government, for example in the **USA**. In other countries the president mainly has ceremonial duties. Clubs, courts and parliaments also have a president.

abschnitte.titel: The President of the Swiss Confederation
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **President of the Confederation** is one of the **seven members of the Federal Council**. He or she is elected by the **United Federal Assembly** in Bern in **December**. The term of office lasts only **one year**; then another member takes over. The president chairs the meetings of the Federal Council and represents Switzerland abroad. He or she has no more power than the other Federal Councillors. For 2026 Parliament elected **Guy Parmelin**, who had already been President of the Confederation in 2021.

**George Washington** became the first President of the United States in **1789**. The capital is named after him. **Abraham Lincoln** was president from 1861 to 1865 and is known for his tall **top hat** and his beard. **Barack Obama** governed from 2009 to 2017 as the first African American president. **Donald Trump** has been back in office since January 2025; he had already been president from 2017 to 2021.

At **Mount Rushmore** in the US state of South Dakota, the giant heads of **four presidents** are carved into the rock. They are George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln. Each head is about as tall as a six-storey building. Many people visit the monument every year.

gewusst: Because the post changes every year, many Federal Councillors have been President of the Confederation more than once.
The heads at Mount Rushmore are each about 18 metres high.

teile.einleitung: The Organization of American States, OAS for short, is an association of the independent countries of the Americas. It works for democracy, human rights and cooperation. Its headquarters is in Washington, D.C.
wichtigste: The OAS Charter was signed in Bogotá in 1948.
Its headquarters is in Washington, D.C.
The OAS has four official languages: Spanish, English, Portuguese and French.
Its predecessor, from 1910, was the Pan American Union.
Cuba was excluded in 1962; the exclusion was lifted in 2009.
Canada only joined in 1990.
Nicaragua left the OAS in November 2023.

abschnitte.text: In 1889 and 1890 the first **International Conference of American States** took place in Washington. A trade office was set up there. In 1910 it became the **Pan American Union**. In 1948 the countries signed the OAS Charter in **Bogotá** in Colombia. This founded the organisation, and the Pan American Union became part of it.

The **independent countries of the Americas** can become members. They include countries in North, Central and South America and in the Caribbean, for example the USA and Brazil. **Canada** stayed away for a long time and only became a member in 1990. Today it is one of the most important funders. The four **official languages** are Spanish, English, Portuguese and French.

The OAS **General Secretariat** is based in **Washington, D.C.**, near the White House. The **Permanent Council** also meets there. An important body is the **Inter-American Commission on Human Rights**. It examines complaints about human rights violations. It too is based in Washington, D.C.

After the communist revolution, **Cuba** was excluded from taking part in the OAS in 1962. In 2009 the exclusion was lifted, but Cuba did not return. **Nicaragua** announced its withdrawal in 2021. The government had rejected criticism of its policies by the OAS. The withdrawal took effect in November 2023.

gewusst: The roots of the OAS go back to 1889, which makes it one of the oldest regional organisations in the world.
Canada only became a member more than 40 years after the OAS was founded.

teile.einleitung: Protectionism is a trade policy by which a country protects its own economy from foreign competition. To do this it makes imports more expensive or restricts them, for example with customs duties.
wichtigste: Protectionism protects domestic firms and jobs from foreign competition.
Its tools are customs duties, quotas, subsidies and strict regulations.
Barriers that are not customs duties are called non-tariff barriers to trade.
The US Smoot-Hawley tariff law of 1930 made the Great Depression worse.
Switzerland protects its farming with tariff quotas.
Customs duties are often paid mainly by buyers in the country itself.

abschnitte.text: With **protectionism**, a country tries to protect its own economy. An important tool is **customs duties**, charges on imported goods. In addition there are **non-tariff barriers to trade**: import restrictions without duties, such as **quotas** or strict **standards**. **Subsidies**, meaning money from the state for domestic firms, can also put foreign suppliers at a disadvantage. The opposite of protectionism is **free trade**.

Supporters say protection preserves **jobs** and important industries. In the 19th century the economist **Friedrich List** argued that **young industries** needed temporary protection until they could compete. This is called an **infant industry tariff**. Critics say customs duties make goods more expensive and in the end harm everyone. A duty makes imports more expensive mainly for **buyers in the country itself**. Other countries also often respond with **retaliatory tariffs**.

In 1930, with the **Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act**, the USA raised customs duties on thousands of goods. Other countries responded with duties of their own. **World trade** collapsed sharply. The law is therefore seen as an example of how protectionism made the **Great Depression** worse. After the Second World War, many countries reduced their customs duties, and today the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** watches over the rules.

When a company sells goods abroad more cheaply than at home, this is called **dumping**. The WTO allows **anti-dumping duties** against it. If imports suddenly rise sharply, a country may take temporary measures under a **safeguard clause**. **Switzerland** protects its **farming** with **tariff quotas**: up to a set quantity a low duty applies, and above it a very high one. At the same time it removes some barriers through the **Cassis de Dijon principle**.

gewusst: On 1 January 2024 Switzerland abolished customs duties on industrial goods.
The Cassis de Dijon principle is named after a French blackcurrant liqueur.

teile.einleitung: The Overland Transport Agreement is a treaty between Switzerland and the European Union. It governs the movement of lorries and trains across borders. It is part of the Bilateral Agreements I.
wichtigste: The agreement is part of the Bilaterals I and has applied since 2002.
Since then, lorries in Switzerland may weigh up to 40 tonnes; before, it was 28 tonnes.
Since 2001 heavy lorries have paid the HVF for every kilometre driven.
Switzerland wants to shift goods from road to rail.
The Alpine Initiative was accepted in 1994.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in 2016.
The night-time and Sunday driving ban for lorries still applies.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is not a member of the EU; it organises its relations through **bilateral agreements**. The **Overland Transport Agreement** is part of the **Bilaterals I** package of seven agreements. It was signed in 1999. In 2000 the Swiss people approved the Bilaterals I. The agreement has been in force since 2002.

In the past, lorries in Switzerland could weigh at most **28 tonnes**, while in the EU the limit was 40 tonnes. With the agreement the limit was raised step by step to **40 tonnes**. In return the EU recognised the **heavy vehicle fee (HVF)**, which is based on performance. It has been charged since 1 January 2001. How much a lorry pays depends on its weight, the kilometres driven and its emissions standard. Part of the money goes into expanding the railways.

Switzerland wants to move as much **transit traffic** through the Alps as possible onto the railways. This is called **modal shift** from road to rail. Its basis is the **Alpine Initiative**, which was accepted on 20 February 1994. Since then, protecting the Alpine region from transit traffic has been written into the **Federal Constitution**. This protects the environment and the people from noise and exhaust fumes.

So that more goods travel by train, Switzerland built the **New Rail Link through the Alps (NRLA)**. It includes the **Lötschberg Base Tunnel**, which opened in 2007. In June 2016 the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** followed, about 57 kilometres long. In 2020 the Ceneri Base Tunnel in Ticino was added. Freight trains can now travel through the Alps on flatter routes and more quickly.

Switzerland was able to keep some of its own rules. The **night-time and Sunday driving ban** for lorries still applies; it protects people from noise. There is also a **ban on cabotage**. Cabotage means transporting goods from one place to another within a foreign country. So a lorry from the EU may not deliver goods from Basel to Zurich.

gewusst: At about 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
In Switzerland lorries are banned from driving at night from 10 pm to 5 am.

teile.einleitung: Free movement of persons means that people may choose freely which country they live and work in. Between Switzerland and the EU there is a separate agreement for this. Its aim is to make it easier for people to work and live in Switzerland and the EU.
wichtigste: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons is meant to make it easier for people to work and live in Switzerland and the EU.
It was signed in 1999 and has applied since 1 June 2002.
It is part of the Bilateral Agreements I between Switzerland and the EU.
Anyone moving to another country usually needs a job or enough money of their own.
Accompanying measures are meant to prevent wages in Switzerland from being pushed down.
Switzerland has voted on the free movement of persons several times.
Thanks to the agreement, Swiss people can also work more easily in the EU.

abschnitte.text: Free movement means being allowed to move freely. Within the EU, the **free movement of persons** is one of the four fundamental freedoms, together with the free movement of goods, services and capital. Switzerland is not an EU member and has therefore concluded its own agreement. It is called the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons**, AFMP for short.

The agreement was signed in 1999 as part of the **Bilateral Agreements I**. In 2000 the Swiss people voted in favour of it, with about 67 per cent saying yes. It has been in force since 1 June 2002 and was gradually extended to new EU countries. Similar rules also apply with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Anyone from an EU country who finds a job in Switzerland receives a **residence permit**. People who study or have enough money to live on may also come. Many people live abroad and work in Switzerland; they are called **cross-border commuters**. In the other direction, people from Switzerland can work in Germany or Spain, for example.

So that companies do not hire cheaper workers on low wages, there are **accompanying measures**. Inspectors check whether the usual wages and working conditions are being respected. Breaches can lead to fines. These rules were introduced in 2004.

The free movement of persons is politically controversial in Switzerland. In 2014 voters narrowly accepted the mass immigration initiative, which wanted to limit immigration. In 2020 they rejected the limitation initiative, which wanted to end the agreement, with about 62 per cent voting no. Supporters stress that the economy needs skilled workers, while opponents worry about housing and traffic.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to choose freely where you live and work.
Agreements between two partners, in this case between Switzerland and the EU.
People who live in one country and travel to another country every day to work.
Permission to live in a country for a longer period.

gewusst: Every day almost 400,000 cross-border commuters travel to work in Switzerland (as of 2024).
The Bilateral Agreements I are linked by the so-called guillotine clause: if one agreement ends, the others end too.

teile.einleitung: NATO is a defence alliance of countries from North America and Europe. Its members promise to help one another if one of them is attacked. Because of its neutrality Switzerland is not a member, but it works with NATO in some areas.
wichtigste: NATO is a defence alliance of countries from North America and Europe.
It was founded on 4 April 1949 in Washington.
The name stands for North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Its headquarters is in Brussels in Belgium.
Under Article 5, an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
Since 2024 NATO has had 32 member states.
Switzerland is neutral and not a member, but it takes part in the Partnership for Peace.

abschnitte.text: NATO is an alliance for joint **defence**. Its full name is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and it is also known as the **North Atlantic Alliance**. The members decide together and by consensus, meaning only when everyone agrees. NATO does not have a large army of its own; instead the member states provide their soldiers and weapons. The organisation is led by a Secretary General; since October 2024 this has been the Dutchman Mark Rutte.

After the Second World War, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other as opponents; this is called the **Cold War**. Many Western European countries feared an attack from the East. So on 4 April 1949 twelve countries, including the USA, Canada, Great Britain and France, founded NATO. As a counterpart, the Soviet Union and its allies founded the **Warsaw Pact** in 1955, which was dissolved in 1991.

The heart of the treaty is **Article 5**. It says that an armed attack on one member is regarded as an attack on all. Each member then helps with the means it considers necessary. This collective defence clause has so far been invoked only once, after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 in the USA. The idea behind it is **deterrence**, because nobody should dare to attack a member.

After the end of the Cold War, many countries from Central and Eastern Europe joined, for example Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary in 1999. After the Russian attack on Ukraine in 2022, Finland and Sweden gave up their long-standing non-alignment. Finland became a member in 2023, Sweden in 2024. This means NATO has had **32 member states** since 2024. In 2014 the members set themselves the goal of spending about 2 per cent of their economic output on defence.

Switzerland is a **neutral state** and does not join any military alliance. But since 1996 it has taken part in the **Partnership for Peace**, a NATO programme for cooperation with non-members. This covers, for example, training, disaster relief and peacebuilding. Since 1999, Swiss soldiers of Swisscoy have helped in the KFOR peacekeeping force in Kosovo, which is led by NATO.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of countries that have joined together to help one another.
A strategy in which an opponent is meant to be kept from attacking by one's own strength.
A neutral country does not take part in wars between other countries and does not join any military alliance.
The period from about 1947 to 1991 in which the USA and the Soviet Union were hostile to each other without fighting a war directly.

gewusst: The collective defence clause under Article 5 was first invoked not for Europe but for the USA.
Iceland is a founding member of NATO, even though it has no army of its own.
NATO's first headquarters was not in Brussels but in Paris; it moved to Belgium in 1967.

teile.einleitung: Resettlement means moving especially vulnerable refugees from a first country of refuge to another country where they can stay permanently.
wichtigste: Resettlement is the transfer of refugees from a first country of asylum to a third country.
The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, proposes people to the receiving countries.
It is one of UNHCR's three durable solutions, alongside voluntary return and local integration.
The refugees enter the country safely and legally.
In Switzerland the Federal Council decides how many people are taken in.
Switzerland took in refugees from Hungary as early as 1956.

abschnitte.text: People fleeing war or persecution often first reach a neighbouring country. This country is called the **first country of asylum**. But some people cannot stay there safely or need special help, for example sick people or families with small children. With **resettlement**, they are taken to another country, a so-called **third country**. There they receive permanent protection.

**UNHCR** is the UN Refugee Agency, based in Geneva. It selects especially vulnerable people and proposes them to receiving countries. These countries then decide for themselves whether to take them in. UNHCR names **three durable solutions**: **voluntary return** to the home country, integration in the country of asylum and resettlement.

A big advantage is that the people enter **safely and legally**. They do not have to undertake a dangerous journey with **smugglers**. The journey is organised, and their admission has been approved in advance. In the new country they receive support to learn the language and settle in.

In Switzerland the **Federal Council** decides how many refugees come through resettlement, usually for two years at a time. The **State Secretariat for Migration (SEM)** carries this out with the cantons. Switzerland has taken in groups in the past too: in 1956 more than 10,000 people from **Hungary**, from the 1960s **Tibetans**, and at the end of the 1970s several thousand Vietnamese **boat people**.

gewusst: One of the largest Tibetan communities outside Asia lives in Switzerland.
Worldwide, only a small proportion of the refugees who need resettlement actually get a place.

t1ru5n16.t: List of the countries of the world

teile.einleitung: There are about 195 countries on Earth. However, the exact number cannot be given, because not all countries are recognised everywhere. The countries vary greatly in size and are spread unevenly across the continents.
wichtigste: Usually about 195 countries are counted.
They include the 193 UN members, Vatican City and Palestine.
With 54 countries, Africa has the most.
There are no countries in Antarctica.
Since 2023 India has had more inhabitants than China.
South Sudan has been independent since 2011 and is regarded as the youngest country.
Australia takes up almost an entire continent.

abschnitte.text: Usually about **195 countries** are counted. They include the **193 members of the UN** as well as **Vatican City** and **Palestine**, which are observers at the UN. Some territories such as **Kosovo** or **Taiwan** are recognised as separate countries by only some states. Switzerland, for example, has recognised Kosovo since 2008. That is why people usually say “about 195”.

**Africa** has 54 countries, more than any other continent. **Asia** is larger, but has fewer countries. In **Antarctica**, at the South Pole, there are no countries, only research stations. An international treaty ensures that it is used peacefully for research. **Australia** is a special case: the whole mainland belongs to a single country, plus the island of Tasmania.

The largest country in the world by area is **Russia**. In America, **Canada** is the largest; it is even slightly bigger than the USA. The smallest country in the world is **Vatican City**, in the middle of Rome. **Monaco** is tiny too, only about 2 square kilometres. With just over 41,000 square kilometres, Switzerland lies somewhere in between.

**India** has the most inhabitants. In 2023 it overtook **China**. Both countries have more than 1.4 billion people. Together, more than a third of all the people in the world live there. Vatican City has the fewest inhabitants, with only a few hundred people.

The number of countries changes over time. After the Second World War many former **colonies** became independent, especially in Africa and Asia. When the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia broke apart, new countries also came into being. The youngest generally recognised country is **South Sudan**. It separated from Sudan in 2011 and became a member of the UN.

gewusst: Russia is so large that it stretches across eleven time zones.
Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre and lies entirely within the city of Rome.

teile.einleitung: Political participation means that people take part in politics. This can be voting in elections and referendums, but also signing a petition or taking part in a demonstration. In Switzerland, with its direct democracy, there are especially many ways to do this.
wichtigste: Political participation means taking part in political decisions.
In Switzerland adults aged 18 and over have been able to vote at federal level since 1991.
Women only received the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971.
In the National Council elections of 2023, turnout was about 47 per cent.
Anyone may submit a petition, including children and people without a Swiss passport.
In the consultation procedure, cantons, parties and associations can give their views on new laws.
People who believe they can make a political difference take part more often.

abschnitte.text: The best-known form is voting in elections and referendums. In Switzerland there are several **voting Sundays** every year. You can also join a party, stand for office or collect signatures for a popular initiative. A federal **popular initiative** needs 100,000 signatures within 18 months.

Political science calls forms outside elections and votes **unconventional**. They include taking part in a demonstration, boycotts or campaigns on social media. A well-known Swiss example is the women's strike of 14 June 1991 and 2019. The climate strikes by young people from 2019 also count.

In Switzerland women only received the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. That was much later than in most European countries. In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, women were only allowed to have a say at cantonal level from 1990. This happened through a ruling of the **Federal Supreme Court**, because the men at the Landsgemeinde (open-air assembly) had previously rejected it.

The **right of petition** belongs to everyone, including children and foreigners. With a petition you can write a request or a proposal to the authorities. The authorities must take note of it. For young people there are also youth parliaments and the Federal Youth Session, where they can put forward their own demands.

In the National Council elections of 2023, only about one in two people entitled to vote went to the polls; turnout was about 47 per cent. More people often take part in votes on controversial topics. Experts speak of **political efficacy** when someone believes they can make a difference through their own actions. People who have this feeling usually take part in politics more often.

begriffe.erklaerung: Taking part or being involved in something.
A written request or proposal to an authority, which anyone may submit.
A procedure in which cantons, parties and associations give their opinion on a new law.
The proportion of people entitled to vote who actually do vote.

gewusst: In the canton of Glarus, young people can take part in the Landsgemeinde and in cantonal votes from the age of 16.
Most Swiss people now vote by post instead of going to the polling station.

teile.einleitung: The Partnership for Peace is a NATO programme for cooperation with countries that are not members. Neutral Switzerland has also taken part since 1996, without giving up its neutrality.
wichtigste: NATO launched the Partnership for Peace in January 1994.
Switzerland joined in December 1996, Austria earlier in 1995.
Cooperation is voluntary, and there is no obligation to provide assistance.
Each country chooses for itself what it takes part in.
In 1997 the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council was set up for political talks.
Switzerland contributes especially through its three Geneva centres.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the **Cold War**, **NATO** wanted to improve relations with other countries in Europe. In January **1994** it set up the **Partnership for Peace**. Through it, non-members can work with NATO on a voluntary basis, for example in training, disaster relief and peacebuilding. **Russia** also joined in 1994. Cooperation with Russia was later largely halted because of conflicts.

The partnership contains **no obligation to provide assistance**. So a partner country does not have to help anyone militarily in the event of war. Each country sets out in an **individual programme** which areas it wants to take part in. Since 1997 there has been the **Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council** for political talks. NATO members and partners meet there.

Switzerland signed the framework document in **December 1996**. A clear principle applies: **neutrality** is preserved. Switzerland only chooses activities that are compatible with it. It focuses, for example, on **training**, **disarmament** and **disaster relief**. Neutral **Austria** has also been a partner since 1995.

The contribution of the **three Geneva centres** is especially important. The **Geneva Centre for Security Policy** offers courses for experts from many countries. The **Centre for Security Sector Governance** helps to place the army and police under democratic control. The **Centre for Humanitarian Demining** supports the clearance of landmines worldwide.

gewusst: Finland and Sweden were partners for a long time and are now members of NATO.
The Partnership for Peace does not mean joining NATO.

teile.einleitung: In principle, the UN Charter forbids countries to use force against one another. An important exception is the right of self-defence: if a country is attacked, it may defend itself. But strict rules apply.
wichtigste: The right of self-defence is set out in Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The condition is an armed attack.
It only applies until the Security Council has taken the necessary measures.
The country must report to the Security Council immediately.
Necessity and proportionality also apply.
NATO invoked collective defence for the first time after 11 September 2001.

abschnitte.text: In Article 2(4), the UN Charter forbids the threat and use of force between countries. **Article 51** allows an exception: the right of **individual and collective self-defence**. The condition is an **armed attack**. According to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), lesser uses of force do not give a right to armed self-defence.

The right of self-defence only exists **until the Security Council** has taken the measures necessary for world peace. So it is only a temporary solution. A country that defends itself must **report immediately** to the Security Council. The ICJ regarded a missing report as a sign against a genuine case of self-defence.

Two further limits from **customary law** also apply: **necessity** and **proportionality**. The response must not go beyond what is needed to repel the attack. This formula goes back to the **Caroline affair** of 1837. At that time British troops destroyed the US steamship Caroline. US Secretary of State **Daniel Webster** demanded that self-defence must be instant and overwhelmingly necessary.

In **collective self-defence**, other countries help the country that has been attacked. In the **Nicaragua** case in 1986, the ICJ required a **request** from the attacked country for this. The USA could not prove such a request. **NATO** is also based on this idea. After the attacks of **11 September 2001**, the NATO Council declared for the first time that collective defence under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty applied.

Things get difficult when an attack is only threatened. Defending against an **imminent** attack is accepted by many; this is called pre-emptive self-defence. **Preventive self-defence** is aimed at a merely possible future danger. It is mostly regarded as not allowed. Neutral Switzerland works for the ban on the use of force to be strictly respected.

gewusst: A rule from an exchange of letters about a steamship in 1837 still applies in international law today.
The first time in its history that NATO invoked collective defence, it was for the USA.

teile.einleitung: The Palace of Westminster in London is the building where the British Parliament works. With its famous clock tower on the bank of the Thames, it is one of the best-known buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Palace of Westminster stands in London right on the Thames.
The House of Commons and the House of Lords of the British Parliament meet here.
In 1834 a great fire destroyed most of the old palace.
The present building in the Gothic Revival style was built afterwards.
In the House of Commons the benches are green, in the House of Lords red.
The House of Commons does not have enough seats for all its members.

abschnitte.text: The **Palace of Westminster** stands in the London district of Westminster, right on the bank of the **Thames**. The English kings used to live here. Today the **British Parliament** works here. It consists of the **House of Commons** and the **House of Lords**. The monarch's residence, on the other hand, is Buckingham Palace.

In October **1834** a great **fire** broke out and destroyed most of the old palace. Afterwards it was rebuilt to plans by the architect **Charles Barry**. **Augustus Pugin** helped with the design. The building, in the **Gothic Revival style**, has many pinnacles and decorations. The old **Westminster Hall** survived the fire and is the oldest part of the building.

At the north end stands the famous clock tower. Since 2012 it has officially been called the **Elizabeth Tower**. Many people simply call it **Big Ben**, but that is actually the name of the largest bell in the tower. Its chimes are known around the world from British radio and television. Together with neighbouring Westminster Abbey, the palace is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The chamber of the **House of Commons** is decorated in **green**, and the leather benches are green too. The government and the opposition sit facing each other. Two **red lines** run in front of the benches. Traditionally it is said that they are **two sword lengths** apart and should not be crossed during a debate. The chamber has only about **427 seats**, far fewer than there are members. When everyone attends, some have to stand.

gewusst: The House of Lords is decorated in red, the House of Commons in green.
In the Second World War, the House of Commons chamber was destroyed by bombs in 1941 and rebuilt afterwards.

teile.einleitung: A microcredit is a very small loan for people who cannot get money from a normal bank. With it they can start a small business, for example. The idea became famous through the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
wichtigste: Microcredits are small loans, often only a few hundred dollars.
Poor people often cannot get a loan from normal banks because they have no collateral.
Most of the Grameen Bank's loans go to women.
Many borrowers form small groups that support each other.
The UN declared 2005 the International Year of Microcredit.
Critics warn of high interest rates and excessive debt.
In 2001 BlueOrchard, one of the first investment funds for microfinance, was set up in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A **microcredit** is a small loan, often only a few hundred dollars. It is aimed at poor people who cannot get a loan from normal banks. Banks usually ask for **collateral** such as land or a house, which these people do not have. In addition, the administrative costs of very small amounts are high in relation to the loan. With a microcredit, someone can buy a sewing machine, chickens or goods for a market stall, for example.

The best-known microcredit bank is the **Grameen Bank** in **Bangladesh**. “Grameen” comes from Bengali and means something like “village” or “rural”. It was founded by the economics professor **Muhammad Yunus**. Most of its borrowers are **women**; in 2007 they made up about 97 per cent. Women are seen as especially reliable and often invest in the family. In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank received the **Nobel Peace Prize**.

Many microcredits are given to **solidarity groups**. The borrowers join together in small groups and support each other. Only when the first members repay regularly do others receive a loan. In this way, trust within the group replaces the missing collateral. The term **microfinance** is broader: it also includes savings accounts, insurance and money transfers for people on low incomes.

Microcredits are not without controversy. The **interest rates** are often more than 20 per cent a year. Some borrowers take out new loans to pay off old ones and fall into a **debt trap**. Around 2010 there was a crisis in the Indian state of **Andhra Pradesh** because of massive **over-indebtedness**. The government then placed tight restrictions on microfinance institutions.

The UN declared **2005** the **International Year of Microcredit**. It saw microcredit as a way to fight poverty. Switzerland plays a role too: in 2001 **BlueOrchard**, one of the first commercial investment funds for microfinance, was set up in **Geneva**. It invests investors' money in microfinance institutions in many countries. Switzerland is regarded as an important centre for such investments.

gewusst: In the 1970s Muhammad Yunus gave his first loans out of his own pocket to women in a village.
The Grameen Bank is largely owned by its own borrowers.

teile.einleitung: Japan is a parliamentary democracy with an emperor at its head. The emperor, however, has no political power; the country is governed by parliament and the prime minister.
wichtigste: Japan's present constitution dates from 1947.
The emperor is the “symbol of the State and of the unity of the people”.
The parliament is called the Kokkai (National Diet) and has two chambers.
The lower house has 465 members.
Parliament elects the prime minister, and the emperor only appoints them formally.
Since 2019 the Reiwa era has been under way, with Emperor Naruhito.
In October 2025 Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first woman prime minister.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Japan received a new **constitution**. It came into force in **1947** and still applies today. It made Japan a **democracy**. Power lies with the people, who elect the parliament. In Article 9, Japan also renounces war as a means of politics.

Japan has an **emperor**. According to the constitution, he is the **“symbol of the State and of the unity of the people”**. He has no political power. The imperial throne is called the **Chrysanthemum Throne**, because the chrysanthemum is the emblem of the imperial family. With each new emperor a new **era** with its own name begins. In 2019 Emperor **Akihito** stepped down because of his advanced age. Since then his son **Naruhito** has reigned, and the **Reiwa era** applies.

The Japanese parliament is called the **Kokkai** (National Diet) and is based in **Tokyo**. As in Switzerland, it consists of **two chambers**: the **House of Representatives** (Shugiin) and the **House of Councillors** (Sangiin). The lower house has **465 members**, who are elected for at most four years. It is the more powerful of the two chambers.

The government is led by the **prime minister**. This person is elected by **parliament**. After that the emperor appoints them only **formally**. The prime minister chooses the ministers of the government. In October **2025**, **Sanae Takaichi** became the first woman to be prime minister of Japan.

gewusst: A special law was needed for Emperor Akihito to step down.
Before the Reiwa era, Emperor Akihito's time was called the Heisei era.

teile.einleitung: In many countries a prime minister leads the government. The office is especially well known in Great Britain, where it has existed for almost 300 years.
wichtigste: The prime minister is the head of the government, not the head of state.
In Great Britain the king is head of state and the prime minister leads the government.
The king officially appoints the prime minister.
The British prime minister sits in the House of Commons.
Every Wednesday he or she answers questions from members there.
In 1979 Margaret Thatcher became the first woman British prime minister.
Canada, Japan and many other countries also have a prime minister.

abschnitte.text: The **prime minister** is the **head of government**. He or she leads the government and helps shape its policies. In many countries there is also a **head of state**, for example a king or a president. **Canada**, Japan and India have a prime minister. In Germany and Austria the office is called **Federal Chancellor**. Switzerland has no head of government: the seven-member **Federal Council** governs together.

In Great Britain the **king** is the head of state. After an election he invites the person who can form a government and officially **appoints** them prime minister. Usually this is the leader of the strongest party. The prime minister is a member of the **House of Commons**. He or she lives and works at **10 Downing Street** in London.

Every **Wednesday** the House of Commons holds **“Prime Minister's Questions”**. Members ask the prime minister questions, often critical ones. The opposition in particular uses the opportunity. The debates are often loud and lively and are broadcast on television.
