**Winston Churchill** led Great Britain through the **Second World War** from 1940. **Margaret Thatcher** became the first woman in the office in 1979. She was called the **“Iron Lady”**. **Liz Truss** was in office for only **49 days** in 2022. That is the shortest term in British history.

gewusst: Robert Walpole, who governed from 1721, is regarded as the first British prime minister.
There is always a police officer outside the door of 10 Downing Street, and a cat often lives in the house to catch mice.

teile.einleitung: The Treaties of Rome were signed in Rome in 1957. They founded the European Economic Community and Euratom and are regarded as an important foundation stone of today's European Union.
wichtigste: The treaties were signed in Rome on 25 March 1957.
They founded the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom.
Six countries signed: Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
They came into force on 1 January 1958.
Customs duties between the member states were abolished by 1968.
As a counterpart, Switzerland, Austria and Great Britain, among others, founded EFTA in 1960.

abschnitte.text: On **25 March 1957** six countries signed two treaties in **Rome**: Belgium, the Federal Republic of Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. The ceremony took place in the **Palazzo dei Conservatori** on the **Capitoline Hill**, in the Hall of the Horatii and Curiatii. After ratification by all six countries, the treaties came into force on **1 January 1958**. These countries had already been working together since 1952 in the Coal and Steel Community.

The first treaty created the **European Economic Community (EEC)**. It was meant to create a **common market** in which goods, people, services and capital could move freely. The second treaty founded **Euratom**, the European Atomic Energy Community. It was meant to promote the **peaceful use of nuclear energy**. The EEC is an important forerunner of today's EU.

**Customs duties** between the EEC countries were to be removed step by step. On **1 July 1968** the last internal duties disappeared and a common **external tariff** was introduced. This happened faster than the treaty had planned. The EEC Treaty also provided for a **Common Agricultural Policy**. It was meant to secure food supplies and support farmers' incomes.

Not all European countries wanted to join the EEC. **Switzerland**, Austria, Great Britain and other countries founded the **European Free Trade Association (EFTA)** in **1960**. They wanted free trade, but not such close cooperation. Switzerland is still a member of EFTA today. It has concluded many **bilateral agreements** with the EU.

gewusst: 25 March is still a day of remembrance for European unity; in 2017 the EU countries met in Rome again for the 60th anniversary.
The customs union was completed in 1968, a year and a half earlier than planned.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a neutral country. This means that it does not get involved in other countries' wars and does not join any military alliance. Even so, it is very active in the world, for example as a mediator in conflicts.
wichtigste: Being neutral means that Switzerland does not get involved in other countries' wars.
Switzerland is permanently neutral, which means in peacetime too.
It has armed neutrality and defends itself with its own army.
Switzerland is not a member of NATO or any other military alliance.
The rules for neutral states are set out in the Hague Conventions of 1907.
Thanks to its neutrality, Switzerland often offers its “good offices” as a mediator.
How strictly neutrality should be interpreted is debated again and again in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A neutral country does not take part in wars between other countries. It sends no soldiers, does not let any party to the war use its territory and does not favour any side with weapons from its own army stocks. These duties are called the **law of neutrality**. They were set down in 1907 in the **Hague Conventions**.

Switzerland wants to be able to defend itself in an emergency. That is why it has its own army, organised on the **militia principle**. Many citizens serve as soldiers and then go back to their jobs. So neutrality does not mean being defenceless, but being impartial.

Because Switzerland does not take sides, both sides of a conflict often trust it. It organises peace talks, for example in Geneva, and provides rooms and experts for negotiations. As a **protecting power**, it represents the interests of one country in another country when the two no longer have relations. For example, since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran.

Besides the fixed rules there is **neutrality policy**. This means how the government puts neutrality into practice day to day. The Federal Constitution obliges the Federal Council and Parliament to safeguard neutrality. Exactly how this is done is decided by politicians depending on the situation.

Since Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022, there has been especially heated debate about neutrality. At that time Switzerland adopted the EU's sanctions against Russia. Some think this fits well with neutrality, others are critical. The question of whether other countries may pass on Swiss weapons also causes debate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country stays out of other countries' wars and does not help any party to a war militarily.
Help from a neutral country so that states in conflict can talk to each other.
A country that represents the interests of another country when that country has no embassy of its own.
Several countries promise to defend one another in war.

gewusst: Switzerland did not fight in either the First or the Second World War.
Besides Switzerland, countries such as Austria and Ireland are also neutral, but each in its own way.
According to surveys, neutrality is very popular with the Swiss population.

teile.einleitung: The Middle East conflict is a long-running dispute between Israel and the Palestinians. It is about land, borders, security and the city of Jerusalem. Each side has its own view of history.
wichtigste: In 1947 the UN adopted a plan to divide Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state.
In the war of 1948 about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven out; they call this the Nakba.
In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, among other areas.
In 1987 the First Intifada, a Palestinian uprising, began.
On 7 October 2023 Hamas carried out a major terrorist attack on Israel, followed by a long war in Gaza.
Israelis and Palestinians both claim Jerusalem as their capital.

abschnitte.text: In November 1947 the **UN General Assembly** adopted a **partition plan**. Palestine was to be divided into a Jewish and an Arab state. The Jewish side agreed, the Arab side refused. In 1948 the state of **Israel** was founded. Then the first war between Israel and its Arab neighbours broke out.

In the war of 1948 about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven out. The Palestinians call this event the **Nakba**, the Arabic word for “catastrophe”. Many descendants of the refugees of that time still live in camps today. The question of whether they may return is an important point of dispute. Israel and the Palestinians see this question very differently.

abschnitte.titel: The Six-Day War and the Intifada
abschnitte.text: The **Six-Day War** lasted from 5 to 10 June 1967. Israel captured the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem, the Golan Heights and the Sinai Peninsula. In 1987 the **First Intifada** began, an uprising against the Israeli occupation. Intifada means “shaking off” in Arabic. Later there were also peace talks, but they did not bring a lasting solution.

The **Gaza Strip** lies on the Mediterranean and borders Egypt in the south at Rafah. **Jerusalem** has holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, such as the Western Wall and the Dome of the Rock. Both sides claim the city as their capital. Its status is one of the most difficult points of dispute. Switzerland works for a peaceful solution through negotiations.

On **7 October 2023**, fighters of **Hamas** broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip. They killed about 1200 people and took hostages. This was followed by a long war in the Gaza Strip. A very large number of people were killed, and large parts of Gaza were destroyed. Many countries and aid organisations are trying to relieve suffering and help bring about peace.

gewusst: Jerusalem is a holy city for three major world religions.
The Six-Day War really did last only six days, from 5 to 10 June 1967.

teile.einleitung: Malala Yousafzai is a campaigner for girls' right to education. She comes from Pakistan and became world-famous as a teenager. In 2014 she became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Malala grew up in the Swat Valley in northern Pakistan.
She campaigns above all for girls' education.
In October 2012 she was shot by the Taliban on her way to school.
She was treated in Birmingham in England.
In 2013 her book “I Am Malala” was published.
In 2014 she received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Kailash Satyarthi.
In 2020 she completed her degree at Oxford.

abschnitte.text: Malala Yousafzai was born in 1997 in the **Swat Valley** in northern **Pakistan**. Her father ran a school and supported her greatly. In her region the **Taliban** took power for a time. They banned girls from going to school. But Malala was determined to keep learning.

Even as a child, Malala wrote a **diary** on the internet. In it she described how important school was to her. She also gave interviews and demanded the **right to education** for all girls. This made her well known in Pakistan. For the Taliban it was a provocation.

In October **2012** a Taliban fighter shot Malala on the school bus. She was seriously injured but survived. She was flown to **Birmingham** in England and treated in a hospital that specialises in serious injuries. Her family then moved to England as well. The attack caused outrage around the world.

In 2013 her book **“I Am Malala”** was published, which she wrote with the journalist Christina Lamb. In 2014, at the age of 17, she received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. She shared it with the Indian **Kailash Satyarthi**, who fights against child labour. In this way the Nobel Committee honoured a Muslim woman from Pakistan and a Hindu from India together. Both work for children.

Malala studied philosophy, politics and economics at the University of **Oxford**. She graduated in 2020. With her father she founded the **Malala Fund**. This organisation supports education projects for girls in many countries. Malala gives speeches all over the world, including at the UN.

gewusst: Malala is the youngest person ever to have received a Nobel Prize.
On her 16th birthday in 2013, Malala gave a speech at the UN in New York.

teile.einleitung: The President of the French Republic is France's head of state. He is elected directly by the people and has a lot of power, more than the heads of state of many other European countries.
wichtigste: The president is the head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
He is elected directly by the people for five years.
A person may be elected at most twice in a row.
He appoints the prime minister, who leads the government.
His official residence is the Élysée Palace in Paris.
Emmanuel Macron was elected in 2017 and 2022.

abschnitte.text: France's present constitution dates from **1958**. It founded the **Fifth Republic**, and its first president was **Charles de Gaulle**. The **president** is the **head of state**. He has a strong say in foreign policy and is **commander-in-chief of the armed forces**. He can also dissolve parliament and call new elections.

In France the citizens elect the president **directly**. This is different from our President of the Confederation, who is elected by Parliament. The term of office lasts **five years**. A person may be elected at most **twice in a row**. If nobody wins a majority in the first round, there is a second round between the two candidates with the most votes. **Emmanuel Macron** was elected in 2017 and 2022.

The president **appoints** a **prime minister**. This person leads the **government** and is answerable to parliament. If the president and the parliamentary majority belong to different political camps, this is called **cohabitation**, meaning “living together”. In that case the prime minister has more influence.

abschnitte.titel: The Élysée and the national day
abschnitte.text: The president's official residence is the **Élysée Palace** in the middle of Paris. On **14 July** France celebrates its **national day**. Then there is a large military parade on the **Champs-Élysées**, watched by the president. At official ceremonies the national anthem, the **Marseillaise**, is played.

gewusst: The French president is also one of the two heads of state of Andorra, with the title of Co-Prince.
Until 2002 the French president's term of office lasted seven years.

teile.einleitung: In the Council of the European Union, the ministers of the member states meet. Together with the European Parliament, it passes most EU laws.
wichtigste: Depending on the topic, the responsible ministers of the member states sit in the Council.
It is also called the Council of Ministers.
Together with the European Parliament it passes most EU laws.
Each country takes over the presidency for six months.
Many decisions are taken by qualified majority; in foreign policy they are usually unanimous.
The Council usually meets in Brussels, and in April, June and October in Luxembourg.

abschnitte.text: In the **Council of the European Union**, the **ministers** of the member states responsible for a given area meet. Which ministers come depends on the topic: for agriculture the agriculture ministers, for the environment the environment ministers. That is why it is often called the **Council of Ministers**, officially simply **“the Council”**. The meetings are prepared by the **Committee of Permanent Representatives**, COREPER for short. There the countries' EU ambassadors meet in Brussels.

The Council is one of the EU's two **lawmakers**. In the **ordinary legislative procedure**, the Council and the **European Parliament** must both agree to a law. Many decisions are taken by **qualified majority**: at least **55 per cent** of the countries must agree, together representing at least **65 per cent** of the EU population. In **foreign and security policy**, on the other hand, **unanimity** is usually needed. There any single country can block a decision.

The chair of the Council, the **Council presidency**, is taken over by each country for **six months**. Then it is another country's turn. In this way every member gets a turn. The country holding the presidency chairs the meetings and tries to find compromises. Normally the Council meets in **Brussels**, but in **April, June and October** in **Luxembourg**.

There are three bodies with similar names. The **Council of the EU** is the Council of Ministers. In the **European Council**, the heads of state and government meet and set the overall direction. The **Council of Europe** in **Strasbourg**, on the other hand, is **not an EU institution** but a separate organisation with 46 member states. **Switzerland** also belongs to the Council of Europe, even though it is not a member of the EU.

gewusst: The EU has 24 official languages, so many Council documents are translated into all of them.
Switzerland has been a member of the Council of Europe since 1963.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has been a member of the United Nations, the UN for short, since 2002. This made it one of the last countries in the world to join, even though an important UN office has long been located in Geneva. Today Switzerland works actively in the UN and has even sat on the Security Council.
wichtigste: Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002.
On 3 March 2002 the people said yes to joining.
In a first vote in 1986 the people had still clearly rejected joining.
Switzerland was admitted as the 190th member on 10 September 2002.
After New York, Geneva is the UN's second most important location.
In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.
UN membership is compatible with neutrality.

abschnitte.text: The **United Nations** was founded in 1945 after the Second World War. Its aims are to secure peace, protect human rights and promote cooperation between countries. Today almost all the countries in the world belong to it, 193 in total. Its headquarters is in New York.

Switzerland worked with the UN for a long time, for example from 1948 with **observer status**. But many feared that membership would not fit with neutrality. In 1986 the people clearly rejected joining, with about 76 per cent voting no. Only a **popular initiative** led to a second vote.

On 3 March 2002 about 55 per cent of voters were in favour of joining. A narrow majority of the cantons also said yes. This made Switzerland the first nation to join the UN through a **popular vote**. On 10 September 2002 it was admitted as the 190th member.

The **Palais des Nations** in Geneva houses the UN's second-largest office. Around Geneva many UN organisations work, for example the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN Refugee Agency and the Human Rights Council. Thousands of people from all over the world work there. For Switzerland this is an important part of its foreign policy.

In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a member of the **Security Council** for the first time. There it worked mainly for peace, the protection of civilians and the climate. Switzerland pays contributions to the UN and sends experts on peace missions. Swiss military observers are deployed in the Middle East and in Africa, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: The United Nations organisation, of which almost all the countries in the world are members.
You may attend meetings but may not vote.
A deployment in which experts or soldiers help to secure peace.
A country that belongs to an organisation.

gewusst: Before joining the UN, Switzerland was already a member of several UN specialised agencies, such as the World Health Organization.
After Switzerland, East Timor joined in 2002, and Montenegro followed in 2006.
From 1920 to 1946 Geneva was the seat of the League of Nations, the forerunner of the UN.

teile.einleitung: The Kosovo War was a war in 1998 and 1999 over the region of Kosovo in South-East Europe. It ended after 78 days of NATO air strikes. Afterwards Kosovo came under international administration.
wichtigste: The NATO air strikes were called Operation Allied Force.
They lasted from 24 March to 10 June 1999, which is 78 days.
Before that, the Rambouillet negotiations had failed.
The operation was controversial because there was no mandate from the UN Security Council.
Resolution 1244 placed Kosovo under international administration.
Switzerland takes part in KFOR with Swisscoy.
For the German armed forces it was the first combat mission since 1945.

abschnitte.text: At that time **Kosovo** belonged to **Serbia**, which together with Montenegro formed the **Federal Republic of Yugoslavia**. The majority of the population were **Kosovo Albanians**. They wanted more self-government or independence. From 1998 the Albanian group **KLA** (UÇK) and Serbian security forces fought each other. Many people had to flee.

In **February and March 1999**, talks were held at the **Château de Rambouillet** near Paris. The aim was an agreement on **autonomy** for Kosovo, meaning extensive self-government. The Yugoslav side rejected the draft. **NATO** then decided to intervene militarily.

On **24 March 1999**, NATO began **Operation Allied Force**. Its aircraft attacked military and strategic targets in Serbia and Kosovo. The attacks ended on **10 June 1999**, after **78 days**. For the German **Bundeswehr** it was the **first combat mission** since the Second World War. It took part with Tornado aircraft.

The operation lacked a **mandate from the UN Security Council**. Russia and China would have blocked such a mandate. Supporters spoke of a **humanitarian intervention** to protect the population. Critics saw it as a breach of the **ban on the use of force** in international law. This question is still debated today.

**Resolution 1244** of 10 June 1999 placed Kosovo under the **UN interim administration UNMIK**. The international security force **KFOR** was to keep the peace. Since 1999 **Switzerland** has taken part with **Swisscoy**, which is made up of volunteers. In 2008 Kosovo declared its independence, which not all countries recognise.

gewusst: Swisscoy is the Swiss Army's largest mission abroad to promote peace.
Resolution 1244 is still in force today.

teile.einleitung: The Red Cross emblem is a red cross on a white background. It is one of the best-known symbols in the world and protects helpers, the wounded and hospitals in wars.
wichtigste: The emblem is a red cross on a white background.
It is often explained as the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.
The first Geneva Convention established it as a protective emblem in 1864.
Besides the Red Cross there are the Red Crescent and the Red Crystal.
Anyone displaying the protective emblem must not be attacked.
Use of the emblem is protected by law.

abschnitte.text: The Red Cross emblem is a **red cross on a white background**. It is often explained as a **reversal of the colours** of the Swiss flag, in honour of Switzerland, where the Red Cross was founded. However, historians point out that this origin is not clearly proven. With the **first Geneva Convention** of **1864**, the emblem was made binding internationally as the identifying sign of the medical services.

In an armed conflict, the emblem is a **protective emblem**. Whoever or whatever displays it, for example **medical staff**, ambulances or **hospitals**, must not be attacked. This is laid down in the **Geneva Conventions**. So that the emblem keeps this effect, its use is **protected by law**. You may not simply use it as a logo for your own products, and unauthorised use can be punished.

The **Red Crescent** was first used by the **Ottoman Empire** in the 1870s and officially recognised in 1929. Many aid societies in predominantly Muslim countries use it. In 1929 the **Red Lion and Sun** was also recognised, which **Iran** used until 1980. Since then Iran has used the Red Crescent. The **Red Crystal** is a red square standing on one of its points, with no religious meaning. It was agreed in 2005 and has applied since 2007.

Two uses are distinguished. The **protective emblem** is large and clearly visible and protects in war. The **indicative emblem** only shows that a person or object belongs to the **Red Cross Movement**. It is smaller and is usually combined with the name of the society, for example in the logo of the **Swiss Red Cross**.

gewusst: The Red Crystal was created so that countries that want to use neither the cross nor the crescent can also take part.
The additional protocol on the Red Crystal came into force on 14 January 2007.

teile.einleitung: The law of the European Union is the set of all rules that apply to the EU and its member states. A central feature is that EU law can apply directly in the member states and takes precedence over national law. This distinguishes the EU from ordinary international treaties.
wichtigste: EU law can apply directly in the member states and takes precedence over national law.
A distinction is made between primary law, meaning the treaties, and secondary law, meaning the rules the EU adopts itself.
Important treaties are the Treaty on European Union and the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU.
Regulations apply directly, while directives must be turned into national laws by each country.
The Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg watches over EU law.
Switzerland is not an EU member, but it adopts many EU rules through bilateral agreements.
The whole body of EU law is also called the “acquis”.

abschnitte.text: The EU is an association of 27 countries that have common rules. These rules form a separate **legal order**. They concern, for example, trade, consumer protection, the environment or travel. Normally international treaties only apply between states, but EU law can create rights directly for individual people.

**Primary law** consists of the founding treaties that all the member states have signed. Their present form comes from the Treaty of Lisbon, which came into force in 2009. **Secondary law** is adopted by the EU institutions themselves, above all by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU together. The proposals for it are made by the European Commission.

A **regulation** applies immediately in all member states, like a law. One example is the General Data Protection Regulation, which has applied since 2018. A **directive**, on the other hand, only sets a goal, and each country must turn it into a law of its own. This leaves the countries some room for manoeuvre.

The **Court of Justice of the European Union** is based in Luxembourg. It decides how EU law is to be interpreted correctly. In famous rulings of 1963 and 1964 it established that EU law can apply directly and takes precedence. Without these rules, each country could undermine EU law with its own laws.

Switzerland does not belong to the EU, but it is closely linked to it. Through about 120 **bilateral agreements** it adopts the same or similar rules in many areas, for example on Schengen or air transport. Switzerland also often adapts its laws to EU law voluntarily; this is called autonomous adoption. In 2024 Switzerland and the EU concluded negotiations on a new package of agreements, which has to be decided on politically in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: When two rules contradict each other, the one with precedence applies.
An EU law that applies directly in all member states.
An EU goal that each country must put into practice with its own laws.
A country that belongs to the EU.

gewusst: Because of an EU rule, almost all mobile phones now have the same charging port, USB-C.
EU laws are translated into all 24 official languages, and every version is equally valid.

teile.einleitung: The right of peoples to self-determination says that a people may decide its political future for itself. It is an important principle of international law. It played a big role above all at the end of the colonial era.
wichtigste: The UN Charter names self-determination as an aim of the UN in Article 1(2).
Both UN human rights covenants of 1966 begin with this right in Article 1.
US President Woodrow Wilson made it widely known in 1918 with his Fourteen Points.
Resolution 1514 of 1960 called for the independence of colonial peoples.
A distinction is made between internal and external self-determination.
A Swiss example is the founding of the canton of Jura.

abschnitte.text: In January **1918** US President **Woodrow Wilson** presented a peace programme, the **Fourteen Points**. It provided for reorganising Europe after the First World War along national lines. The Russian revolutionary leader Lenin also promoted self-determination. Since then the term has become an essential part of world politics.

In **Article 1(2)**, the **UN Charter** names as an aim friendly relations based on equal rights and the **self-determination** of peoples. Article 55 takes up the principle again. The two **UN human rights covenants** of 1966, the Civil and Political Covenant and the Economic, Social and Cultural Covenant, both begin with this right in identical words in **Article 1**. This made it binding treaty law.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the colonial era
abschnitte.text: For a long time European countries ruled large areas of Africa and Asia as **colonies**. In 1960 the General Assembly adopted **Resolution 1514**. It called for the independence of colonial countries and peoples and gave **decolonisation** a strong boost. New states often kept the old administrative borders. This principle is called **uti possidetis**. It is meant to prevent border conflicts after independence.

Two forms are distinguished. **Internal self-determination** means having a say and **autonomy** within an existing state. **External self-determination** means choosing one's international status, up to and including **independence**. Whether there is a general right to break away from a state is disputed. In its 2010 advisory opinion on **Kosovo**, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) only decided that its declaration of independence did not violate international law.

There is a well-known example in Switzerland too. The Jura belonged to the canton of **Bern** for a long time. Many people in the north of the Jura wanted a canton of their own. After several **votes** in the 1970s, the northern Jura districts separated from Bern. The **canton of Jura** has existed since **1979**. Here self-determination within the federal state was achieved through votes.

gewusst: The canton of Jura is Switzerland's youngest canton.
Both major UN human rights covenants begin with exactly the same article on self-determination.

teile.einleitung: Nuclear deterrence means that a country possesses nuclear weapons so that nobody dares to attack it. The idea is that an attacker would itself be destroyed. This thinking shaped above all the Cold War between the USA and the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: MAD stands for Mutually Assured Destruction.
Second-strike capability means being able to strike back after an attack.
The nuclear triad consists of land-based missiles, submarines and bombers.
In the 1950s the USA threatened massive retaliation.
In 1967 NATO adopted the strategy of flexible response.
The ABM Treaty of 1972 limited missile defence.
In 1983 Stanislav Petrov recognised a missile alert as a false alarm.

abschnitte.text: **Deterrence** means keeping an opponent from attacking by means of a threat. With nuclear weapons the threat is especially great. People speak of **MAD**, Mutually Assured Destruction. Because an attacker would itself be destroyed, nobody is supposed to start a nuclear war. Whether this logic always works is disputed.

**Second-strike capability** is important. A country must still be able to strike back even after an enemy attack. Then an attack is pointless. That is why nuclear powers spread their weapons across the **nuclear triad**: land-based intercontinental missiles, missiles on submarines and strategic bombers. This way an opponent cannot knock out all systems at the same time.

In 1954 US Secretary of State **John Foster Dulles** presented the strategy of **massive retaliation**. Any Soviet attack was to be answered with an all-out nuclear strike. This soon seemed hardly credible, because the Soviet Union could itself threaten the USA. In 1967 NATO adopted **flexible response**. Depending on the attack, the response was to be conventional or with different nuclear weapons.

In 1972 the USA and the Soviet Union concluded the **ABM Treaty**. In it they limited their **missile defence**. That sounds strange, but there was a reason. An effective defence could have allowed one side to risk a first strike. By limiting it, both remained vulnerable and therefore deterred.

In September 1983 a Soviet early-warning system reported supposed missiles coming from the USA. The officer **Stanislav Petrov** judged the alert to be a false alarm. He did not pass it on as an attack. In this way he may have prevented a counter-strike. The case shows how risky deterrence can be because of technical faults.

gewusst: The English word “mad” also means “crazy”, which suits the abbreviation MAD well.
In the ABM Treaty, two superpowers voluntarily gave up a large part of their protection.

teile.einleitung: A political ideology is a set of ideas about what a state and a society should be like. Examples are liberalism, conservatism, socialism and anarchism. Ideologies help us understand why parties have such different aims.
wichtigste: A political ideology is a world view with ideas about how state and society should work.
Liberalism puts the freedom of the individual at the centre; John Locke laid important foundations for it in 1689.
Edmund Burke, with his work of 1790, is regarded as the founder of modern conservatism.
According to Karl Marx, communism aims at a classless society without private ownership of the means of production.
Social democracy relies on reforms instead of revolution.
Anarchism rejects every form of rule and state coercion.
The terms “left” and “right” come from the seating arrangement of the French National Assembly of 1789.

abschnitte.text: **Liberalism** puts the freedom of every person at the centre. In 1689 the Englishman John Locke wrote the “Two Treatises of Government”, in which he described rights to life, liberty and property. In 1859, in “On Liberty”, John Stuart Mill formulated the **harm principle**. It says that the state may only restrict a person's freedom in order to prevent harm to others.

**Conservatism** wants to preserve what has proved its worth and to approach change only cautiously. Its founder is regarded as the Irishman Edmund Burke, with his “Reflections on the Revolution in France” of 1790. He criticised the revolutionaries for wanting to overturn everything at once. Conservatives often value tradition, family, religion and order.

**Socialism** arose in the 19th century, when many factory workers lived in great poverty. In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published “The Communist Manifesto”. Communism aims at a classless society in which factories and land belong to everyone in common. **Social democracy**, by contrast, wants to improve the situation of workers through reforms within democracy.

**Anarchism** rejects any rule of people over people, including the state. An important meeting place of the early anarchists in 1872 was Saint-Imier in the Bernese Jura. Dictatorships are completely different: an authoritarian dictatorship bans opposition, while a **totalitarian** dictatorship wants to control every area of people's lives. Examples of totalitarian rule are National Socialism and the Soviet Union under Stalin.

During the French Revolution in 1789, the supporters of change sat on the left in the National Assembly and the supporters of the king on the right. This gave rise to the terms **left** and **right**. Today parties on the left tend to want more equality and a strong welfare state. Parties on the right tend to stress tradition, personal responsibility and national independence, and in between lies the political centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: A set of ideas and beliefs about how the world should be.
Things used to make goods, for example factories, machines and land.
A step-by-step change without overturning everything.
Rule that tries to control every area of people's lives.

gewusst: Swiss parties can be roughly linked to different ideologies, for example the FDP to liberalism and the SP to social democracy.
Since the 1970s, environmentalism has also become a political movement of its own.
After 1849 Karl Marx lived in London for many years, where he wrote his main work, “Das Kapital” (Capital).

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, the UN for short, is an association of almost all the countries in the world. Switzerland only joined in 2002, after the people had agreed. Even so, it has long been closely linked to the UN, because an important UN office is in Geneva.
wichtigste: Switzerland officially became a UN member on 10 September 2002.
It was the 190th member.
In 1986 about three quarters of voters said no to joining.
In 2002 about 55 per cent said yes.
The Palais des Nations, the UN's large office in Europe, is in Geneva.
In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland sat on the Security Council for the first time.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the people decide on joining the UN. In the first vote in **1986**, about three quarters of voters said **no**. Many feared for **neutrality**. In March **2002** about 55 per cent voted **yes**. The result among the cantons was also very close.

On **10 September 2002** the General Assembly admitted Switzerland. It became the **190th member** of the UN. East Timor followed shortly afterwards. Even before that, Switzerland had worked in many UN organisations and had observer status. Today the UN has 193 member states.

The **League of Nations**, the forerunner of the UN, used to work in Geneva. It built the **Palais des Nations** there. Today it houses the UN's large office in Europe. Many other organisations are also based in Geneva, such as the World Health Organization or the International Committee of the Red Cross. That is why important conferences often take place there.

In front of the Palais des Nations stands a giant wooden chair, the sculpture **“Broken Chair”**. One of its legs is **broken off**. The chair is a reminder of the people who have been injured by **landmines**. It is meant to remind countries to ban such weapons. The chair is a popular subject for photos.

Switzerland also takes part in peace missions. **Swisscoy** has been deployed in **Kosovo** since 1999. Its basis is a decision of the UN Security Council. In 2022 Switzerland was elected to the **Security Council** by the General Assembly. In 2023 and 2024 it sat there for the first time as a non-permanent member.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries to have joined the UN after a popular vote.
Even before Switzerland joined, Geneva was one of the most important UN locations in the world.

teile.einleitung: The War Material Act governs whether Swiss companies may sell weapons and ammunition abroad. It is meant to stop Swiss war material from reaching conflict zones. Since the war in Ukraine it has been the subject of fierce debate.
wichtigste: Licences are granted by SECO, together with the FDFA.
As a rule, nothing is delivered to countries involved in an armed conflict.
With a non-re-export declaration, buyers promise not to pass anything on without permission.
In 2022 Germany was not allowed to pass Swiss ammunition for the Gepard on to Ukraine.
Denmark was not allowed to pass on Piranha armoured vehicles either.
In 2009 the people rejected an export ban, with 68.2 per cent voting no.
Since 1 May 2022 the licensing criteria have been set out in the act itself.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, exporting **war material** requires a **licence**. Applications are examined by the **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs** (SECO) together with the **FDFA**. Difficult cases are decided by the **Federal Council**. As a rule, exports are ruled out if the receiving country is involved in an **armed conflict**. On top of this comes the **principle of equal treatment** under the law of neutrality.

Anyone who buys Swiss war material often signs a **non-re-export declaration**. With it, the buying country promises **not to pass the material on** to third parties **without Switzerland's consent**. This is meant to stop weapons from reaching conflict zones by roundabout routes. This rule became especially important after Russia attacked Ukraine.

**Germany** had supplied Ukraine with **Gepard** anti-aircraft tanks. It wanted to pass on Swiss **35-millimetre ammunition** for them. It had originally been developed by **Oerlikon**. Switzerland refused in 2022. **Denmark** was not allowed to pass **Piranha** wheeled armoured personnel carriers made by the firm **Mowag** from Kreuzlingen on to Ukraine either.

On **29 November 2009** the people voted on a **ban on exports of war material**. **68.2 per cent** said no, and all the cantons rejected it too. Later came the **“Correction Initiative”**, which wanted stricter rules. Its counter-proposal came into force on **1 May 2022**: the licensing criteria are now set out in the **act** instead of an ordinance. This means Parliament decides on changes, and the initiators withdrew their initiative.

abschnitte.titel: The dispute over relaxing the rules
abschnitte.text: The **arms industry** warns about the strict rules. It fears that foreign customers will no longer buy Swiss parts if they are not allowed to pass them on in an emergency. This, it says, puts jobs and the country's own defence industry at risk. Others stress **neutrality** and protection against supplying weapons to wars. Since then, Parliament has been debating whether to relax the rules.

gewusst: The Gepard has two cannons and its own radar to detect aircraft.
The firm Mowag in Kreuzlingen also supplies Piranha vehicles to the Swiss Army.

teile.einleitung: The Schuman Plan was a proposal from 1950: France and Germany were to manage their coal and steel jointly. This was meant to make a war between the two countries impossible. The plan is regarded as the beginning of European unification.
wichtigste: Robert Schuman presented the plan in Paris in 1950 as French foreign minister.
Coal and steel were to be managed jointly.
The aim was to make a war between France and Germany impossible.
The plan was drawn up mainly by Jean Monnet.
German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer agreed quickly.
Schuman was born in Luxembourg in 1886.

abschnitte.text: France and Germany had fought each other three times in less than a hundred years. After the Second World War, politicians looked for a way to lasting peace. Schuman wrote that a war between the two countries should become “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible”. Materially here means that they would no longer even have the means for it.

At that time **coal** and **steel** were industry's most important raw materials. They were also needed to build tanks, cannons and ships. Anyone who manages them jointly can hardly rearm in secret. That is why the plan proposed a joint **High Authority**. Other European countries were also allowed to join.

The plan was drawn up mainly by **Jean Monnet** and his team. Monnet was a French economic expert. **Robert Schuman**, as French **foreign minister**, made the plan his political proposal. He presented it in **Paris** on 9 May 1950. German Chancellor **Konrad Adenauer** agreed immediately.

In 1951 six countries signed a treaty in Paris: France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. This created the **European Coal and Steel Community**, also called the Montan Union. Today's European Union grew out of it step by step. Switzerland is still not a member of the EU.

Robert Schuman was born in **Luxembourg** in 1886 and later became a French politician. After his time as foreign minister he remained committed to Europe. In 1958 he became the first president of the **European Parliamentary Assembly**. Today's European Parliament grew out of it. He chaired it until 1960.

gewusst: 9 May, the day of the declaration, is now Europe Day in the EU.
A complex of EU buildings in Brussels bears the name Schuman, as do a square and a metro station.

teile.einleitung: The Olympic Museum stands in Lausanne, right on Lake Geneva. It shows the history of the Olympic Games from ancient times to today. Lausanne is also the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee.
wichtigste: The museum is in Ouchy on the shore of Lake Geneva.
It opened in 1993 and reopened in 2013 after a renovation.
There you can see torches, medals, sports equipment and clothing.
The museum is surrounded by a park with sculptures.
The Olympic flame is lit at Olympia in Greece.
St Moritz hosted the Olympic Winter Games in 1928 and 1948.

abschnitte.text: The **Olympic Museum** stands in **Ouchy**, a district of Lausanne in the canton of Vaud. It lies right on the shore of **Lake Geneva**. From the museum you can see across the lake to the Alps. It opened its doors in 1993. After a major renovation it reopened in 2013.

The museum shows the history of the Olympic Games from **ancient times** to today. You can see sports equipment, clothing and many souvenirs. There are also many **medals**: gold for first place, silver for second and bronze for third. Around the museum there is a **park** with sculptures and works of art on the theme of sport. You can stroll there and enjoy the view.

Many **torches** are on display in the museum. They were used to carry the **Olympic flame** to the Games. Each edition has its own torch with its own design. The flame is lit with the sun's rays at ancient **Olympia** in Greece. Then runners carry it to the host city.

Lausanne calls itself the **Olympic Capital** because the International Olympic Committee has its headquarters there. Olympic Games have also been held in Switzerland. **St Moritz** in the canton of the Grisons hosted the Olympic Winter Games in 1928 and 1948. No other place in Switzerland has hosted the Winter Games for adults so far. In 2020 Lausanne hosted the Winter Youth Olympic Games.

gewusst: The Olympic flame is lit with a concave mirror and the rays of the sun.
Lausanne is officially allowed to call itself the “Olympic Capital”.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it belongs to the Schengen area. This is called association with Schengen. As a result, there are no longer any systematic checks on people at the borders with the neighbouring countries.
wichtigste: In 2005 voters said yes to Schengen and Dublin.
Since 12 December 2008 Schengen has applied at Switzerland's land borders.
At the airports, the checks ended on 29 March 2009.
Goods are still checked by customs.
The Swiss police are connected to the Schengen Information System.
Liechtenstein joined Schengen in December 2011.

abschnitte.text: The **Schengen area** is a region in Europe where you can travel from one country to another without systematic passport checks. The name comes from the village of **Schengen** in Luxembourg, where the first agreement was signed in 1985. Switzerland approved it in a popular vote in **2005**. From **12 December 2008** systematic checks on people ended at the **land borders**. At the **airports** this followed on **29 March 2009**, because Schengen and non-Schengen flights had to be separated.

Schengen only concerns the **movement of people**. Switzerland is not part of the **EU customs union** and has its own **customs duties**. That is why the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** still checks **goods** at the border. Anyone bringing in a lot of meat from abroad, for example, must declare it. Spot checks on people are also possible.

So that the end of border checks does not weaken security, the Schengen countries work closely together. In the **Schengen Information System (SIS)**, wanted people, missing persons and stolen property are listed. The Swiss police can also access it. Since October 2025 the **Entry/Exit System (EES)** has recorded the entries and exits of people from non-Schengen countries with a facial image and fingerprints, including at Swiss airports.

If the EU changes Schengen law, Switzerland must adopt the new rules, otherwise the cooperation is at risk. The people can vote on this. On **19 May 2019** they accepted the stricter **EU Firearms Directive** with 63.7 per cent voting yes. On **15 May 2022** they approved, with 71.5 per cent, a higher contribution to **Frontex**, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency. Neighbouring **Liechtenstein** only became part of Schengen on 19 December 2011.

gewusst: The Schengen area is named after a small wine-growing village in Luxembourg.
The Entry/Exit System is gradually replacing the stamping of passports at the external borders.

teile.einleitung: Rescue dogs search for missing or buried people. With their sensitive noses they find people under rubble, in snow or in forests, often faster than people with equipment.
wichtigste: A rescue dog finds people with its nose.
Avalanche dogs search for people buried in snow.
When the dog has found someone, it barks or scratches.
In Switzerland the association REDOG trains search and rescue dogs.
The St Bernard Barry from the Great St Bernard Pass is the most famous rescue dog.
Dog and handler work together as a team.

abschnitte.text: Dogs can smell much better than people. They can pick up the **scent** of a person even when that person is lying under **rubble** or under **snow**. That is why they are so valuable in a search. When the dog has found someone, it **barks** or **scratches** at the spot. This way the rescuers know where to dig.

There are different kinds of rescue dogs. **Avalanche dogs** search for buried people after an avalanche. **Rubble search dogs** search collapsed buildings, for example after an earthquake. Area search dogs comb through forests and fields. A **mantrailer** sniffs an item of clothing belonging to the missing person and then follows exactly that person's scent trail.

A rescue dog never works alone, but with its **handler**. The two often train together for years until they are ready for missions. On a mission the dog often wears a **high-visibility vest**. This way the rescuers can see it easily, and everyone knows that it is working. In Switzerland the association **REDOG** trains dogs and their handlers. The teams search for missing people at home and also help abroad after earthquakes.

abschnitte.titel: Barry from the Great St Bernard
abschnitte.text: On the **Great St Bernard**, an Alpine pass in Valais, the monks of the hospice kept large dogs. These helped to find travellers who had lost their way in the snow. The **St Bernard** breed developed from them. The most famous dog was called **Barry**. He is said to have rescued about 40 people around 1800.

gewusst: Today Barry can be seen, stuffed, in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
A mantrailer can find a person again from a single item of clothing.

teile.einleitung: Protection status S is a special form of protection in Switzerland. It applies to people fleeing a serious general danger such as a war. It was used for the first time in 2022 for people from Ukraine.
wichtigste: The S stands for “schutzbedürftig”, meaning in need of protection.
Protection status S was created by the Asylum Act of 1998.
The Federal Council activated it for the first time in March 2022.
No detailed asylum procedure is needed for each individual person.
The status is geared towards return once the war is over.
People from Ukraine with status S may work straight away, with a permit.

abschnitte.text: The **S** stands for the German word **“schutzbedürftig”**, meaning in need of protection. People in need of protection are those who flee their country because of a serious general danger such as **war**. In Switzerland they receive the **S permit**. With it they may stay here for a certain time. At federal level the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) is responsible.

The status was included in the **Asylum Act of 1998** after the experiences with the wars in the former **Yugoslavia**. After that it went unused for more than 20 years. After Russia attacked **Ukraine**, the **Federal Council** activated the status for the first time on 11 March **2022**. In this way many people from Ukraine quickly found protection in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Fast instead of case by case
abschnitte.text: In the normal **asylum procedure**, the authorities examine every individual case in detail. This often takes a long time. With status S **no detailed asylum procedure** is needed. This way a very large number of people can receive protection in a short time. The status is **geared towards return**: it applies as long as the danger in the country of origin continues, and the Federal Council can lift it again.

In 2022 the Federal Council decided that people with status S may work **without a waiting period**. However, the employer must report the job or have it approved. After **five years**, people in need of protection can in principle receive a temporary **B residence permit**. This applies until the protection is lifted.

The European Union also has a similar instrument: **temporary protection**. The directive on it dates from 2001. It too was applied for the first time in March 2022, for people from Ukraine. This way refugees in Switzerland and in the EU received similar protection.

gewusst: Protection status S existed only on paper for more than 20 years before it was first used in 2022.

teile.einleitung: New START was a treaty between the USA and Russia. It limited the number of strategic nuclear weapons held by both countries. The treaty was in force from 2011 until February 2026.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed in Prague on 8 April 2010.
It was signed by Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev.
It came into force in February 2011.
Each side was allowed at most 1550 deployed strategic warheads.
700 deployed delivery systems were allowed.
In 2023 Russia suspended its participation.
The treaty expired on 5 February 2026.

abschnitte.text: On **8 April 2010**, US President **Barack Obama** and Russian President **Dmitry Medvedev** signed the treaty in Prague. At that time the two wanted to revive relations between their countries. The treaty was seen as a success of this rapprochement. It came into force in February 2011. START is an English abbreviation for Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty.

**Strategic nuclear weapons** are weapons with a very long range. Each side was allowed at most **1550** deployed, ready-to-use warheads. In addition, **700** deployed **delivery systems** were allowed, for example intercontinental missiles and heavy bombers. Together with non-deployed systems, the limit was 800. This was much less than in earlier agreements.

So that both sides could trust each other, there were **inspections** and an exchange of data. Experts were allowed to visit the other country's sites. There were simple rules for counting. Each deployed heavy bomber counted as **one warhead**, no matter how many it could carry. This rule made checking easier.

The treaty first ran for ten years. Shortly before it expired, the USA and Russia agreed in 2021 on the one possible **extension** of five years. In February 2023 President Putin announced that Russia was **suspending** its participation. However, Russia did not formally withdraw. After that there were no more inspections or data exchanges, and on **5 February 2026** the treaty finally expired.

gewusst: Under the rules of New START, a single heavy bomber counted as only one warhead.
The treaty could only be extended once.

teile.einleitung: A school meal is a meal that children receive at school. In many poor countries it is the most important meal of the day for children and a good reason to go to school at all.
wichtigste: The UN World Food Programme (WFP) provides meals in schools in many countries.
Where there is food at school, more children come to lessons.
Hungry children find it hard to concentrate.
In “home-grown” programmes, the food comes from local farmers.
Some programmes give children food rations to take home to their families.
In Switzerland many schools have a lunch club, and at break children eat their “Znüni”.

abschnitte.text: Around the world, many children do not have enough to eat every day. The UN **World Food Programme**, **WFP** for short, helps people in need with food. One of its most important tasks is providing meals in schools. The WFP is one of the largest providers of school meals worldwide. It often works with the governments of the countries so that they can later run the programmes themselves.

In poor families there is often not enough food for everyone. Some children then have to work instead of learning. If there is a guaranteed meal at school, parents are more willing to send their children to school. In some programmes children, often girls, also receive **food rations** to take home for the family. This way going to school pays off for the whole family.

Thinking is hard on an empty stomach. Hungry children quickly get tired and find it hard to **concentrate**. A healthy school meal gives them energy to learn. It should be varied and contain **vegetables**, **cereals** and **protein**, for example from beans, lentils, milk or eggs. This way children grow up healthy.

In **home-grown programmes**, schools buy their food from local farmers. The English word means grown at home. This way the children get fresh food and the farmers earn money. The money stays in the region and helps other people there too. In this way a school meal can benefit several groups at once.

In Switzerland many children go home at lunchtime. But because both parents often work, many municipalities and schools offer a **lunch club** (“Mittagstisch”). There the children eat together and are looked after. In the morning many children eat a **“Znüni”** at break, such as an apple or a piece of bread. In the afternoon there is the **“Zvieri”**, an afternoon snack.

gewusst: The World Food Programme has its headquarters in Rome and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
The name “Znüni” comes from the Swiss German “z Nüni”, meaning “at nine o'clock”.

teile.einleitung: The Schengen Agreement provides for the removal of passport checks at the shared borders of the countries taking part. So anyone travelling in the Schengen area can usually go from one country to another without being checked. Switzerland has also taken part since 2008.
wichtigste: The Schengen Agreement provides for the removal of passport checks at shared borders.
It was signed in 1985 in the small village of Schengen in Luxembourg.
The Schengen area includes 29 countries in Europe (as of 2025).
Switzerland takes part, even though it is not a member of the EU.
Swiss voters said yes to Schengen in 2005.
In return, the external borders of the Schengen area are checked more strictly.
The countries' police work closely together and share a common database of wanted persons.

abschnitte.text: **Schengen** is a small wine-growing village in Luxembourg, where Luxembourg, Germany and France meet. There, on 14 June 1985, five countries signed the agreement on a boat on the Moselle. They were Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The border checks were actually removed from 1995.

Within the **Schengen area**, there are normally no fixed passport checks at the borders any more. But you still have to carry a valid passport or identity card. The police may also carry out spot checks near the border. In special situations, countries may temporarily reintroduce checks.

So that free movement stays safe, the **external borders** of the Schengen area are checked carefully, for example at airports. People coming from outside need a **visa**, depending on their country of origin. A Schengen visa is valid for all the countries taking part. The border agency Frontex supports the countries at the external borders.

An important tool is the **Schengen Information System**, SIS for short. This is a shared database in which wanted people and stolen property such as cars are stored. The police in all Schengen countries can access it. This way, for example, a car stolen in Italy can be recognised in Switzerland.

Switzerland concluded the Schengen Agreement with the EU as part of the **Bilateral Agreements II**. On 5 June 2005 the people approved it with just under 55 per cent. Since December 2008 there have been no systematic checks on people at the land borders, and at the airports since March 2009. However, customs still checks goods, because Switzerland is not in the EU customs union.

begriffe.erklaerung: The countries between which there are no regular border checks.
The border between the Schengen area and other countries.
Permission to enter a country.
Checks on goods brought across a border, often with charges to pay.

gewusst: Not all EU countries belong to the Schengen area; Ireland, for example, does not take part.
Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Switzerland are in the Schengen area, even though they do not belong to the EU.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a kingdom in South-East Asia. At the head of the state is a king, while a prime minister leads the government. The king is deeply revered in Thailand.
wichtigste: Thailand is a monarchy and its head of state is a king.
Maha Vajiralongkorn has been king since 2016; he is also called Rama X.
His father Bhumibol reigned from 1946 to 2016, about 70 years.
The capital is Bangkok, where the Grand Palace stands.
Thailand used to be called Siam.
In cinemas, people stand up when the royal anthem is played.

abschnitte.titel: A king as head of state
abschnitte.text: Thailand is a **constitutional monarchy**. This means there is a king, but also a constitution, a parliament and a government. Until 1932 the king held all the power; then the **absolute monarchy** was abolished. Today the government is led by a **prime minister**. The king is seen as a symbol of the country's unity. Criticising the king is forbidden in Thailand by strict laws and can be punished severely.

Today's royal family is called the **Chakri dynasty** and has ruled since 1782. Its kings also carry the title **Rama** with a number. The number shows which king of the family it is. Today's king, **Maha Vajiralongkorn**, is Rama X, the tenth. He became king in 2016 and was formally crowned in 2019.

King **Bhumibol** reigned from 1946 to 2016, a total of 70 years. He was one of the rulers who sat on a throne the longest. In his youth he lived in Switzerland for a long time, in **Lausanne**. There he went to school and studied at the university. Many Thai people revered him deeply. After his death the whole country mourned for a year.

**Bangkok** is the capital and the largest city in Thailand. It is home to the **Grand Palace**, which was built from 1782 onwards. For a long time it was where the kings lived. Today it is used mainly for ceremonies and visited by many tourists. Within the palace grounds there is also a famous temple with the **Emerald Buddha**.

For a long time the country was called **Siam**. The name **Thailand** was introduced in 1939 and has been final since 1949. It means something like “land of the free”. The word **Siamese cat**, for example, comes from the old name. In the cinema, the **royal anthem** is often played before the film, and everyone stands up out of respect.

gewusst: Thailand was never ruled as a colony by a European power.
King Bhumibol spent a large part of his youth in Lausanne on Lake Geneva.

t9voif9.t: Member states of the European Union

teile.einleitung: The European Union (EU) is an association of European countries. Since Great Britain left in 2020, it has had 27 members. Switzerland does not belong to it, but it is surrounded by EU countries.
wichtigste: Since 2020 the EU has had 27 member states.
The European Economic Community was founded by six countries in 1957.
Germany has the most inhabitants, France the largest area.
Malta is the smallest member, both by area and by population.
In 2004 ten countries joined at once.
Luxembourg is the only grand duchy in the world.
Switzerland organises its relations with the EU through bilateral agreements.

abschnitte.text: The history of the EU begins after the Second World War. In 1957 six countries signed the **Treaties of Rome** and founded the **European Economic Community**. The founders were **Belgium**, **Germany**, **France**, **Italy**, **Luxembourg** and the **Netherlands**. They wanted to secure peace through cooperation. This later developed into the European Union.

Gradually more countries joined. The largest **enlargement** took place on 1 May **2004**: ten countries joined at once, including **Poland** and the **Czech Republic**. Most of them came from Central and Eastern Europe, along with **Malta** and **Cyprus**. The most recent country to join was **Croatia** in 2013. In 2020 **Great Britain** left the EU, and since then it has had **27 members**.

**Germany** has more than 80 million inhabitants and is the EU country with the largest population. **France** is the largest by area, followed by Spain and Sweden. The smallest member is the island state of **Malta**, with only about 316 square kilometres. **Luxembourg** is a **grand duchy**, with a Grand Duke at its head. Other EU countries are monarchies too, such as Spain, Belgium or Sweden.

**Cyprus** lies in the eastern Mediterranean and joined the EU in 2004. The island is divided: since 1974 the north has been controlled by **Turkey**. In practice EU law does not apply there. The UN has been working for decades to reunite the island. So far this has not succeeded.

Four of Switzerland's neighbours are in the EU: **Germany**, **France**, **Italy** and **Austria**. Switzerland itself is not a member. In 1992 the people narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. Since then Switzerland has organised its relations through **bilateral agreements**, for example on the **free movement of persons** or on **Schengen**. This gives it access to the **single market** in certain areas.

gewusst: Malta is just under half the size of the canton of Glarus and is still a full EU member.
Great Britain is so far the only country to have left the EU again.

teile.einleitung: A supply chain covers all the steps a product goes through, from raw material to customer. Today companies from many countries are often involved. If one link in the chain fails, people all over the world feel it.
wichtigste: A supply chain includes extracting raw materials, manufacturing, transport and sale.
Many goods travel in containers, measured in TEU, the size of a 20-foot container.
With just-in-time, parts are delivered exactly when they are needed.
In March 2021 the “Ever Given” blocked the Suez Canal for six days.
In 2021 and 2022 there was a worldwide shortage of computer chips, which slowed down the car industry.
Cargo ships reach as far as Basel via the Rhine.
The Responsible Business Initiative failed in 2020 because it did not win a majority of the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A **supply chain** shows the path of a product. It begins with a **raw material**, for example cocoa, cotton or ore. This is then processed, assembled into a product, transported and sold. A mobile phone is made of parts from many different countries. That is why people often speak of **global supply chains**.

A large part of world trade travels on **container ships**. Containers come in standard sizes and fit on ships, trains and lorries. Cargo is measured in **TEU**, which stands for “Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit”. This means a container **20 feet** long, about 6 metres. Switzerland is connected to the sea via the **Rhine**: cargo ships travel up to the **Swiss Rhine Ports** in Basel.

Many factories work on the **just-in-time** principle. Parts are delivered exactly when they are needed. This means the factory hardly needs a warehouse and saves money. But if a delivery fails, production quickly comes to a standstill. This method became well known mainly through the Japanese carmaker Toyota.

In March 2021 the huge container ship **“Ever Given”** ran aground in the **Suez Canal**. It blocked the canal for six days, and hundreds of ships were stuck in a queue. During the **coronavirus pandemic**, **computer chips** (semiconductors) became scarce. In 2021 and 2022 many car factories therefore had to stop production at times. Disruptions like these show how strongly countries depend on one another.

Supply chains can involve problems such as **child labour** or environmental damage. The **Responsible Business Initiative** wanted to make Swiss companies liable for this. On 29 November 2020 it won a narrow majority of the votes. However, most cantons rejected it, so it failed because it did not win the **majority of the cantons**. After that, a counter-proposal by Parliament came into force which, among other things, requires large companies to publish reports.

gewusst: The largest container ships can carry more than 20,000 containers at once.
The Responsible Business Initiative was one of the few initiatives that won a majority of the people and still failed.

teile.einleitung: Every four years the USA elects a president. The election attracts great attention worldwide and works differently from most elections, because what counts are the votes of the electors.
wichtigste: A US president's term of office lasts four years.
The election is held in November, always on a Tuesday.
Since 1951 a person may be elected at most twice.
A candidate must be at least 35 years old.
There are 538 electors, and you need at least 270 to win.
The next presidential election will take place in 2028.

abschnitte.text: The USA elects a president **every four years**. The election takes place in **November**, always on a **Tuesday**. This has been fixed since the 19th century: it is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. The term of office begins the following **January**. The last election was in **2024**, and the next will take place in **2028**.

The US **Constitution** sets conditions. Anyone who wants to become president must be at least **35 years** old and a US citizen from birth. Since a constitutional amendment of **1951**, a person may be elected president at most **twice**. Before the actual election, the parties decide in **primaries** who will stand for them.

There are two big parties in the USA: the **Republicans** and the **Democrats**. Their candidates have the best chance of winning the election. The Republicans have an **elephant** as their symbol, the Democrats a **donkey**. There are other parties too, but they hardly ever win any electoral votes.

The people do not elect the president directly. Each state has a certain number of **electors**, depending on its population. In most states the winner gets **all the electors** of that state. There are **538** electors in total. Whoever has more than half, at least **270**, wins. That is why someone can win fewer votes nationwide and still win.

gewusst: Tuesday was chosen in the past so that farmers had enough time after Sunday to travel to the polling station.
The capital, Washington D.C., also has three electors, even though it is not a state.

teile.einleitung: A passport is an identity document that allows you to travel to other countries. It shows who you are and what nationality you have. The Swiss passport also has its special features.
wichtigste: The Swiss passport is red and bears the white Swiss cross.
For adults it is valid for 10 years, for children and young people under 18 for 5 years.
Every child needs their own identity document for travelling abroad.
A chip stores the passport photo, among other things.
You apply for a passport at your canton's passport office.
For the USA an identity card is not enough; you need a passport.

abschnitte.text: At the border, the passport shows who you are and which country you come from. It contains your name, date of birth, nationality and a photo. Some countries also require a **visa**. This is **permission to enter**, which is often stuck into the passport or issued electronically. For many European countries, Swiss citizens only need their **identity card**, but for the **USA** you need a passport.

The Swiss passport has a **red cover** with the **white cross**, the symbol of Switzerland. For adults aged 18 and over it is valid for **10 years**. For children and young people it is only valid for **5 years**, because their appearance changes more quickly. Every child needs **their own identity document**; children can no longer be entered in their parents' passport.

The Swiss passport contains a **chip**. The data from the passport and the **passport photo** are stored on it. For people aged 12 and over, **fingerprints** are added. Thanks to the chip the passport is hard to forge, and at some airports it can be checked at machines.

You apply for a new passport at the **passport office** or identity document centre of your **canton**. First you register, often online. At the passport office a photo and fingerprints are taken. The finished passport then arrives by post. Anyone planning to travel should check early enough whether their passport is still valid.

Besides the normal passport there are special passports. **Diplomats** receive a **diplomatic passport** for their work abroad, which shows their role. For other people working for the state there is the **service passport**. These passports are also red in Switzerland.

gewusst: Since 2022 Switzerland has issued a newly designed passport with pictures of Swiss landscapes.
A diplomatic passport makes work easier, but it does not replace accreditation by the host country.

teile.einleitung: Mercosur is an association of countries in South America. It is meant to make trade between its members easier. The name means “Common Market of the South”.
wichtigste: Mercosur was founded in 1991 with the Treaty of Asunción.
Its founders were Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Venezuela has been suspended since 2016.
Bolivia became a full member in 2024.
Chile is only an associate member.
The main languages are Spanish and Portuguese.
Brazil has the largest economy in Mercosur.

abschnitte.text: **Mercosur** is short for **Mercado Común del Sur**. “Mercado” means market, “común” common and “sur” south. In Portuguese the organisation is called **Mercosul**. The aim is for goods, services and people to cross borders more easily. The secretariat is based in **Montevideo**, the capital of Uruguay.

On 26 March 1991, **Argentina**, **Brazil**, **Paraguay** and **Uruguay** signed the **Treaty of Asunción**. It is named after the capital of Paraguay, where it was signed. In 1994 the **Protocol of Ouro Preto** followed. It gave Mercosur its own **legal personality** and set up its bodies. From 1995 there was also a **customs union** with a common **external tariff** towards other countries.

**Venezuela** became a member in 2012 but was **suspended** in December 2016 because it did not keep to the bloc's rules. **Bolivia** signed the accession protocol in 2015 and became a full member in 2024. This means Mercosur has five active full members. **Chile** and other South American countries are only **associate members**. They cooperate, but they are not part of the customs union.

In **Brazil** people speak **Portuguese**, in the other member countries mainly **Spanish**. In Paraguay the indigenous language **Guaraní** is also widely spoken. Brazil is the largest country in South America by area and by population. Its economy is bigger than those of all the other members put together. Important exports of Mercosur include soya, meat and ore.

Mercosur also negotiates **free trade** with other parts of the world. **EFTA**, to which Switzerland belongs, concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement with Mercosur in 2025. The **European Union** also negotiated such an agreement for many years. In Europe this is controversial: supporters expect more trade, while critics worry about farming and the rainforest.

gewusst: Mercosur's founding treaty is named after Asunción, the capital of Paraguay.
Brazil is so large that it borders almost all the other countries of South America.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit, SHA for short, sends Swiss experts to countries affected by disasters or crises. Its members help, for example, after earthquakes, floods or in war zones.
wichtigste: The SHA was founded in 1973.
It used to be called the Swiss Disaster Relief Unit.
It has about 700 experts ready for deployment.
It is a militia unit: its members have other jobs.
The SHA is part of the FDFA and carries out SDC projects.
It is divided into 11 specialist groups.

abschnitte.text: The unit was founded in **1973**. It was originally called the **Swiss Disaster Relief Unit**. Later it was renamed the **Humanitarian Aid Unit**. This showed that it helps not only in natural disasters but also in crises and conflicts. Today it is one of the most important tools Switzerland uses to help abroad.

The SHA comes under the **Federal Department of Foreign Affairs**, **FDFA** for short. It mainly carries out projects of the **Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation** (SDC). It helps wherever the federal government provides humanitarian aid. The SHA also makes experts available to **UN organisations** such as the World Food Programme. Such postings are called **secondments**.

About **700** experts are on standby in the SHA. The SHA is a **militia unit**. This means that its members normally work in their own jobs, for example as doctors, engineers or logistics specialists. When a disaster strikes, they are **called up** for a mission. This way Switzerland can send suitable experts abroad at short notice.

The SHA is divided into **11 specialist groups**. They range from **logistics** and **construction** to **health** and **rescue**, and on to security, information and protection. An important group is **water, sanitation and hygiene**. Clean water is especially important after disasters, so that diseases do not spread. The right experts are chosen for each mission.

gewusst: In everyday life the members of the SHA work in quite ordinary jobs and only travel abroad for missions.
The unit has existed for more than 50 years.

teile.einleitung: Nuclear sharing is part of NATO's deterrence. The USA stores nuclear weapons in some European countries. In an emergency, aircraft of these host countries could use them, but only with the USA's approval.
wichtigste: Nuclear sharing involves American B61 aircraft bombs.
In Germany, Büchel air base is regarded as a storage site.
Further storage sites are thought to be in Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Turkey.
In peacetime the USA controls the weapons.
Germany wants to replace the Tornado with the F-35A fighter jet.
NATO's Nuclear Planning Group advises on nuclear policy.

abschnitte.text: Only a few NATO countries have their own nuclear weapons. With **nuclear sharing**, other members are also involved in deterrence. For this, the USA stores free-falling **B61** nuclear bombs in some European countries. In an emergency, aircraft of the **host countries** would deliver the bombs to their target. This way several countries share responsibility and risk.

In Germany, **Büchel air base** in Rhineland-Palatinate is regarded as a storage site. According to public estimates there are other stores in Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Turkey. Places such as Kleine Brogel, Volkel, Aviano, Ghedi and Incirlik are mentioned. The governments do not officially confirm this. But they do not deny it either.

In peacetime the weapons remain under the guard of **American soldiers**. The USA also holds the codes to arm them. Only after approval by the **US President** and with NATO's consent could pilots of the host countries use them. Nuclear policy is discussed by the **Nuclear Planning Group**. It was set up in the 1960s, and France is the only member that does not take part.

In Germany this task has so far been carried out by the **Tornado**. It is outdated and has to be replaced. In 2022 the German government decided to buy **F-35A** jets from the USA for this. Every year NATO practises the procedures in the exercise **Steadfast Noon**, without real warheads. For some years NATO has been informing the public about this exercise.

gewusst: No real nuclear weapons are ever carried during the Steadfast Noon exercise.
France has its own nuclear weapons but does not take part in the Nuclear Planning Group.

teile.einleitung: Multilateralism means that many countries work together and keep to common rules. Instead of each country acting alone, they solve problems such as climate change, diseases or wars together. The United Nations in New York and Geneva is the best-known example.
