wichtigste: Multilateralism is cooperation between many countries according to common rules.
The word comes from the Latin “multi” for many and “latus” for side.
The most important example is the UN, founded in 1945.
The opposite is unilateralism, where one country acts alone.
Geneva is one of the most important centres of multilateral cooperation.
Switzerland joined the UN in 2002 after a popular vote.
Small countries benefit especially, because the rules apply to everyone.

abschnitte.text: In **multilateralism**, three or more countries work together according to rules they have agreed on jointly. When only two countries make a treaty, this is called **bilateralism**. When a country acts entirely alone without regard for others, this is called **unilateralism**. The basic idea is that many problems do not stop at national borders. Air pollution, epidemics or movements of refugees affect many countries at once.

After the First World War, the **League of Nations** was founded in 1920, based in Geneva, to prevent wars. However, it failed because important countries were missing and it could not prevent the Second World War. So in 1945 the **United Nations**, the UN for short, was set up with its headquarters in New York. Today 193 countries belong to it. In the General Assembly each country has one vote, whether it is large or small.

Besides the UN there are many other multilateral organisations. The **World Health Organization** (WHO) looks after health and is based in Geneva. The World Trade Organization (WTO), also in Geneva, sets rules for international trade. Agreements such as the Paris Agreement on climate protection are also multilateral treaties.

Switzerland only joined the UN on 3 March 2002 after a popular vote, as one of the last countries to do so. The UN's European headquarters is in Geneva, in the **Palais des Nations**. In addition there are dozens of international organisations, for example the International Committee of the Red Cross. For 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a member of the UN Security Council for the first time. As a neutral country it works especially for international law and peace talks.

A big advantage is that common rules prevent disputes and also protect small countries. It is not the strongest who wins, but what has been agreed. However, negotiations between many countries often take a long time, and sometimes they only agree on small steps. In addition, in the UN **Security Council** five permanent members can block decisions with their veto.

begriffe.erklaerung: Between two sides, for example a treaty between two countries.
The rules that apply between countries, for example treaties and the ban on wars of aggression.
The right to stop a decision on your own.
The assembly of the UN in which all member states are represented.

gewusst: With its many international organisations and missions, Geneva is regarded as one of the largest centres of diplomacy in the world.
Switzerland worked in many UN organisations long before it joined.
The USA was missing from the League of Nations, even though its president Woodrow Wilson had strongly promoted the idea.

teile.einleitung: A prince is a member of a royal or princely family. Usually he is the son or grandson of a king, a queen or a reigning prince.
wichtigste: The son of a king or queen is a prince.
A crown prince is meant to become king later.
Prince William has been Prince of Wales since 2022.
His sons are called George and Louis.
Prince Harry has lived in the USA with his family since 2020.
The husband of a reigning queen is often called the prince consort.

abschnitte.text: A **prince** belongs to a **royal family** or a princely family. Usually he is the **son** of a king or a queen. The word comes from the Latin **“princeps”**, which means “the first”. The prince who is next in line to become king is called the **crown prince**. He will wear the crown later.

The eldest son of King **Charles III** is **Prince William**. Since 2022 he has held the title **“Prince of Wales”**, which is traditionally given to the heir to the British throne. William's eldest son **George** was born in London in 2013, and his youngest son **Louis** in 2018. William's brother **Prince Harry** moved with his family to **California** in the USA in 2020. He no longer works for the royal family.

When a woman is the reigning **queen**, her husband usually does not become king. He is often called the **prince consort**. He accompanies and supports her but does not rule himself. A well-known example is **Prince Philip**. He was Queen Elizabeth II's husband for more than 70 years.

Right next to Switzerland lies the **Principality of Liechtenstein**. There the head of state is a **prince**. His son and successor holds the title of **Hereditary Prince**. Since 2004 Hereditary Prince **Alois** has carried out many of the prince's duties. Monaco also has a ruling prince, called “Prince” in French.

gewusst: Princes appear in many fairy tales, such as “The Frog Prince” or “Sleeping Beauty”.
The title “Prince of Wales” has been given for more than 700 years.

teile.einleitung: Russia is the largest country in the world by area. It stretches from Europe to the Pacific and is so huge that it has many time zones.
wichtigste: With about 17 million square kilometres, Russia is the largest country on Earth.
The capital is Moscow.
Russia lies in Europe and Asia, with the Urals forming the border.
The country has 11 time zones.
The flag has the colours white, blue and red.
The Trans-Siberian Railway runs from Moscow to Vladivostok.

abschnitte.text: Russia covers about **17 million square kilometres**, which makes it the **largest country on Earth**. It is almost as big as the whole of South America. Switzerland has about 41,000 square kilometres, so it would fit into Russia **more than 400 times**. Russia is so wide from west to east that it has **11 time zones**. When it is evening in Moscow, it is already the next morning in the east.

Russia lies in **Europe and Asia**. The **Ural** mountains run through the country from north to south and are regarded as the border between the continents. To the west lies Europe, to the east Asia. About a quarter of the area lies in Europe, but most people live there. The large Asian part is called **Siberia** and is very cold in winter.

The capital and largest city is **Moscow**. **St Petersburg** used to be the capital. In the middle of Moscow stands the **Kremlin**, an old fortress with walls, towers, churches and palaces. The Russian president has his official seat there. Next to it is the famous **Red Square**.

The **Trans-Siberian Railway** runs from Moscow to **Vladivostok** on the Pacific. The route is **more than 9000 kilometres** long and one of the longest railway lines in the world. The train takes about a week for the whole journey. On the way it crosses many large rivers and runs along Lake Baikal.

Russia's **flag** has three horizontal stripes: **white** at the top, **blue** in the middle and **red** at the bottom. Russia has huge forests, the **taiga**, and in the north the treeless **tundra**. The **Volga** is the longest river in Europe. **Lake Baikal** in Siberia holds more fresh water than any other lake in the world.

gewusst: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth.
A journey on the Trans-Siberian Railway passes through seven time zones.

teile.einleitung: The Secretariat is the administration of the United Nations. It is one of the UN's principal organs and is led by the Secretary-General. Its staff work in New York, Geneva, Vienna and many other places.
wichtigste: According to Article 97 of the Charter, the Secretary-General is the UN's chief administrative officer.
Under Article 99 he may draw the Security Council's attention to threats to peace.
The staff may not accept instructions from governments.
The headquarters stands in New York, and Le Corbusier was involved in its design.
The office in Geneva is led by a Director-General.
OCHA coordinates humanitarian aid worldwide.

abschnitte.text: At the head of the Secretariat is the **Secretary-General**. According to **Article 97** of the Charter, he is the organisation's **chief administrative officer**. He leads the Secretariat but has no power to give orders to countries. Under **Article 99** he may bring to the attention of the **Security Council** any matter which in his opinion threatens world peace. António Guterres has been Secretary-General since 2017, and his deputy is **Amina Mohammed** from Nigeria (as of 2026).

**Article 100** of the Charter requires the staff to be **independent**. The staff may not seek or accept instructions from **governments**. They work for the whole world and not for their home country. For official travel they receive their own travel document, the **laissez-passer**. Many countries recognise it like a passport.

The UN **headquarters** stands in **New York** on the East River. In 1947 it was designed by an international team of architects led by Wallace Harrison. The team included **Le Corbusier**, who was born in **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. The Secretariat tower block was completed in 1952. It is still one of the best-known buildings in the city.

The Secretariat also has large offices outside New York. The **United Nations Office at Geneva** is led by a **Director-General**. In **Vienna** there is the Vienna International Centre on the Danube, opened in 1979. People call it **UNO City**. **OCHA** coordinates humanitarian aid in disasters and, besides New York, has an important office in Geneva.

Since the UN was founded in 1945, there have been several Secretaries-General from different regions of the world. **U Thant** from Burma, today's Myanmar, led the UN from 1961 to 1971. He took over the post after the death of his predecessor Dag Hammarskjöld. U Thant was the **first Secretary-General from Asia**.

gewusst: UN staff may not accept orders from their own government.
The architect Le Corbusier from La Chaux-de-Fonds was involved in designing the UN headquarters.

teile.einleitung: With a sponsorship you regularly support a child, a village, a project or even an animal. Many aid organisations and zoos offer sponsorships so that they can plan for the long term.
wichtigste: With a sponsorship you donate money regularly.
Usually you pay a fixed amount every month.
A person who takes on a sponsorship is called a sponsor.
Regular help allows the aid organisation to plan further ahead.
Sponsors often receive reports and photos.
Before taking on a sponsorship, you check whether the aid organisation is trustworthy.

abschnitte.text: With a **sponsorship** you promise to support a child, a village or a project over a longer period. Usually you pay a fixed amount **every month**. The person who does this is called a **sponsor**. The German word for it, “Patenschaft”, originally comes from the church: at a baptism, a godparent takes on responsibility for a child. In Switzerland godparents are also called **“Götti”** (godfather) and **“Gotte”** (godmother).

When money comes in every month, an **aid organisation** knows what it can count on. This lets it plan projects over **several years**, for example building a school or running a well. Many aid organisations send sponsors **reports, letters or photos**. This way the sponsors see what happens with their money.

In the past, a **child sponsorship** often supported just one child. Today many aid organisations use the money to help the child's **whole village**. This way all the children there benefit, for example from clean water or a better school. In Switzerland there are also sponsorships for **mountain municipalities** that need money for important projects.

Many **zoos** and animal protection organisations offer **animal sponsorships**. The money helps pay for food and care. Before taking on a sponsorship, you should check whether the aid organisation is **trustworthy**. In Switzerland the **Zewo** quality seal helps with this. It shows that an organisation handles donations carefully.

gewusst: In Switzerland there has been a sponsorship scheme for mountain municipalities since 1940.
School classes sometimes take on an animal sponsorship together.

teile.einleitung: A coronation is a solemn ceremony in which a new king or queen has the crown placed on their head. It shows everyone that the country now has a new head. Coronations in Great Britain are especially well known.
wichtigste: At a coronation, the crown is ceremonially placed on a new ruler's head.
British kings and queens have been crowned in Westminster Abbey in London for almost 1000 years.
The Archbishop of Canterbury places the crown on the British king's head.
King Charles III was crowned on 6 May 2023.
The king travels to the coronation in a magnificent horse-drawn coach.
Afterwards the royal family waves from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.
The coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953 was broadcast on television.

abschnitte.text: A **coronation** is the solemn start of the reign of a king or queen. The **crown** is a sign of power and dignity. Other symbols often go with it, for example a **sceptre** (a decorated rod) and an **orb** (a ball with a cross). In the past many people believed that a king received his power from God. That is why coronations usually took place in a church.

In Great Britain, coronations take place in **Westminster Abbey**, a large, old church in London. The ceremony is led by the **Archbishop of Canterbury**, the senior clergyman of the Church of England. The king sits on an ancient coronation chair. He takes an oath and promises to serve the country. A particularly solemn moment is the **anointing** with holy oil. Only after that is the crown placed on his head.

The king travels to the coronation in a magnificent **coach** pulled by horses. Soldiers in colourful uniforms accompany the procession through the streets. Many people line the roads and cheer. After the ceremony the royal family appears on the **balcony of Buckingham Palace**. Thousands of people wait below and wave back.

Queen **Elizabeth II** was crowned on 2 June 1953. Her coronation was broadcast on **television**, and millions of people watched. Many families bought a television set especially for it. Her son **Charles III** was crowned on 6 May 2023. His wife Camilla was crowned queen together with him.

Not all monarchies crown their rulers. In Spain, Denmark or the Netherlands there is no longer a coronation; there the new king takes office with a ceremony or an oath. In the Middle Ages emperors were crowned too: **Charlemagne** was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome in the year 800. Switzerland is a republic and has no king, so there are no coronations here.

gewusst: In 1804 in Paris, Napoleon placed the imperial crown on his own head, even though the Pope was present.
The British Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London and can be visited.

tfq20sz.t: Switzerland on the UN Security Council

teile.einleitung: In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland sat on the UN Security Council for the first time. This body is responsible for peace and security in the world. Switzerland was one of its ten non-permanent members.
wichtigste: The Security Council is meant to maintain world peace and international security.
The General Assembly elects the non-permanent members for two years.
Switzerland was elected in June 2022 with 187 votes, together with Malta.
Its motto was “A plus for peace”.
Switzerland had no veto.
Ambassador Pascale Baeriswyl represented Switzerland in New York.

abschnitte.titel: What does the Security Council do?
abschnitte.text: Under the **UN Charter**, the Security Council has the main responsibility for **world peace** and international security. It can, for example, decide on **sanctions** or **peace missions**. The Council has 15 members. Five of them are permanent: China, France, Great Britain, Russia and the USA. The other ten are **non-permanent members**.

The non-permanent members are elected by the **General Assembly**, in which every UN state has one vote. Every year five of the ten seats are filled anew. Members are elected for **two years**, and immediate re-election is not possible. On 9 June 2022 Switzerland received **187 votes**; a two-thirds majority was needed. At the same time **Malta** was elected for the group of Western European and other states.

Switzerland stood with the motto **“A plus for peace”**. It refers to the cross on the Swiss flag, which looks like a plus sign. Switzerland wanted to work especially for peace, the protection of civilians and the climate. Before the candidacy there was also debate in Switzerland about whether a seat fits with **neutrality**.

Only the five permanent members can block decisions with a **veto**. As a non-permanent member, Switzerland voted normally. In New York, Ambassador **Pascale Baeriswyl** represented Switzerland. She headed Switzerland's Permanent Mission to the UN and spoke for Switzerland in the Council. Important decisions were agreed with the Federal Council in Bern.

The presidency of the Security Council changes every month. Switzerland held it in May 2023 and in **October 2024**. In October 2024 President of the Confederation **Viola Amherd** chaired the annual debate on women, peace and security. Federal Councillor **Ignazio Cassis** chaired a meeting on scientific and technological developments.

gewusst: Switzerland has only been a UN member since 2002, and just over twenty years later it was already sitting on the Security Council.
The presidency rotates every month in the alphabetical order of the countries' names in English.

teile.einleitung: There are still about a dozen monarchies in Europe today. In them a king, a queen or a prince is at the head of the state. Almost everywhere, parliament holds the real power.
wichtigste: Liechtenstein, our neighbour, is a principality.
Felipe VI has been King of Spain since 2014.
Frederik X has been King of Denmark since January 2024.
Since August 2026 Haakon VIII has been King of Norway.
Philippe has been King of the Belgians since 2013.
Willem-Alexander has been King of the Netherlands since 2013.
Sweden has a king; Germany, Italy and Austria are republics.

abschnitte.text: The kingdoms in Europe are **Belgium**, **Denmark**, the **Netherlands**, **Norway**, **Sweden**, **Spain** and the **United Kingdom**. In addition there are the principalities of **Liechtenstein** and **Monaco** and the Grand Duchy of **Luxembourg**. **Andorra** and **Vatican City** also have a special form of monarchy. Our neighbouring countries **Germany**, **Italy**, **France** and **Austria**, on the other hand, are republics. Almost all monarchies in Europe are **parliamentary monarchies**.

**Felipe VI** has been King of **Spain** since 2014. He succeeded his father **Juan Carlos**, who abdicated. **Philippe** has been King of the **Belgians** since 2013. His title is deliberately “King of the Belgians” and not “King of Belgium”. Belgium lies between France and the Netherlands.

**Willem-Alexander** has been King of the **Netherlands** since 2013. He succeeded his mother Beatrix, who abdicated. He lives in **The Hague**, where the government and parliament also sit. The royal family is called the **House of Orange**. That is why on **King's Day** on 27 April many people wear **orange** clothes and celebrate in the streets.

In **Sweden**, **Carl XVI Gustaf** has been king since 1973. **Frederik X** became King of **Denmark** in January 2024, after his mother Margrethe II abdicated. In **Norway**, King **Harald V** died in August 2026. His son **Haakon** became the new king and is now called **Haakon VIII**. In all three countries the king mainly has ceremonial duties.

Switzerland's neighbour with a prince is **Liechtenstein**. It lies between Switzerland and Austria. Unlike in most monarchies, the prince there still has quite a lot of political power. **Monaco** on the Mediterranean is also a principality, ruled by the Grimaldi family. And in **Luxembourg** a **Grand Duke** is at the head of the state.

gewusst: In Sweden, since 1980, the eldest child becomes heir to the throne, whether a girl or a boy.
Andorra has two heads of state: the French president and a Spanish bishop.

teile.einleitung: A princess is a female member of a royal or princely family. Usually she is the daughter of a king or the wife of a prince.
wichtigste: The daughter of a king or queen is a princess.
The wife of a prince is also often called a princess.
The daughter of Prince William and Catherine is called Charlotte.
Princess Diana died in a car accident in Paris in 1997.
Princess Anne has held the title “Princess Royal” since 1987.
Prince Harry's daughter is called Lilibet.

abschnitte.text: A **princess** belongs to a **royal family** or a princely family. Usually she is the **daughter** of a king or a queen. When a prince marries, his wife is often also called a **princess**. If the prince later becomes king, she is called **queen**. A princess who is meant to become queen herself one day is called a **crown princess**, like Victoria in Sweden.

**Princess Charlotte** is the daughter of Prince William and Catherine. She was born in London in 2015. Prince Harry also has a daughter: **Lilibet**, born in 2021. Her name comes from Queen Elizabeth II's **pet name**. The eldest daughter of a British king or queen can be given the honorary title **“Princess Royal”**.

**Princess Anne** is the sister of King Charles III. She has held the title **“Princess Royal”** since 1987. She was a very good **horse rider**. In 1976 she even took part in the **Olympic Games** in Montreal. She is regarded as one of the hardest-working members of the royal family and attends many events every year.

**Princess Diana** was Charles's first wife and the mother of William and Harry. She worked for the sick and the poor and drew attention to the suffering caused by **landmines**. In 1997 she died in a **car accident** in Paris. People all over the world mourned her. Many called her the **“People's Princess”**.

gewusst: Princess Anne's daughter Zara Tindall also became a rider and won a silver medal at the 2012 Olympic Games.
In Spain, Princess Leonor is expected to become queen one day.

teile.einleitung: Arms control means that countries agree in treaties which weapons, and how many, they may possess. This is meant to make wars less likely and build trust between countries.
wichtigste: Arms control aims to limit weapons and make them verifiable.
The INF Treaty of 1987 banned land-based intermediate-range missiles.
With New START, the USA and Russia limited their strategic nuclear warheads from 2010.
The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 bans biological weapons.
The Conference on Disarmament meets in Geneva.
Switzerland has not signed the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons of 2017.

abschnitte.text: In **arms control**, countries conclude **treaties** on weapons. They lay down how many weapons are allowed or which are banned altogether. **Verification** is also important: inspectors check whether everyone is keeping to the rules. This builds **trust**. The **Conference on Disarmament** in **Geneva** is the most important forum for such negotiations.

In 1987 **Ronald Reagan** and **Mikhail Gorbachev** signed the **INF Treaty** in Washington. It banned land-based **intermediate-range missiles** with a range of 500 to 5500 kilometres. In 2019 the USA withdrew and the treaty ended. In 2010 the **USA and Russia** concluded the **New START** treaty. It limited their strategic **nuclear warheads**; in 2023 Russia suspended its participation.

The **Biological Weapons Convention** was signed in **1972** and came into force in 1975. Bans on chemical weapons and landmines followed later. The **Convention on Cluster Munitions** was negotiated in Dublin in May 2008 and signed in **Oslo** in December 2008. The **Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons** of 2017 came into force in 2021; Switzerland has not signed it so far.

The **Treaty on Open Skies** allowed unarmed **observation flights** over other states parties. This allowed countries to keep an eye on military activities. The UN **Arms Trade Treaty** of **2013** regulates the international trade in **conventional weapons** such as tanks or rifles. Conventional means: not nuclear, biological or chemical weapons. Its secretariat is in **Geneva**.

gewusst: Geneva is a centre of disarmament: the Conference on Disarmament and the secretariat of the Arms Trade Treaty are based there.
With the INF Treaty, a whole category of nuclear missiles was completely abolished for the first time.

teile.einleitung: The Kurds are a people with their own language and culture who live in the Middle East. They are often described as the largest people without a state of their own. The Kurdish conflict is about their rights, their self-government and the question of a state of their own.
wichtigste: The area where Kurds live lies mainly in Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria.
Most Kurds live in Turkey.
The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 made no provision for a Kurdish state.
Abdullah Öcalan founded the PKK in 1978, which fought against the Turkish state from 1984.
In northern Iraq there is an Autonomous Kurdistan Region with its capital Erbil.
In 1988 the town of Halabja was attacked with poison gas.
In May 2025 the PKK announced that it would dissolve.

abschnitte.text: The area where many Kurds live is called **Kurdistan**. It is not a state; it stretches across **Turkey**, **Iraq**, **Iran** and **Syria**. The Kurds speak **Kurdish** and have their own traditions. An important festival is **Newroz**, the New Year festival in spring. Many Kurds now also live in Europe, including Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Treaties after the First World War
abschnitte.text: After the First World War, the Ottoman Empire broke apart. The **Treaty of Sèvres** of 1920 still held out the prospect of self-government for the Kurds. But it was never put into effect. In 1923 it was replaced by the **Treaty of Lausanne**, which was signed in the Swiss city of Lausanne. It fixed the borders of present-day Turkey and no longer mentioned a Kurdish state.

In Turkey, Kurds were for a long time not allowed to use their language freely. In 1978 **Abdullah Öcalan** founded the **Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK)**. From 1984 it waged an armed struggle against the Turkish state in which many people died. Turkey, the EU and the USA classify the PKK as a terrorist organisation. Öcalan was captured in Kenya in 1999 and has been held on the prison island of İmralı ever since. In May 2025, following his call, the PKK announced its **dissolution** and the end of its armed struggle.

Under the dictator **Saddam Hussein**, the Kurds in Iraq were severely persecuted. In the **poison gas attack on Halabja** in March 1988, several thousand civilians died. Today northern Iraq has the **Autonomous Kurdistan Region** with its own government and parliament in **Erbil**. Its self-government is set out in the Iraqi constitution of 2005. In a **referendum** in September 2017, more than 90 per cent voted for independence. The Iraqi government and most countries rejected the result, and it was not put into effect.

In the **Syrian civil war**, Kurdish groups took control of areas in the north of the country. There they also fought against the terrorist militia “Islamic State”. Many Kurds also live in **Iran**, mainly in the west of the country. There too, Kurdish groups are demanding more rights. The governments of the countries concerned, on the other hand, want to preserve their borders and their unity.

gewusst: The borders of present-day Turkey were fixed in Switzerland in 1923, in the Treaty of Lausanne.
The Kurdish New Year festival Newroz is celebrated on 21 March, at the start of spring.

thxoj6q.t: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development

teile.einleitung: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD for short, is an association of countries that promotes economic growth. Its members share experience and look together for good solutions for the economy, education and the environment. Many pupils know the OECD from the PISA study.
wichtigste: The OECD is an association of countries that promotes the economy.
It was founded in 1961 and is based in Paris.
Its predecessor was the OEEC, which from 1948 organised the rebuilding of Europe after the Second World War.
The OECD has 38 member countries (as of 2025).
Switzerland has been a member since it was founded.
The OECD collects data, compares countries and makes recommendations.
The OECD's PISA study compares the performance of 15-year-olds worldwide.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Europe was in ruins. Reconstruction was organised with money from the USA, the **Marshall Plan**, and the OEEC was set up for this in 1948. In 1961 it became the **OECD**, which now also included the USA and Canada. Its headquarters is the Château de la Muette in Paris.

Today 38 countries belong to the OECD (as of 2025). They include most European countries, the USA, Canada, Japan, Australia, Mexico and Chile. They are mainly wealthy countries with a **democracy** and a market economy. Other countries are applying for membership.

The OECD is a kind of think tank for governments. Its experts collect **statistics** on the economy, taxes, work, health and the environment. They compare the countries with one another and show what works well. The recommendations are usually not binding, but they carry great weight.

Since 2000 the OECD has regularly carried out the **PISA study**. In it, 15-year-olds in many countries solve tasks in reading, maths and science. The results show how well the school systems compare. Switzerland usually does better than average in maths.

In 1961 Switzerland was one of the founding members. A well-known example of the OECD's work is the worldwide **minimum tax** of 15 per cent for large companies. In 2023 Swiss voters approved a proposal to put this minimum tax into practice. The OECD also regularly examines the Swiss economy and writes reports on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Collected figures that measure something and make it comparable.
An aid programme of the USA that financed the rebuilding of Europe after 1948.
A type of economy in which supply and demand set the prices.
A tax that large companies must pay at least in all the countries taking part.

gewusst: The OECD publishes thousands of reports and data collections every year.
The word PISA stands for “Programme for International Student Assessment”.

teile.einleitung: The Pacific Islands Forum is an organisation of the countries of the South Pacific. Its members work together to tackle shared problems such as climate change, security and the economy of their islands.
wichtigste: The forum was founded in Wellington in 1971 as the South Pacific Forum.
Since 2000 it has been called the Pacific Islands Forum.
Its secretariat is in Suva, the capital of Fiji.
Besides many island states, Australia and New Zealand are also members.
The Boe Declaration of 2018 calls climate change the greatest threat to the region.
The Treaty of Rarotonga of 1985 makes the South Pacific a nuclear-weapon-free zone.

abschnitte.text: In the Pacific there are many small **island states**, such as Fiji, Samoa, Tonga or Kiribati. They are far apart from one another and often have few inhabitants. Together they carry more weight in the world. So in 1971 they founded the **South Pacific Forum** in **Wellington** in New Zealand. In 2000 it was given its present name. The **secretariat** is in **Suva** in Fiji.

Besides the island states, **Australia and New Zealand** have been members since it was founded. They pay a large part of the budget. The heads of state and government meet every year for a summit. Sometimes there are disputes: **Kiribati** left in 2022 because of a dispute over the post of Secretary General. After mediation it returned in 2023.

abschnitte.titel: Climate change as the greatest worry
abschnitte.text: Many islands lie only a little above sea level. If the sea rises, houses, fields and drinking water are in danger. In the **Boe Declaration**, adopted in Nauru in 2018, the forum declared **climate change** the single greatest threat to the security and livelihoods of the region. That is why the members work together at international climate conferences for more climate protection.

In the **Treaty of Rarotonga** of 1985, the South Pacific became a **nuclear-weapon-free zone**. Possessing, stationing and testing nuclear weapons are banned there. One reason was the French nuclear tests in Polynesia. After unrest in the **Solomon Islands**, members of the forum sent a mission led by Australia from 2003. It was meant to restore law and order and lasted until 2017.

gewusst: The territory of the member states covers huge areas of sea but only a little land.
The mission to the Solomon Islands was known by the abbreviation RAMSI.

teile.einleitung: The Nuremberg trials were court proceedings against leading figures of Nazi Germany after the Second World War. For the first time, senior politicians and military leaders had to answer before an international court. The trials have shaped international law to this day.
wichtigste: The main trial began on 20 November 1945 in the Nuremberg Palace of Justice.
The court was made up of the USA, Great Britain, the Soviet Union and France.
Its basis was the London Charter.
The chief prosecutor for the USA was Robert H. Jackson.
Twelve defendants were sentenced to death and three were acquitted.
The Nuremberg Principles state that acting on orders does not free anyone from punishment.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, the victorious powers wanted to put those mainly responsible on trial. The **USA**, **Great Britain**, the **Soviet Union** and **France** formed the **International Military Tribunal**. Each power provided a chief judge and a deputy as well as its own prosecutors. In the **London Agreement** they agreed on the charter of the court. It laid down which crimes would be charged and how the proceedings would run.

The main trial opened on **20 November 1945**. It took place in courtroom 600 of the **Nuremberg Palace of Justice**. The chief prosecutor for the USA was **Robert H. Jackson**, a judge of the US Supreme Court. For Great Britain, Hartley Shawcross led the prosecution. The charges included war crimes and crimes against humanity.

In October 1946 the verdicts were delivered. **Twelve** defendants were sentenced to death, one of them in his absence. Three were acquitted, and the rest received prison sentences. **Hermann Göring** escaped execution by taking his own life in his cell the night before the executions. How he obtained the poison has still not been fully explained.

After the main trial there were further proceedings in Nuremberg. In the **Doctors' Trial**, doctors were convicted who had carried out criminal experiments on people in concentration camps. This led in 1947 to the **Nuremberg Code**. It sets out ethical rules for experiments on humans. An important rule is the voluntary and informed consent of the person being tested.

The principles of the trials were set down in the **Nuremberg Principles**. Anyone who commits a crime under international law on **orders** is still responsible. At most, the order can reduce the punishment. Even high-ranking officials can be punished. These ideas are the basis for later courts such as the International Criminal Court.

gewusst: Courtroom 600 in Nuremberg can be visited today as a memorial site.
The trials were interpreted simultaneously into several languages, which was a technical innovation at the time.

teile.einleitung: With the cohesion contribution, Switzerland supports poorer member states of the EU. The money goes into projects meant to reduce differences within Europe. It used to be called the enlargement contribution.
wichtigste: Its basis is the Eastern Europe Cooperation Act, accepted in 2006 with about 53 per cent.
The first contribution came to about 1.3 billion francs in total.
Poland received the largest share.
The SDC and SECO carry out the projects.
The money goes into projects, not into the EU budget.
The Switzerland-EU package plans 350 million francs per year for 2030 to 2036.

abschnitte.text: **Cohesion** means holding together. In the EU there are richer and poorer regions. Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it has access to its **single market**. With the contribution it helps to reduce the **economic and social differences** in Europe. This also strengthens its relations with the EU.

The basis is the **Federal Act on Cooperation with the States of Eastern Europe**, known as the Eastern Europe Cooperation Act. A **referendum** was launched against it. On **26 November 2006** the people accepted the act with **53.4 per cent** voting yes. This allowed Switzerland to make the contribution.

At first **1 billion francs** was planned for the ten countries that had joined the EU in **2004**. Later, contributions for **Bulgaria**, **Romania** and **Croatia** were added. In total it came to about **1.3 billion francs**. **Poland**, the new member with the largest population, received the biggest share. Projects in transport, the environment and research, for example, were supported.

Switzerland does **not pay the contribution into the EU budget**. It funds **specific projects** that it agrees on with the partner countries. The **Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation** (SDC) and the **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs** (SECO) look after them. For the part on migration, the State Secretariat for Migration is also involved.

In the **Switzerland-EU package**, the contribution is to be made **legally binding** for the first time. It will be set for **seven years** at a time, matching the EU's financial framework. For the years **2030 to 2036**, **350 million francs per year** are planned. The package is the subject of political debate in Switzerland, as supporters and opponents judge it very differently.

gewusst: Switzerland decides together with the partner countries which projects it supports.
In the EU enlargement of 2004, Poland was the largest new member.

teile.einleitung: Every year many people from Africa and Asia try to reach Europe across the Mediterranean. Several routes are distinguished. The crossing in boats that are often overcrowded is very dangerous.
wichtigste: There is a western, a central and an eastern Mediterranean route.
The central route runs mainly from Libya and Tunisia to Italy.
The small island of Lampedusa is often the first place people arrive.
The central route is regarded as the deadliest.
The western route runs from Morocco to Spain, the eastern route from Turkey to Greece.
The border agency Frontex is based in Warsaw.
In 2022 Swiss voters approved a higher contribution to Frontex.

abschnitte.text: Three main routes across the Mediterranean are distinguished. The **western route** runs from **Morocco** to **Spain**, across the Strait of Gibraltar or to the Spanish territories of **Ceuta** and **Melilla** in North Africa. The **central route** runs from **Libya** or **Tunisia** to **Italy**. The **eastern route** runs from **Turkey** to Greek islands in the Aegean. There the distance is in places only a few kilometres.

The small Italian island of **Lampedusa** is closer to Africa than to the Italian mainland. That is why many boats arrive there. Many set off from **Libya**, where there has been great insecurity since Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011. **Smugglers** take advantage of this and demand a lot of money for the crossing. The route is long and the boats are often overcrowded. According to the **International Organization for Migration**, more people die on this route than on any other.

In October 2013 a boat capsized off Lampedusa and more than 360 people died. After that the **Italian navy** launched Operation **“Mare Nostrum”**. Within a year it rescued a great many people in distress at sea. Today private aid organisations also operate rescue ships. How sea rescue should be organised is politically disputed in Europe.

The European border agency **Frontex** was founded in 2004 and is based in **Warsaw**. It helps countries protect the **external borders of the Schengen area**. Switzerland is a member of Schengen and therefore takes part in Frontex. In May 2022 Swiss voters approved an increase in the contribution, with about **71 per cent** in favour. Supporters stressed security, while opponents criticised the way refugees are treated.

On the Greek island of **Lesbos** there was the **Moria** camp. It had been built for far fewer people, but at times more than 12,000 people lived there in cramped conditions. In September 2020 the camp burned down. The residents lost their shelter. The fire sparked debates across Europe about taking in refugees.

gewusst: Lampedusa is closer to Tunisia than to Sicily.
Between the Turkish coast and some Greek islands there are only about ten kilometres of sea.

teile.einleitung: The Ottawa Treaty is an international treaty against landmines that injure or kill people. It bans these weapons completely and obliges countries to destroy mines and clear mined areas.
wichtigste: The treaty bans the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel mines.
It was signed in December 1997 in Ottawa, the capital of Canada.
It has been in force since 1 March 1999.
Anti-tank mines and other mines aimed at vehicles are not banned.
The USA, Russia and China have not joined.
Switzerland is one of the early states parties.
The Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining is based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: An **anti-personnel mine** is an explosive charge that is usually hidden in the ground. According to the treaty, it is set off by the **presence, proximity or contact of a person**. Mines often remain dangerous for many years, long after a war has ended. That is why they often hit people who are not fighting at all, for example farmers or children at play.

Many organisations joined together in the **International Campaign to Ban Landmines**. They persuaded many governments to negotiate a ban. In December 1997 the treaty was opened for signature in **Ottawa** in Canada. It came into force on **1 March 1999**. Today well over 150 countries belong to it.

Any country that joins the treaty may never again use, produce or pass on such mines. The countries must **destroy their stockpiles** and **clear** mined areas. They are also meant to help mine victims. **Anti-tank mines**, which are intended for vehicles, are not covered.

Switzerland supported the ban from the start. In 1998 the **Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining** was founded in **Geneva**. It helps countries all over the world to find and remove mines safely. However, major military powers such as the **USA, Russia and China** have not joined the treaty. In 2025, in addition, some countries in Eastern Europe announced that they would withdraw.

gewusst: In 1997 Princess Diana walked through a minefield in Angola, drawing worldwide attention to the suffering caused by mines.
The campaign against landmines received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1997.

teile.einleitung: The territorial sea is the strip of sea directly off a country's coast. There, the sea belongs to the country almost as much as the land itself. The rules for it are set out in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
wichtigste: The territorial sea is at most 12 nautical miles wide, which is about 22 kilometres.
It is measured from the baseline, usually the low-water line along the coast.
The country has sovereignty over the water, the seabed and the airspace.
Foreign ships have the right of innocent passage.
Harbours and bays behind the baseline are internal waters.
The contiguous zone reaches up to 24 nautical miles, for example for customs and immigration.

abschnitte.text: The **territorial sea** is also called territorial waters. It reaches at most **12 nautical miles** out to sea. A nautical mile measures 1852 metres, so 12 nautical miles are about 22 kilometres. In this strip the coastal state exercises its **sovereignty**. It covers the water, the seabed, the ground beneath it and the **airspace** above it.

The territorial sea is measured from the **baseline**. The normal baseline follows the **low-water line**, the line at low tide. On very jagged coasts with many bays and islands, straight lines may be drawn between certain points. Everything on the land side of the baseline, such as harbours and bays, counts as **internal waters**. They are fully part of the country's territory.

Foreign ships may pass through the territorial sea. This is called the **right of innocent passage**. However, the ships must not disturb the peace and security of the coastal state. They are not allowed to fish or extract raw materials there. In internal waters this right of passage does not exist as a rule.

abschnitte.titel: From the cannon to 12 nautical miles
abschnitte.text: In the past the **cannon-shot rule** applied: the sea belonged to the country as far as a cannon could fire from the shore. That was about three nautical miles. Later many countries demanded wider zones. The **United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea** of 1982 set the limit at 12 nautical miles. The convention came into force in 1994.

Directly beyond the territorial sea lies the **contiguous zone**, which reaches up to 24 nautical miles. There the country may, for example, enforce customs and immigration rules and pursue smugglers. The **exclusive economic zone** reaches up to 200 nautical miles; only the coastal state may fish and use raw materials there. Beyond that begin the **high seas**, which are open to all countries.

gewusst: Although Switzerland has no sea, there are ocean-going ships under the Swiss flag with Basel as their home port.
A nautical mile is as long as one minute of arc on a meridian of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's neutrality has a long history. Officially, Switzerland has been regarded as permanently neutral since the Congress of Vienna in 1815. This stance accompanied the country through two world wars and still shapes its foreign policy today.
wichtigste: Since the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Switzerland has officially been regarded as permanently neutral.
Many see the defeat at Marignano in 1515 as the start of Switzerland's restraint in foreign wars.
The European great powers expressly recognised its neutrality in 1815.
Switzerland was spared in both world wars and did not fight.
In the Second World War the army withdrew to the Alpine fortress known as the Réduit.
For a long time neutrality was also given as a reason against joining the UN.
Today Switzerland is neutral but works in many international organisations.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages, the Confederates were feared warriors. In 1515 they lost to France at the **Battle of Marignano** in northern Italy. After that they hardly fought any more wars of conquest of their own. However, many Swiss continued to fight as paid mercenaries for foreign rulers.

After the Napoleonic Wars, Europe's rulers met in Vienna in 1814 and 1815 to reorganise Europe. At the **Congress of Vienna** and in the Treaty of Paris of November 1815, the great powers recognised Switzerland's permanent neutrality. At that time Switzerland's borders were also largely fixed as they still are today. The great powers promised not to attack Swiss territory.

In the First World War, from 1914 to 1918, the army under General Ulrich Wille guarded the borders. In the Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, Switzerland was surrounded by Germany and Italy. General **Henri Guisan** had the army withdraw into a fortress in the Alps, the **Réduit**. However, Switzerland also traded with Germany and turned refugees away at the border, which is viewed critically today.

After 1945 the West and the Eastern bloc were hostile to each other. Switzerland stayed neutral, but economically and culturally it clearly belonged to the West. Geneva became a venue for important meetings, for example in 1985 between the presidents of the USA and the Soviet Union. In 1986 the people still clearly rejected **joining the UN**.

After the end of the Cold War, Switzerland opened up more. In 1996 it joined NATO's **Partnership for Peace**, and in 2002 it became a member of the UN. In 2023 and 2024 it even sat on the UN Security Council. Neutrality still applies, but it is debated again and again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Meeting of European rulers in 1814 and 1815 to reorganise Europe after Napoleon.
The Alpine fortress into which the Swiss Army withdrew during the Second World War.
A soldier who fights for a foreign country in return for payment.
A very powerful country with great influence in the world.

gewusst: The Pontifical Swiss Guard in the Vatican is still a reminder today of the time of the Swiss mercenaries.
Napoleon occupied Switzerland around 1800 and turned it into the Helvetic Republic, before it became independent and neutral again in 1815.

teile.einleitung: A consulate is a smaller mission of a country that helps its citizens abroad. It deals with passports, emergencies and questions from people who live or travel abroad. Unlike an embassy, it is often not in the capital.
wichtigste: A consulate helps its own citizens abroad.
An embassy mainly represents a country towards the government of the host country.
Consulates issue passports and identity cards, for example.
They help in emergencies such as accidents, theft or arrest.
The rules are set out in the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations of 1963.
A consulate general is a larger consulate.
An honorary consul works for a country on a voluntary basis.

abschnitte.text: A **consulate** is an office of a country in a city abroad. It is there mainly for people, not for government politics. The person in charge is called the **consul**. Larger consulates are called consulates general. A country can have several consulates in different cities of another country.

An **embassy** is usually in the capital and represents the country towards the government. The ambassador works there. A consulate, on the other hand, deals with practical questions from citizens. An embassy often has a consular section too. Switzerland, for example, has an embassy in Rome and a consulate general in Milan.

A consulate issues **passports** and identity cards. It reports births, marriages and deaths abroad to the home country. It helps when someone has an accident, is robbed or is arrested abroad. For foreigners who want to enter the country, it often issues visas. It also supports companies and encourages contacts in culture and business.

The tasks and rights of consulates are set out in the **Vienna Convention** on Consular Relations of 1963. It says, for example, that a consulate may visit an arrested person from its country. The premises of a consulate are specially protected. The police of the host country may only enter them with permission. Consuls enjoy a certain protection, but less than diplomats in an embassy.

More than 800,000 Swiss people live abroad. For them and for travellers, the Swiss missions are important places to turn to. The foreign ministry, the FDFA, also runs a **helpline** that can be reached around the clock. Before a trip you can register with the Travel Admin app. Voluntary honorary consuls help in places where there is no embassy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who runs a consulate.
Permission to enter a foreign country.
A person who represents a country in a city on a voluntary basis.
Swiss people who live permanently in another country.

gewusst: The word consul comes from ancient Rome, where the consuls were the highest officials of the state.
Many honorary consuls are business people who work for another country alongside their job.

teile.einleitung: Reporters Without Borders is an organisation that campaigns for press freedom. It helps journalists who are threatened or persecuted because of their work.
wichtigste: Reporters Without Borders works for press freedom and the protection of journalists.
The organisation was founded in Montpellier in 1985.
Its international headquarters is in Paris.
In French it is called Reporters sans frontières, RSF for short.
Since 2002 it has published a press freedom ranking every year.
From 2017 to 2024 Norway came first every year.

abschnitte.text: **Press freedom** means that newspapers, radio, television and online media may report freely. The state may not tell them what to write. Press freedom is important for **democracy**, because people need good information to form an opinion. In Switzerland media freedom is protected in the Federal Constitution.

Reporters Without Borders was founded in **1985** in **Montpellier** in the south of France. Today its international headquarters is in **Paris**. In French it is called **Reporters sans frontières**, and the abbreviation **RSF** is used worldwide. The organisation has sections in several countries and is **independent of governments**.

RSF helps **persecuted journalists**, for example with legal aid or support in fleeing. The organisation makes it public when media workers are arrested, threatened or attacked. It also campaigns against **censorship** on the internet. Censorship means that content is banned or suppressed.

Since **2002** RSF has published a **press freedom ranking** every year. It compares how freely journalists can work in about **180 countries**. It assesses, for example, political interference, economic pressure and violence against media workers. From 2017 to 2024 **Norway** came first every year. For years Switzerland has been one of the countries with good press freedom.

gewusst: 3 May is World Press Freedom Day.
Although RSF was founded in Montpellier, its headquarters is now in Paris.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland itself has hardly any raw materials. Even so, it is one of the most important trading centres in the world for oil, metals, gold and agricultural goods such as coffee.
wichtigste: Geneva is the most important location, especially for the oil trade.
Many commodity firms are based in the canton of Zug, including Glencore in Baar.
Lugano is also an important trading centre.
In transit trade, the goods never even come to Switzerland.
There are large gold refineries in Ticino.
Companies value low taxes and political stability.

abschnitte.text: **Raw materials** are materials from nature that are processed further. There are **energy raw materials** such as oil, **metals** such as copper and aluminium, and **agricultural raw materials** from farming such as coffee, wheat or sugar. Standardised raw materials that are traded in large quantities on exchanges are called **commodities**.

Switzerland never sees most of the raw materials that Swiss firms trade. This is called **transit trade**. A company buys copper in Chile, for example, and sells it to China. The ship sails directly there, but the deal is handled in Switzerland. This requires banks, insurers, shipping companies and inspection firms.

**Geneva** is regarded as the most important location. Several of the world's largest **oil trading firms** are based there. In second place is the canton of **Zug**, which from the 1950s attracted trading firms with low taxes. The group **Glencore** has its headquarters in **Baar**. The third important centre is **Lugano**, where mainly firms trading metals and agricultural goods are active.

Several of the world's largest **gold refineries** are in **Ticino**. There gold is purified and cast into **bars**, which are traded worldwide. A large part of the world's gold passes through a Swiss refinery at some point.

Companies come because of **low taxes**, **political stability**, a strong financial centre and the central location in Europe. The industry brings jobs and tax revenue. However, critics call for more responsibility for the environment and human rights in the countries where the raw materials are extracted. In 2020 the Responsible Business Initiative won a narrow majority of the voters but failed because it did not win a majority of the cantons.

gewusst: Switzerland has almost no raw materials of its own and is still a centre of the world's commodity trade.
In transit trade, the goods being traded never cross the Swiss border.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations (UN) was founded in 1945. Since then the world has changed greatly, which is why there has been debate for decades about reforming the UN and especially the Security Council.
wichtigste: The Security Council has five permanent members with a veto: the USA, Russia, China, France and Great Britain.
Since 1965 the Council has had 15 members instead of 11; this was the only enlargement so far.
The G4 (Germany, Japan, India, Brazil) want permanent seats.
The Uniting for Consensus group, led by Italy, rejects new permanent seats.
In the Ezulwini Consensus, Africa demands at least two permanent seats.
Since 2009 the reform has been discussed in intergovernmental negotiations in the General Assembly.

abschnitte.text: When the UN was founded in 1945, the victorious powers of the Second World War were given permanent seats on the **Security Council**. Each of these five countries has a **veto**: it can prevent a decision on its own. Today the UN has many more members than then, and countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America have become more important. Many countries therefore think that the Council no longer reflects today's world well.

In 1963 the member states decided to enlarge the Security Council. The change came into force in **1965**. Since then the Council has had 15 members instead of 11, because the **non-permanent seats** rose from six to ten. The non-permanent members are each elected for two years. There has been no further enlargement since then.

The **G4**, Germany, Japan, India and Brazil, support one another for permanent seats. The **Uniting for Consensus** group, formerly called the “Coffee Club”, is against this. It includes countries such as Italy, Pakistan, Argentina and South Korea and would rather have more non-permanent seats. In the **Ezulwini Consensus** of 2005, the African Union demands at least two permanent seats with a veto. Since 2009 **intergovernmental negotiations** have been held on this every year, so far without agreement.

In 2004 a **High-level Panel** presented two models. **Model A** provided for six new permanent seats without a veto and three more non-permanent seats. Model B wanted a new kind of seat with a four-year, renewable term. In 2005 Secretary-General **Kofi Annan** published the report **“In Larger Freedom”**, which linked development, security and human rights.

abschnitte.titel: What has been achieved so far
abschnitte.text: At the World Summit in 2005 the **Peacebuilding Commission** was created. It helps countries rebuild after a war so that violence does not break out again. In 2006 the **Human Rights Council**, based in Geneva, was also set up. Switzerland has been a member of the UN since 2002 and in 2023 and 2024 was a non-permanent member of the Security Council for the first time.

gewusst: The name Ezulwini Consensus comes from a valley in Eswatini where African countries met.
A change to the UN Charter needs the approval of all five permanent members, which is why reforms are so difficult.

teile.einleitung: A monarchy is a form of state in which a king, a queen or a prince is at the head of the country. The office is usually passed down within the family. Switzerland is not a monarchy but a republic.
wichtigste: In a monarchy, a king, a queen or a prince is the head of state.
A country with a king or queen is called a kingdom.
Usually a child of the king inherits the office; this is called a hereditary monarchy.
A king usually reigns until his death.
A king is addressed as “Majesty”.
In Great Britain, Parliament makes the laws, not the king.
Switzerland has no king; it is a republic.

abschnitte.text: The word **monarchy** comes from Greek and means “rule by one person”. At the head is a **monarch**: a king, a queen, a prince or an emperor. A country with a king or a queen is called a **kingdom**, for example Spain or Denmark. A country with a prince is called a **principality**, like Liechtenstein. A king's wife is usually called the **queen**, and together they are the **royal couple**.

Usually you are born into the royal family. A child of the king or queen later inherits the office. That is why it is called a **hereditary monarchy**. The person who will be the next king is called the **heir to the throne**. A king usually reigns for life, until his death. But some give up the office voluntarily in old age; this is called **abdication**.

In the past many kings held all the power; this is called an **absolute monarchy**. Today most monarchies in Europe are **parliamentary monarchies**. There the king has little power. In **Great Britain**, for example, **Parliament** passes the laws and an elected government runs the country. The king mainly represents the country at ceremonies and state visits.

Kings and queens are addressed as **“Your Majesty”**. This is an old, very polite form of address. For princes, the German-speaking world uses the title **“Durchlaucht”**, which corresponds to “Serene Highness”. A monarchy often also includes a crown, a sceptre and magnificent palaces. Many people are interested in the lives of royal families.

Switzerland has **no king**. It is a **republic**. The people elect the parliament and can vote themselves on many questions. Instead of a king there is the **Federal Council** with seven members who govern together. Interestingly, the famous ruling family of the **Habsburgs** originally came from the area of today's Switzerland; their ancestral castle stands in the canton of Aargau.

gewusst: The Pope is the head of Vatican City and is elected, not born into the role: an elective monarchy.
Habsburg Castle in the canton of Aargau is the ancestral seat of one of the most powerful ruling families in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Muhammad Yunus is an economist from Bangladesh. He became known through the Grameen Bank, which gives small loans to poor people. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.
wichtigste: Muhammad Yunus was born in 1940 near Chittagong, which today belongs to Bangladesh.
He studied economics and gained his doctorate in the USA.
After that he was professor of economics at the University of Chittagong.
He founded the Grameen Bank, which gives small loans to poor people.
In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize.
He promotes social business, meaning companies that solve social problems.
From August 2024 until after the elections in February 2026 he led an interim government in Bangladesh.

abschnitte.text: Yunus studied **economics**, the study of how a country manages its economy. He gained his doctorate in the USA and returned home after Bangladesh became independent in 1971. At the University of Chittagong he headed the economics department. There he saw how poor many people in the surrounding villages were. He did not just want to teach theories, but to help in practical ways.

Many poor people could not borrow money from normal banks because they had no collateral. So Yunus began lending small amounts himself. This grew into the **Grameen Bank**, which means something like “village bank”. It gives **microcredits**, very small loans, often to women. With the money people can, for example, set up a small business.

In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank jointly received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The Nobel Committee honoured their work for development from below. The idea behind it: people who escape poverty live more safely and peacefully. After that, microcredits were copied in many countries. However, some experts view the effect of microcredits critically.

Yunus coined the term **social business**. By this he means companies that want to solve a social or environmental problem. The profit is not shared out to owners but put back into the company. This way the business is meant to grow and help even more people. Yunus has written books about it and gives talks all over the world.

In summer 2024 there were large protests in Bangladesh, and the prime minister resigned. On 8 August 2024 Yunus became head of an **interim government**. An interim government runs a country for a limited time until new elections are held. After the elections of February 2026, Yunus stepped down from the post.

gewusst: The name Grameen comes from the Bengali language and is related to the word for village.
Yunus did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize alone, but together with his bank.

teile.einleitung: The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, Quad for short, is a forum of four countries in the Indo-Pacific region. In it, the USA, Japan, India and Australia cooperate on security and other issues.
wichtigste: The Quad is made up of the USA, Japan, India and Australia.
It is not a formal military alliance.
Its roots lie in the relief effort after the tsunami of 2004.
Japanese Prime Minister Shinzō Abe proposed the dialogue in 2007.
Australia temporarily pulled out in 2008.
In 2017 the Quad was revived, and in 2021 the first summit of the leaders took place.

abschnitte.text: In December **2004** a massive **tsunami** devastated many coasts around the **Indian Ocean**. At that time the USA, Japan, India and Australia coordinated their navies for **disaster relief**. This gave rise to the idea of a regular dialogue. **Quadrilateral** means “four-sided”, so the name stands for the four countries.

Japanese Prime Minister **Shinzō Abe** proposed the **Quad dialogue** in **2007**. He promoted cooperation between the democracies of the **Indo-Pacific**, the region between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. But in **2008** **Australia** under Kevin Rudd pulled out. The government did not want to strain its relations with **China**. After that the dialogue lay dormant for about ten years.

In **2017** representatives of the four countries met again on the sidelines of a summit in Manila. An important reason was China's growing presence in the region. In March **2021** the four leaders met for the first time by video, and in September 2021 in person in **Washington**. This gave the Quad considerably more weight. China views the Quad critically.

The Quad is **not a military alliance** with an obligation to provide assistance. Even so, the navies train together. The **Malabar** exercise began as an exercise between **India and the USA**. Since Australia returned in **2020**, all four Quad countries have taken part. The four countries also cooperate on topics such as health, technology and the climate.

gewusst: Shinzō Abe also coined the idea of a “free and open Indo-Pacific”.
The four Quad countries lie on three different continents.

teile.einleitung: New Zealand is an island country in the South Pacific, far away from Switzerland. The country consists mainly of two large islands. It is known for its nature, the kiwi bird and the culture of the Māori.
wichtigste: The capital is Wellington, and the largest city is Auckland.
Wellington is the southernmost capital of any country in the world.
New Zealand consists mainly of the North Island and the South Island.
The Māori lived in New Zealand before the Europeans.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first country to give women the vote nationwide.
The kiwi is the symbol of the country.

abschnitte.text: New Zealand lies in the **South Pacific**, south-east of Australia. It consists mainly of the **North Island** and the **South Island**, plus many smaller islands. The country has mountains, volcanoes, glaciers and long beaches. Because it is in the southern hemisphere, it is summer there when it is winter here. The largest city is **Auckland**.

The capital is called **Wellington**. It lies at the southern tip of the North Island. No other national capital is further south. In Wellington there is a round parliament building that is called the **Beehive** because of its shape. The ministers work inside it.

The **Māori** came to New Zealand across the sea in boats many hundreds of years ago. They lived there long before Europeans arrived. Their language is now an **official language** of the country. In the Māori language New Zealand is called **Aotearoa**. This means something like “land of the long white cloud”.

In **1893** women in New Zealand were allowed to vote throughout the country. This made New Zealand the first country in the world with **women's suffrage** at national level. In Switzerland it took much longer. Here women only received the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. That is a difference of almost 80 years.

The **kiwi** is a small bird that cannot fly. It lives only in New Zealand and is mostly active at night. With its long beak it searches the ground for worms and insects. The kiwi is the symbol of the country. The people of New Zealand often call themselves “Kiwis”.

gewusst: When it is winter in Switzerland, it is summer in New Zealand.
The kiwi fruit was named after the bird because it looks similarly brown and fluffy.

teile.einleitung: Since April 2023 there has been war in Sudan. The army and the RSF militia are fighting for power in the country. Millions of people have had to flee, and many are suffering from hunger.
wichtigste: Since April 2023 the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been fighting.
The army is led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the RSF by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti.
The RSF grew out of the Janjaweed militias.
The ruler Omar al-Bashir was overthrown in 2019.
Sudan has the largest displacement crisis in the world (as of 2025).
The army government moved its seat to Port Sudan.

abschnitte.text: **Omar al-Bashir** had ruled Sudan since **1989**. The **International Criminal Court** wanted him for crimes in Darfur. After large **protests**, the military removed him in **April 2019**. After that the country was meant to move towards democracy. In 2021, however, the army and the RSF carried out a coup together.

In **April 2023** the two sides began fighting each other. The **army** is led by **Abdel Fattah al-Burhan**. The **Rapid Support Forces** (RSF) militia is led by **Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo**, known as **Hemedti**. Both want power in the country. Because of the fighting in the capital **Khartoum**, the army government moved its seat to **Port Sudan** on the Red Sea.

The RSF grew out of the **Janjaweed** militias. From 2003 these were involved in serious crimes during the **Darfur conflict**. Under al-Bashir they were reorganised as the RSF in 2013. In **Darfur**, in the west of the country, the population is again badly affected by violence. In October 2025 the RSF captured the city of **El Fasher**, the army's last major stronghold in Darfur.

According to the UN, more than **12 million people** have been displaced (as of 2025). This makes Sudan the **largest displacement crisis in the world**. Many fled to neighbouring countries such as **Chad**, **Egypt** and **South Sudan**. In August 2024 an expert panel declared a **famine** in the **Zamzam** camp near El Fasher. Sieges and blocked aid deliveries are seen as the main causes.

Other countries also play a role. Experts and UN reports often accuse the **United Arab Emirates** of supplying the RSF with weapons. The Emirates deny this. Aid organisations are calling for the fighting to stop and for aid to be allowed through to the people.

gewusst: South Sudan has been a separate country since 2011; its capital is Juba.
In Khartoum the White Nile and the Blue Nile flow together.

teile.einleitung: In a representative democracy, the people elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf. These representatives sit in parliament and pass laws. In Switzerland this system is supplemented by popular votes; this is called semi-direct democracy.
wichtigste: Representative means acting on behalf of others: elected members decide for the people.
The Swiss Parliament consists of the National Council with 200 members and the Council of States with 46.
The 200 National Council seats are distributed among the cantons according to their resident population.
Within a canton the seats are distributed among the lists using the Hagenbach-Bischoff method.
Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.
The United Federal Assembly elects the members of the Federal Council.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau believed that the general will could not be represented by elected members.

abschnitte.text: In large countries, not everyone can discuss every law themselves. That is why they elect **representatives** to act for them. Together these representatives form the **parliament**. They are elected for a certain period and must then stand for election again.

The Federal Assembly consists of two chambers: the **National Council** with 200 members and the **Council of States** with 46 members. The National Council seats are distributed among the cantons according to their resident population, but every canton has at least one seat. In the Council of States most cantons have two seats and six cantons only one. Together the two councils form the United Federal Assembly, which elects the Federal Council.

The National Council is elected every four years, and since 1919 by **proportional representation**. Under this system the parties receive roughly as many seats as their share of the vote. The seats are distributed among the lists using the Hagenbach-Bischoff method. Anyone who writes people from different lists on their ballot paper is **splitting their vote** (in German “panaschieren”), and anyone who writes a name twice is cumulating it.

Under Article 161 of the Federal Constitution there is a **ban on instructions**. This means that members vote without instructions and need only follow their conscience. Nobody may tell them how to vote. Even so, they usually coordinate with their party and their parliamentary group.

The thinker Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who was born in Geneva, viewed representation by elected members critically. He believed that the general will, the **volonté générale**, could not be expressed by representatives. Switzerland combines both ideas: Parliament makes the laws, but the people can have a say through the referendum and the popular initiative. That is why it is called a semi-direct democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Elected people who decide in parliament on behalf of the people.
An electoral system in which seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote.
Writing candidates from different lists on one ballot paper.
A parliament whose members often have another job besides politics.

gewusst: Most Swiss members of parliament have another job besides their seat in parliament.
Parliament meets in the Federal Palace in Bern, normally in four sessions of three weeks each per year.

teile.einleitung: The ordinary legislative procedure is the normal way laws are made in the European Union. In it, the European Parliament and the Council of the EU decide as equal partners. Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it adopts some EU rules through treaties.
wichtigste: The European Commission proposes new laws.
Parliament and the Council must agree to the same text.
The procedure is set out in Article 294 TFEU.
Before the Treaty of Lisbon it was called the co-decision procedure.
There are at most three readings.
If Parliament and the Council cannot agree, the Conciliation Committee helps.
As a rule the Council decides by qualified majority.

abschnitte.text: In the EU, the **European Commission** normally has the **right of initiative**. This means that only it can propose new laws. Parliament and the Council can only ask it to take action. This is different from Switzerland, where members of parliament and the people can also make proposals. After that, Parliament and the Council discuss the proposal.

In the ordinary procedure, the **European Parliament** and the **Council of the EU** decide as equals. The Council is made up of ministers from the member states. Both must agree to the same text. The Council usually decides by **qualified majority**, a special, larger majority. This is set out in **Article 294** of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, TFEU for short.

A **reading** is a round of discussion on a draft law. There are at most **three readings**. In the second reading, Parliament basically has three months, which can be extended by one month. If it lets the deadline pass, the Council's position is regarded as adopted. If Parliament rejects it by a majority of its members, the law has failed.

If Parliament and the Council cannot agree after the second reading, the **Conciliation Committee** is convened. It is made up of equal numbers of representatives of the Council and Parliament. They have six weeks to find a joint draft. If they succeed, the **third reading** follows. There Parliament and the Council must approve the draft once more.

abschnitte.titel: From co-decision to the normal case
abschnitte.text: The procedure was introduced with the **Treaty of Maastricht**. At that time it was called the **co-decision procedure**. With the **Treaty of Lisbon** it was given its present name. Since then it has been the normal procedure for most EU laws. This made the directly elected Parliament stronger.

gewusst: In the EU it is not Parliament but the Commission that proposes almost all laws.
An EU law can count as adopted if Parliament simply does not decide anything in the second reading.

teile.einleitung: “Persona non grata” is an expression from diplomacy. It describes a diplomat who is no longer accepted by the host country and therefore has to leave.
wichtigste: “Persona non grata” is Latin for “unwelcome person”.
The declaration is governed by the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961.
A country can make it at any time and without giving reasons.
The sending country must then recall the person.
A person can be declared unwelcome even before arriving in the country.
The country affected often responds with expulsions of its own.

abschnitte.text: **Diplomats** represent their country in another state, usually at an **embassy**. They enjoy special protection, **diplomatic immunity**. This means that as a rule they cannot be put on trial in the host country. The rules for this are set out in the **Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations** of 1961. Switzerland, with Bern and Geneva, is home to many diplomats.

The Latin expression **“persona non grata”** means **“unwelcome person”**. A country can declare a diplomat to be one **at any time** and **without giving reasons**. The **sending country** must then **recall** the person or end their work at the embassy. If it does not do so in time, the person is no longer recognised as a diplomat. The declaration is even possible before the person has entered the country at all.

Expelling diplomats is a **retorsion**. In international law, this is the name for a **permitted but unfriendly** response to another country's behaviour. The country affected often responds according to the principle of **reciprocity**: it expels a similar number of diplomats in return. There have been such waves of expulsions, for example, between Russia and Western countries.

The expression “persona non grata” applies to the **head of mission** and the **diplomatic staff**. For the other employees of an embassy, such as administrative staff, the convention uses the expression **“not acceptable”**.
