The effect is similar, though: the person may not continue working in the host country.

gewusst: In everyday life people sometimes jokingly say that someone is “persona non grata” somewhere when they are no longer welcome there.
Because diplomats enjoy immunity, expulsion is often the strongest measure a host country can take.

teile.einleitung: The Oslo Accords of 1993 were an important attempt to resolve the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians peacefully. For the first time, Israel and the PLO recognised each other and agreed on Palestinian self-government.
wichtigste: The secret preliminary talks took place in Norway from January 1993.
The first agreement was signed on 13 September 1993 in front of the White House in Washington.
Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat shook hands, with US President Bill Clinton standing between them.
Israel and the PLO recognised each other in letters.
The Palestinian Authority grew out of the agreement.
Rabin, Arafat and Shimon Peres received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994.
The Oslo II Accord of 1995 divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Israel and the **PLO**, the Palestine Liberation Organization, did not talk to each other officially. So from January 1993 Norwegian diplomats organised **secret meetings**. Away from the public eye, both sides could talk more openly. Because the talks began in Norway, the agreement bears the name of its capital, Oslo.

On 13 September 1993 the **Declaration of Principles** was signed in front of the White House in Washington. Israeli Prime Minister **Yitzhak Rabin** and PLO leader **Yasser Arafat** shook hands. Shortly before, both sides had exchanged letters: the PLO recognised **Israel's right to exist** and renounced violence. Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people.

Oslo I was **not a finished peace treaty**. It only set out principles for a transitional period. The new **Palestinian Authority** was to govern parts of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank itself. Difficult questions such as borders, Jerusalem, refugees and settlements were put off to later negotiations. With **Oslo II** in 1995, the West Bank was divided into **Areas A, B and C**. In Area C, the largest part, Israel kept full control.

For their efforts, Rabin, Arafat and the Israeli foreign minister **Shimon Peres** received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1994. But there were opponents of the agreement on both sides. On 4 November 1995, after a peace rally in Tel Aviv, Rabin was **murdered** by an Israeli extremist. Later negotiations did not bring a final peace. To this day there is dispute over how the conflict can be resolved.

gewusst: The agreement bears the name of Oslo but was signed in Washington.
The Palestinian Authority is now based in Ramallah in the West Bank.

teile.einleitung: On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a large-scale attack on Ukraine. This began the largest war in Europe since the end of the Second World War in 1945.
wichtigste: The full-scale attack began on 24 February 2022.
Russia had already annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014.
Volodymyr Zelensky has been President of Ukraine since 2019.
At the end of February 2022 Switzerland adopted the EU's sanctions.
In 2022 Turkey and the UN brokered a grain deal.
Millions of people fled Ukraine, including to Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Ukraine** has been an independent country since 1991. In March **2014** Russia occupied the Ukrainian peninsula of **Crimea** and annexed it. This breaks **international law**, the rules between countries, and most countries do not recognise it. In the same year fighting began in the east of Ukraine, in the **Donbas**.

In the early hours of **24 February 2022**, Russian troops attacked Ukraine from the north, east and south. President **Volodymyr Zelensky**, in office since 2019, stayed in Kyiv and has led the country through the war. Russian troops withdrew from the Kyiv region in spring 2022. Afterwards many civilians who had been killed were found in the suburb of **Bucha**, which caused horror around the world.

The port city of **Mariupol** was besieged in 2022. The last defenders had dug in at the **Azovstal** steelworks and surrendered in May 2022. In July 2022 **Turkey** and the UN brokered a **grain deal** in Istanbul. It allowed ships carrying grain out of Ukrainian ports until Russia pulled out in 2023. In August 2024 Ukrainian troops made a surprise advance into the Russian region of **Kursk**.

On **28 February 2022** the Federal Council decided to adopt the **EU's sanctions** against Russia. This attracted international attention because Switzerland is **neutral**. For refugees from Ukraine, Switzerland used **protection status S** for the first time in 2022. In June 2024 an international conference on peace in Ukraine took place on the **Bürgenstock**.

gewusst: Protection status S had existed in Swiss law for a long time, but it was used for the first time in 2022.
In March 2022 the UN General Assembly condemned the attack by a large majority.

teile.einleitung: Every parliament needs someone to chair the sittings and keep order. This person is called the president of parliament, or in Great Britain and the USA the “Speaker”.
wichtigste: The speaker chairs the sittings and gives members the floor.
He or she is meant to be fair and neutral towards all parties.
In Switzerland the President of the National Council is often called the “highest Swiss”.
The British Speaker calls “Order!” when it gets too noisy.
In the Bundestag the President keeps order with a bell.
In the US House of Representatives the Speaker uses a wooden gavel.

abschnitte.text: The **president** or **speaker of parliament** chairs the sittings. He or she gives members the floor, calls votes and makes sure the rules are kept. The speaker also represents parliament to the outside world. Because the speaker is meant to treat all members equally, **neutrality** is especially important.

In Switzerland the President of the **National Council** is elected anew every year. Whoever chairs the National Council ranks first in the country according to **protocol**. That is why people speak of the **“highest Swiss”**. The **Council of States** also has its own president. When both chambers meet together, the President of the National Council chairs the sitting.

In the British House of Commons the chair is called the **Speaker**. If things get too rowdy, he calls out **“Order!”**. After being elected, the Speaker leaves his **party** in order to be completely neutral. Normally he does not vote; only in a **tie** does his vote decide. A new Speaker pretends not to want the job, and the members jokingly **drag** him to his chair.

In the German Bundestag there is a **bell** on the presiding table. The President rings it when it gets too noisy. In March 2025 **Julia Klöckner** was elected President of the Bundestag. In the **US House of Representatives** the Speaker uses a small **wooden gavel**. With it he opens the sittings and keeps order.

gewusst: Dragging the new Speaker to the chair is a reminder of earlier times, when the job could be dangerous.
In the USA the Speaker is next in line to succeed the President after the Vice President.

teile.einleitung: Consular protection is the help a country gives its citizens abroad. For Switzerland, embassies and consulates of the FDFA take care of this. They help in emergencies, but not with everything.
wichtigste: If you lose your passport abroad, you contact the Swiss embassy or consulate.
The mission can issue a provisional passport.
People who are arrested have the right to contact their consulate.
The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations dates from 1963.
Honorary consuls work on a voluntary basis and often live in the host country.
You have to pay fines abroad yourself.
Before travelling it is worth looking at the FDFA's travel advice.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has **missions** in many countries. The **embassy** mainly looks after political relations with the host country. The **consulate** takes care of citizens, for example with identity documents or emergencies. Often both tasks are combined in the same building. In Switzerland the responsible body is the **FDFA**, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.

If you lose your **passport** abroad or it is stolen, you report to the Swiss **embassy** or **consulate**. The mission can issue a **provisional passport**. With it you can continue your journey or return home. However, it is only valid for a short time. It is also best to report a theft to the local police.

The rules for consulates are set out in the **Vienna Convention on Consular Relations** of **1963**. It governs the tasks and rights of consulates. **Article 36** is important: if a foreigner is **arrested**, the authorities must tell them that they can have their consulate informed. Consular officials may then visit them.

There is not a separate embassy everywhere. In that case **honorary consuls** often help. They are usually respected local people who work for a country on a **voluntary basis**. They often live in the host country and know their way around well. Switzerland has many such **honorary representations**.

Abroad, the principle of **personal responsibility** applies. The embassy helps in real emergencies. But it does not pay **fines**, bail or lawyers' fees. Anyone who travels should prepare well. In its **travel advice**, the FDFA gives information about dangers such as unrest, crime or natural hazards.

gewusst: The FDFA runs a helpline that can be reached around the clock.
Even in countries where Switzerland has no mission, an honorary consul can often help.

teile.einleitung: The Red Cross is a worldwide aid organisation that was founded in Geneva in 1863. It helps people in wars, in disasters and in everyday life, no matter where they come from.
wichtigste: The Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863 by five men.
Henry Dunant and General Dufour were members of the Committee of Five.
Its emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.
In many countries the organisation is called the Red Crescent.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is based in Geneva.
In Switzerland there is the Swiss Red Cross (SRC).

abschnitte.text: In 1859, after the Battle of Solferino in Italy, **Henry Dunant** from Geneva saw thousands of wounded soldiers without any help. He wrote a book about it and wanted there to be aid societies for the wounded. In **1863** he founded a committee with four other Genevans, including **General Dufour**. Because there were five men, it is called the **Committee of Five**. It grew into the Red Cross.

The emblem is a **red cross on a white background**. The colours of the **Swiss flag** were reversed: the white cross on red became a red cross on white. In many countries the organisation is called the **Red Crescent** and helps in exactly the same way. Since **2005** there has also been the **Red Crystal**, a red square standing on one of its points.

In war, the Red Cross helps especially the **wounded and prisoners**. It does not matter which side they are on. The **International Committee of the Red Cross**, **ICRC** for short, is based in Geneva. It visits prisoners of war, brings relief supplies and helps families who have lost each other in war to find one another again.

In Switzerland there is the **Swiss Red Cross**, **SRC** for short. It helps, for example, with **blood donation**: the blood donation service collects blood for sick and injured people. The SRC also organises transport services for older people, trains care assistants and helps in disasters at home and abroad. Many volunteers work with it.

gewusst: In 1901 Henry Dunant received the very first Nobel Peace Prize.
8 May, Henry Dunant's birthday, is World Red Cross Day.

teile.einleitung: The Reichstag building stands in Berlin and is the seat of the German Bundestag, the parliament of Germany. With its glass dome, it is one of the best-known buildings in Germany.
wichtigste: The Bundestag has its plenary chamber in the Reichstag building.
The building was built more than 100 years ago.
Since 1916 the words “Dem deutschen Volke” (“To the German people”) have stood above the entrance.
In 1995 Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the building in fabric.
The architect Norman Foster rebuilt it in the 1990s.
You can climb the glass and steel dome by a ramp.

abschnitte.text: The Reichstag building was built at the end of the 19th century to plans by the architect **Paul Wallot**. At that time the Reichstag, the parliament of the German Empire, met here. Today the **Bundestag** has its **plenary chamber** here, the large debating hall. There the members discuss and pass Germany's laws.

Above the entrance, in large letters, are the words **“Dem deutschen Volke”**, meaning “To the German people”. The inscription was put up in **1916**, in the middle of the First World War. The letters were cast from the metal of old cannons. The words are a reminder that parliament works for the people of the country.

In 1933 the building burned in the **Reichstag fire**, and in the Second World War it was badly damaged. Afterwards it stood for a long time right next to the Berlin Wall. After German reunification in 1990, it was decided that the Bundestag should meet here again. Since 1999 parliament has worked in the rebuilt building.

In **1995** the artists **Christo and Jeanne-Claude** wrapped the whole building in shimmering silver **fabric**. The artwork could be seen for about two weeks. Millions of people came to Berlin to marvel at it. After that the major rebuilding began.

The British architect **Norman Foster** gave the building a new **dome of glass** and steel. Visitors walk up a **ramp** in a spiral to the top and can see far across Berlin. In the middle hangs a **funnel made of 360 mirrors**. It directs daylight down into the plenary chamber. The transparent dome is also meant to show that politics should be open and visible.

gewusst: From the dome you can watch the members in the plenary chamber from above.
The letters of the inscription were cast from captured cannons.

tqfxm6i.t: Swiss contribution to the enlarged EU

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a member of the European Union. Even so, it supports poorer EU countries with money, especially those that have joined since 2004. This is called the Swiss contribution to the enlarged EU, or cohesion contribution.
wichtigste: The contribution is meant to reduce differences between poor and rich EU regions.
In 2006 the people approved the law for the first enlargement contribution.
In the first contribution, Poland received the most money.
The second contribution amounts to about 1.3 billion francs.
Its focus areas are cohesion and migration.
Parliament finally released the second contribution in 2021.

abschnitte.text: **Cohesion** means holding together. In the EU there are rich and poorer regions. With the **cohesion contribution**, Switzerland helps to reduce these differences. The money supports **projects** in economically weaker EU countries. Switzerland chooses the projects together with the partner countries. It does not pay the money into the EU's coffers, but directly into the projects.

On 26 November **2006** the people accepted the Federal Act on Cooperation with the States of Eastern Europe, with about 53 per cent in favour. The first **enlargement contribution** is based on it. It supported the countries that had joined the EU in 2004 and later. **Poland** is the largest of these countries and received the biggest share. Small countries such as **Malta** received much less.

The **second Swiss contribution** amounts to **1.302 billion francs** and is spread over about ten years. It has two focus areas: **cohesion** and **migration**. About 1.1 billion francs go to the 13 countries that have joined the EU since 2004, for example Poland, Hungary and Romania. About 200 million francs help countries that are strongly affected by migration.

Parliament approved the second contribution in 2019 but attached a **condition** to it: the EU was not to treat Switzerland unfairly. Because there was a dispute with the EU, the money was at first blocked. On 30 September **2021** Parliament finally released the contribution. It is regarded as an important signal in relations between Switzerland and the EU.

Many projects strengthen **vocational training**, for example in Bulgaria, Romania or Slovakia. Switzerland contributes its experience with **apprenticeships**, meaning training in a company combined with vocational school. Other projects improve, for example, the environment, health or security. Swiss experts and companies also work on some projects.

gewusst: Switzerland is not an EU member and still voluntarily supports poorer EU countries.
Switzerland's dual system of vocational training serves as a model in several partner countries.

teile.einleitung: The Olympic flag shows five interlocking rings on a white background. It is the best-known symbol of the Olympic Games. It was designed by Pierre de Coubertin.
wichtigste: The flag has five rings in blue, yellow, black, green and red.
The background is white.
There are three rings at the top and two at the bottom.
The rings stand for the inhabited continents.
Pierre de Coubertin drew the flag in 1913.
In 1920 it flew at the Games for the first time, in Antwerp.

abschnitte.text: The Olympic flag has **five rings**. There are three in the top row and two in the bottom row. All the rings are **linked together**. The colours are blue, yellow, black, green and red. They are on a white background.

The rings stand for the inhabited **continents**. The fact that they are linked shows that athletes from all over the world come together. The colours were also chosen on purpose. Together with the white, **every national flag** at that time contained at least one of these colours. This way every country was meant to find itself in the flag.

The flag comes from **Pierre de Coubertin**. He was a Frenchman who founded the modern Olympic Games. He drew the rings in 1913. At the 1920 Summer Games in **Antwerp** in Belgium, the flag flew in the stadium for the first time. Coubertin later lived in Lausanne, where the International Olympic Committee has its headquarters today.

At the opening ceremony the Olympic flag is solemnly raised. It flies in the stadium throughout the Games. At the **closing ceremony** it is lowered again. It is then handed over to the city that will host the **next Games**. In this way the flag travels from host to host.

gewusst: The Swiss flag also contains colours of the rings: red and white.
The Olympic rings are among the best-known symbols in the whole world.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a small country in the middle of Europe with four national languages and 26 cantons. It has five neighbouring countries and is known for its neutrality, its direct democracy and the city of Geneva as a centre of world politics. Although it is small, it plays an important role internationally.
wichtigste: Switzerland has five neighbouring countries: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
It covers about 41,300 square kilometres and has about 9 million inhabitants (as of 2024).
The national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Switzerland is a federal state of 26 cantons, with Bern as its federal city.
It has been neutral since 1815 and does not belong to any military alliance.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it is closely linked to it by many agreements.
Numerous international organisations are based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland lies in the heart of Europe and borders **Germany**, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. About 60 per cent of its area is the Alps, plus the Central Plateau and the Jura. The highest point is the Dufourspitze at 4634 metres. Large rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône flow out of the Swiss Alps, which is why Switzerland is also called the water tower of Europe.

Modern Switzerland was founded in 1848 as a **federal state**. It is made up of 26 cantons, which can decide a lot for themselves. It is governed by the Federal Council with seven members, and laws are made by Parliament in Bern. Through **direct democracy**, the people can vote on many questions themselves.

About 9 million people live in Switzerland (as of 2024), about a quarter of them without a Swiss passport. German is spoken most, followed by French and Italian. **Romansh** is spoken mainly in the Grisons. The variety of languages and cultures is part of the country's identity.

Switzerland is **neutral** and not a member of NATO or the EU. It has been a member of the UN since 2002, and in 2023 and 2024 it sat on the UN Security Council. It is linked to the EU through **bilateral agreements**, for example on Schengen or the free movement of persons. It is also a member of EFTA, the OECD and the Council of Europe.

The UN's European headquarters, the International Committee of the Red Cross and many other organisations are based in **Geneva**. Switzerland often offers its good offices and mediates between countries that are in dispute. As a protecting power, it also represents countries that have no direct relations with each other. In addition, it provides development cooperation and humanitarian aid all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state made up of several member states that can decide a lot for themselves; in Switzerland these are the cantons.
One of the 26 member states of Switzerland.
The European Free Trade Association, a trade alliance of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
The people themselves decide on issues and laws.

gewusst: Switzerland has no official capital; Bern is called the “federal city”.
The official Latin name is Confoederatio Helvetica, which is where the abbreviation CH comes from.
The red cross on a white background is the Swiss flag reversed, in honour of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Helsinki Final Act was signed on 1 August 1975. It was the result of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE) and a high point of détente in the Cold War.
wichtigste: The Final Act was signed in Helsinki on 1 August 1975.
35 countries signed it, including the USA and Canada.
It is not a treaty but a politically binding declaration.
It is divided into three “baskets”: security, economics and human contacts.
Albania was the only European country that did not take part.
President of the Confederation Pierre Graber signed for Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: East and West at one table
abschnitte.text: In the **Cold War**, the West with the USA faced the East with the **Soviet Union**. In the 1970s both sides tried to reduce the tensions. At the **Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE)** they negotiated together, partly in **Geneva**. On **1 August 1975** the Final Act was signed in **Helsinki**, the capital of Finland.

It was signed by **35 countries**: 33 European countries plus the **USA and Canada**. This meant both blocs and the neutral countries took part. Only **Albania** stayed out. The communist country under **Enver Hoxha** rejected the conference and only joined the CSCE in 1991. For Switzerland, President of the Confederation **Pierre Graber**, head of the Political Department (today's FDFA), signed it.

The Final Act is divided into **three baskets**. **Basket I** dealt with **security**, including the **inviolability of borders**. This was especially important to the Soviet Union, because it confirmed the borders drawn after 1945. **Basket II** concerned economic cooperation. **Basket III** covered **human contacts** and the **exchange of information**, such as reuniting families and travel.

The Final Act is **not a treaty under international law** but a **politically binding declaration**. Even so, its impact was great. Civil rights activists in the East referred to the **human rights** that had been promised. In Czechoslovakia, **Charter 77** was founded in 1977, and **Václav Havel** was one of its spokespeople. In 1995 the CSCE became the **OSCE**, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

gewusst: At the CSCE, Switzerland worked actively in the group of neutral and non-aligned countries.
Václav Havel, a spokesman of Charter 77, later became president of his country.

teile.einleitung: The Responsibility to Protect, R2P for short, is an idea from world politics. It says that every state must protect its population from the most serious crimes. If it fails to do so, the international community bears responsibility.
wichtigste: The term was coined in 2001 by an international commission set up by Canada.
The commission was led by Gareth Evans and Mohamed Sahnoun.
At the 2005 World Summit in New York, UN member states committed to it for the first time.
It applies to four crimes, including ethnic cleansing.
The first pillar: every state must protect its own population.
In 2011 the Security Council referred to it in the case of Libya.

abschnitte.text: In the past the rule was that what happens inside a state is none of other states' business. The diplomat **Francis Deng** shaped a new view: **sovereignty as responsibility**. Sovereignty means not only rights but also duties towards one's own population. If a state fails in this, responsibility can pass to the **international community**.

In the 1990s the world looked on as serious crimes were committed in **Rwanda**. In **Kosovo**, countries intervened without a mandate from the Security Council. Both led to great debate. The **Canadian** government then set up a commission, the **ICISS**. It was led by the former Australian foreign minister **Gareth Evans** and the Algerian diplomat Mohamed Sahnoun. In 2001 it coined the term “Responsibility to Protect”.

At the **2005 World Summit** in New York, the heads of state and government recognised the Responsibility to Protect in the outcome document. It is a **political commitment**, not a treaty. It applies only to four crimes: **genocide**, **war crimes**, **ethnic cleansing** and **crimes against humanity**. Other threats such as natural disasters are not covered.

The **first pillar** says that every state must protect its own population. The **second pillar** concerns help from the international community so that states can manage this. The **third pillar** allows decisive joint action if a state fails. This is first about diplomacy and help. Military means are only intended as a last step and with the Security Council.

In 2011 the **Security Council** referred to the Responsibility to Protect in **Libya**. With Resolution 1973 it authorised a no-fly zone and the protection of civilians. Critics later accused the intervening countries of using the mandate for **regime change**. Since then the concept has become more controversial. Supporters nevertheless see it as important protection for people.

gewusst: The Responsibility to Protect is not a treaty, yet Security Council resolutions refer to it.
The Responsibility to Protect appears in only two paragraphs of the 2005 outcome document.

teile.einleitung: In German, “Präsidentin” is the female form of “Präsident”. For a long time almost only men led countries, but for several decades more and more women have been leading countries and organisations.
wichtigste: In 1960 Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first woman head of government in Ceylon, today's Sri Lanka.
In 1980 Vigdís Finnbogadóttir became the first woman president elected by the people, in Iceland.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf from Liberia was Africa's first elected woman president.
Since 2019 Ursula von der Leyen has been the first woman to lead the EU Commission.
In 2024 Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first woman president.
In 1977 Elisabeth Blunschy was the first woman President of the National Council.

abschnitte.titel: The first women at the top
abschnitte.text: The world's first woman **head of government** is regarded as **Sirimavo Bandaranaike**. In **1960** she became prime minister of **Ceylon**, today's **Sri Lanka**. In **Iceland**, the people elected **Vigdís Finnbogadóttir** in **1980**. She was the world's first woman **president** to be elected by the people. In **Liberia**, **Ellen Johnson Sirleaf** won the election in 2005 and from 2006 was Africa's first elected woman president.

In **India**, **Pratibha Patil** became the first woman president in 2007 and stayed in office until 2012. In **Mexico**, **Claudia Sheinbaum** took office as the first woman president in October **2024**. In **Japan**, **Sanae Takaichi** became the first woman prime minister in October 2025. Many countries in Europe have also had women presidents.

abschnitte.titel: At the head of the EU
abschnitte.text: **Ursula von der Leyen** has led the **European Commission** since December **2019**. She is the first woman in this post. The Commission proposes new laws for the European Union and makes sure the rules are kept. Von der Leyen had previously been a minister in Germany.

In Switzerland women only received the **right to vote and stand for election** at federal level in **1971**. As early as **1977**, **Elisabeth Blunschy** became the first woman to chair the **National Council**. This made her the first “highest Swiss” woman. In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp became the first woman Federal Councillor. **Ruth Dreifuss** was Switzerland's first woman **President of the Confederation** in **1999**.

gewusst: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir remained President of Iceland for 16 years.
Sirimavo Bandaranaike was prime minister three times in total.

teile.einleitung: The Sahel is a dry belt south of the Sahara. Since 2012, violence by armed groups has been spreading there. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger are especially affected.
wichtigste: The Sahel lies between the Sahara Desert and the savannah.
The crisis began in Mali in 2012.
From 2014 to 2022 France fought terrorist groups with Operation Barkhane.
The UN mission MINUSMA left Mali at the end of 2023.
In 2023 Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger founded the Alliance of Sahel States.
Russia became Mali's most important security partner.

abschnitte.text: The **Sahel** stretches from the **Atlantic** to the **Red Sea**. It lies between the **Sahara** Desert in the north and the savannah in the south. The climate is dry and there are often **droughts**. Countries such as **Mali**, **Burkina Faso** and **Niger** suffer from poverty. On top of that, there has been violence by armed groups for years.

In **2012** the **Tuareg** rebelled in the north of Mali. After that, **jihadist groups** took over large areas. These are armed groups that pursue their aims with violence and in the name of a radical interpretation of Islam. From Mali the violence spread to Burkina Faso and Niger. One important group is **JNIM**, which is linked to **al-Qaeda**.

**France** intervened in Mali in 2013 with Operation **Serval**. From **2014** it extended the mission to the whole Sahel as Operation **Barkhane**. After tensions with the new military governments, Barkhane ended in **2022**. The UN had been in Mali since 2013 with the **MINUSMA** mission, one of the most dangerous UN missions. At the request of the military government it ended at the **end of 2023**.

In **Mali**, **Burkina Faso** and **Niger**, the military took power in coups. In **2023** the three countries founded the **Alliance of Sahel States** (AES). At the start of 2025 they left the West African economic community **ECOWAS**. From the end of 2021 Mali brought Russian mercenaries of the **Wagner Group** into the country. Since 2025 the **Africa Corps** of the Russian Ministry of Defence has taken over this role.

Around **Lake Chad**, the terrorist group **Boko Haram** is active, in Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon. In **2014** it kidnapped about 276 schoolgirls in **Chibok** in Nigeria. This sparked the worldwide campaign **“Bring Back Our Girls”**. Many people in the region have had to flee from the violence.

gewusst: The word “Sahel” comes from Arabic and means something like “shore”, meaning the shore of the desert.
In the Sahel, groups linked to al-Qaeda and to the “Islamic State” compete for influence.

teile.einleitung: **Austria** is Switzerland's eastern neighbour. As in Switzerland, there are many mountains, and people speak German. The capital is **Vienna**.
wichtigste: Austria lies east of Switzerland, and its capital is Vienna.
The flag is red, white and red.
People in Austria speak German.
Vorarlberg and Tyrol border Switzerland.
The Danube flows through Vienna.
Mozart was born in Salzburg.
The highest mountain is the Grossglockner.

abschnitte.text: Austria lies **east of Switzerland**. The country is a federal state with nine **federal states** (Bundesländer), similar to Switzerland's cantons. The westernmost federal state is **Vorarlberg**. It borders the cantons of St Gallen and the Grisons, and **Tyrol** also borders Switzerland. The flag has three horizontal stripes: red at the top, white in the middle and red again at the bottom.

**Vienna** is the capital and the largest city in Austria. The **Danube**, one of the longest rivers in Europe, flows through the city. In the middle of Vienna stands **St Stephen's Cathedral**, the city's landmark. The people of Vienna affectionately call it “Steffl”. **Schönbrunn Palace**, the imperial family's summer palace, is also famous, and very many people visit it today.

People in Austria speak **German**. But many words sound different from Swiss German; for example, Austrians say “Paradeiser” for tomato. Austrian cooking is well known, with Wiener Schnitzel and sweet dishes. The **Sachertorte** is a chocolate cake with apricot jam. It was invented in 1832 by **Franz Sacher**.

Austria is famous for its **music**. **Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart** was born in **Salzburg** in 1756. You can visit the house where he was born there today. Other well-known composers also lived and worked in Vienna. To this day there are large concert halls and the famous State Opera there.

A large part of Austria lies in the **Alps**. The highest mountain is the **Grossglockner** at about 3798 metres. In winter many people go skiing there, and in summer they go hiking. In the west, Austria, Germany and Switzerland share **Lake Constance**.

gewusst: The small Principality of Liechtenstein also lies between Vorarlberg and Switzerland.
Austria has been a member of the European Union since 1995 and pays with the euro, whereas Switzerland uses the franc.

teile.einleitung: The Nobel Prize is a very well-known award for outstanding achievements. Since 1901 it has been awarded every year to people and organisations who have done something great for humanity. It was founded by the Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel.
wichtigste: The Nobel Prize is regarded as the most important award in the world in several fields.
It goes back to the will of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite.
It is awarded in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and for peace.
Since 1969 there has also been a prize for economics.
The prizes are presented on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, the other prizes in Stockholm.
The first Nobel Peace Prize went to Henry Dunant from Geneva in 1901.

abschnitte.text: **Alfred Nobel** lived from 1833 to 1896 and came from Sweden. He invented **dynamite** and became very rich from his factories. In his will of 1895 he decided that his fortune should be used for prizes. The prizes were to go to those who had brought the greatest benefit to humanity.

Since 1901 there have been prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The Swedish central bank later founded a prize for **economics**, which has been awarded since 1969. Up to three people can be honoured for each prize. For the Nobel Peace Prize, organisations can also be honoured.

Various expert bodies choose the winners, for example the Swedish Academy for literature. The **Nobel Peace Prize** is awarded by a committee elected by the Norwegian Parliament. Only certain people may make nominations, such as professors or members of parliament. The names of those nominated are kept secret for 50 years.

In October the winners are announced, which makes news around the world. On 10 December they receive a gold medal, a diploma and **prize money** in Stockholm and Oslo. Recently the prize money was about 11 million Swedish kronor per prize (as of 2025). In Stockholm there is a large banquet afterwards.

**Henry Dunant** from Geneva, the founder of the Red Cross, received the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. The International Committee of the Red Cross has even been honoured three times. Albert Einstein received the physics prize in 1921; he was a Swiss citizen at the time. In 2019 the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz received the physics prize for discovering a planet orbiting another star.

begriffe.erklaerung: A document in which someone sets out what is to happen to their property after their death.
An explosive that was used, for example, in building tunnels.
Money that you receive together with an award.
A group of people who make decisions together.

gewusst: Marie Curie was the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes, in 1903 for physics and in 1911 for chemistry.
Malala Yousafzai was only 17 years old when she received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.
Since 1991 there has also been the “Ig Nobel Prize”, a joke prize for research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think.

teile.einleitung: The Parliament Building in Vienna is the seat of the Austrian Parliament. It looks like a Greek temple and stands on the Ringstrasse in the middle of the city.
wichtigste: The architect Theophil Hansen designed the building.
It was completed in 1883.
Its model was the architecture of ancient Greece.
In front of the building is a fountain with a large statue of the goddess Pallas Athena.
The National Council and the Federal Council work in the building.
After a long renovation it reopened in January 2023.

abschnitte.text: The Parliament stands on the **Ringstrasse**, a grand boulevard in **Vienna**. It was designed by the architect **Theophil Hansen** and completed in **1883**. Its model was **ancient Greece**. That is why the building has columns like a Greek temple. Greece is regarded as the birthplace of **democracy**, and the building was meant to show this.

In front of the Parliament there is a fountain with a large statue of the goddess **Pallas Athena**. For the ancient Greeks, Athena was the goddess of **wisdom**. She is meant to remind people that decisions in Parliament should be made wisely. The statue is a **landmark** of the building and appears in many photos.

Two chambers work in the building: the **National Council** and the **Federal Council**. The National Council has **183 members**. The Federal Council represents the nine federal states. In Switzerland it is different: there the chambers are called the National Council and the Council of States, and the National Council has 200 members. In Switzerland the Federal Council is the government.

The old building urgently needed to be modernised. From **2017** until early **2023** it was completely renovated. During this time Parliament met in the **Hofburg**, the former imperial palace in Vienna. In **January 2023** the Parliament Building was ceremonially reopened. Today visitors can see it on guided tours.

gewusst: Theophil Hansen came from Denmark and also built in Athens.
The Republic of Austria was proclaimed on the ramp in front of the Parliament in 1918.

teile.einleitung: “Max Havelaar” is first of all a famous novel from the Netherlands. It denounced the exploitation of coffee farmers. Later a fair trade label was named after it, which you can also find in Swiss shops.
wichtigste: The novel “Max Havelaar” was written by Eduard Douwes Dekker under the name Multatuli.
It was published in 1860 and is set on the island of Java.
In 1988 the first Fairtrade label, called Max Havelaar, was launched in the Netherlands.
A Max Havelaar Foundation was set up in Switzerland in 1992.
Migros and Coop took part from the very beginning.
Max Havelaar bananas have been available in Switzerland since 1997.

abschnitte.text: In 1860 the Dutchman **Eduard Douwes Dekker** published the novel **“Max Havelaar”**. He used the pen name **Multatuli**, which means “I have endured much” in Latin. The novel is set on the island of **Java** in the **Dutch East Indies**, today's Indonesia. It describes how the local farmers were oppressed. They had to grow coffee for export instead of enough food for themselves. The book became a classic of Dutch literature.

In 1988 the first **Fairtrade label** was launched in the **Netherlands**, named after the novel. Behind it were the church organisation **Solidaridad** and the priest **Frans van der Hoff**. At first it was about coffee from small farmers in Mexico. The farmers receive a **minimum price** and also a **premium** for community projects. Other countries took up the idea in the following years.

In Switzerland the **Max Havelaar Foundation** was founded in 1992 by several Swiss aid organisations. The federal government paid a start-up grant, but only on one condition: the two largest retailers, **Migros** and **Coop**, had to sell fair products. This way the label quickly reached many shops. After coffee, honey, cocoa, sugar and tea, **bananas** followed in March 1997. They became one of the most successful Fairtrade products in Switzerland.

gewusst: A novel from 1860 gave its name to a modern label more than 120 years later.
In Switzerland fair trade bananas are especially popular; they are among the best-known Fairtrade products in the country.

teile.einleitung: Finland and Sweden were militarily non-aligned for a long time. After the Russian attack on Ukraine in 2022, both countries applied for NATO membership. Finland joined in 2023, Sweden in 2024.
wichtigste: Finland and Sweden submitted their applications in May 2022.
The trigger was the Russian attack on Ukraine in February 2022.
Finland became NATO's 31st member on 4 April 2023.
Sweden became the 32nd member on 7 March 2024.
Turkey and finally Hungary only agreed to Sweden joining at a late stage.
Finland has a border with Russia about 1340 km long.

abschnitte.text: **Non-aligned** means that a country does not belong to any military alliance. Sweden had not fought a war since 1814 and stayed non-aligned for more than 200 years. Finland also kept out of alliances after the Second World War. But both countries had already been working closely with NATO before. Like Switzerland, they did not want to tie themselves firmly to one side.

In February 2022 Russia attacked **Ukraine**. After that, opinion in Finland and Sweden changed sharply. In May 2022 the two countries submitted their applications for membership together. For a country to join, all NATO members must agree. This approval is called **ratification**.

Finland deposited its instrument of accession in Washington on **4 April 2023**. This made NATO grow from 30 to 31 members. The date was special: on 4 April 1949 the **North Atlantic Treaty**, on which NATO is based, had been signed. With Finland, NATO's land border with Russia roughly doubled. The Finnish-Russian border is about 1340 km long.

In Sweden's case it took longer. **Turkey** and finally **Hungary** delayed their approval until 2024. On **7 March 2024** Sweden was finally admitted. Since then the alliance has had 32 members. This ended Sweden's long period of non-alignment.

gewusst: Finland joined exactly on the anniversary of the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty.
Sweden was not involved in any war for more than two centuries.

teile.einleitung: Monaco is a tiny principality on the Mediterranean coast. After Vatican City it is the second-smallest country in the world. It is known for its Formula 1 race, its casino and the princely Grimaldi family.
wichtigste: Monaco is a principality with a prince at its head.
Albert II has been Prince of Monaco since 2005.
The Grimaldi family has ruled for more than 700 years.
Monaco lies on the Mediterranean and on the land side borders only France.
It is only about 2 square kilometres in size.
The Formula 1 Monaco Grand Prix takes place every year.
The official language is French.

abschnitte.titel: A tiny state by the sea
abschnitte.text: Monaco lies on the **Côte d'Azur** on the **Mediterranean**. On the land side it borders only **France**. At about **2 square kilometres** it is one of the smallest countries in the world. Only **Vatican City** is smaller. Because many people live in so little space, there are many tower blocks. Monaco is regarded as the country with the highest population density in the world.

Monaco is a **principality**. At its head is a **prince**. The **Grimaldi** family has ruled the country for more than **700 years**. Since 2005 **Albert II** has been Prince of Monaco. He succeeded his father **Rainier III**, who was married to the American actress Grace Kelly. The prince lives in the **Prince's Palace** on a rock above the harbour.

Every year Monaco hosts the **Monaco Grand Prix**. **Formula 1 cars** race right through the narrow streets of the city. The track runs past houses and the harbour and through a tunnel. Overtaking there is very difficult. The race is regarded as one of the most famous in the world.

The official language in Monaco is **French**. There is also the old national language, **Monégasque**, which can be learned at school. People pay with the **euro**, even though Monaco is not a member of the EU. A well-known district is **Monte Carlo** with its famous casino. The **Oceanographic Museum** with its large aquarium is also worth seeing.

gewusst: Monaco is smaller than many Swiss municipalities, for example smaller than the city of Zurich.
For a long time the Oceanographic Museum in Monaco was directed by the famous ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Solferino took place in northern Italy in 1859. It is famous not only because of the war, but above all because it moved Henry Dunant from Geneva to found the Red Cross.
wichtigste: The battle took place near Solferino on 24 June 1859.
It was part of the Austro-Sardinian War, also called the Second Italian War of Independence.
France and Sardinia-Piedmont fought against Austria.
Emperor Napoleon III led the French troops himself.
Afterwards Henry Dunant organised help for the wounded of all sides.

abschnitte.text: In 1859 Italy was not yet a single state. Austria ruled the north, including **Lombardy**. The Kingdom of **Sardinia-Piedmont** wanted to unite Italy and allied itself with **France**. This began the **Austro-Sardinian War**, also called the **Second Italian War of Independence**. On **24 June 1859** the armies met near **Solferino**, south of Lake Garda.

The French emperor **Napoleon III** led his troops himself. The Austrian emperor Franz Joseph I was also on the battlefield. It was one of the largest battles of the 19th century, with a great many dead and wounded. **Austria** lost and had to give up **Lombardy**. This was an important step towards the unification of Italy.

The Geneva businessman **Henry Dunant** was actually travelling to meet Napoleon III on business. After the battle he saw thousands of wounded lying there without care. In the nearby town of **Castiglione delle Stiviere** he organised **help for the wounded** together with local women. The women cared for soldiers of all armies. Their words **“Tutti fratelli”**, meaning “All are brothers”, became a symbol of this.

abschnitte.titel: The path to the Red Cross
abschnitte.text: In 1862 Dunant wrote down his experiences in the book **“A Memory of Solferino”**. In it he proposed aid societies for the wounded in every country. The book attracted attention throughout Europe. In **1863** the committee from which the **Red Cross** grew was founded in **Geneva**, and in 1864 the first **Geneva Convention** followed.

gewusst: The war was officially ended in November 1859 by the Peace of Zurich.
For his work Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

teile.einleitung: The principle of non-refoulement is an important principle of international law. It forbids sending people back to a country where they face persecution or torture. It is also called the ban on returning people to danger.
wichtigste: The French word “refouler” means to push back.
The principle is set out in Article 33 of the Geneva Refugee Convention.
The convention has an exception where the security of the country is in danger.
Protection from torture under Article 3 of the ECHR, on the other hand, applies without exception.
In Switzerland the protection is laid down in Article 25 of the Federal Constitution.
In Switzerland, popular initiatives that violate peremptory international law are invalid.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the French **refouler**, which means to push back. Under **Article 33 of the Geneva Refugee Convention**, no country may expel a refugee to a territory where their life or freedom is threatened. A **refugee** is a person who had to leave their country because of persecution. The ban also applies at the border, not only inside the country. It is one of the most important rules for protecting refugees.

The Refugee Convention has an exception in **Article 33, paragraph 2**. It applies if a refugee is a danger to the security of the country or has been convicted of a particularly serious crime. Protection from **torture** goes further. Under **Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights** (ECHR), it applies without exception, even to criminals. Article 3 of the UN Convention against Torture is equally absolute.

In Switzerland the protection is set out in **Article 25 of the Federal Constitution**. It forbids deporting or extraditing refugees to a state that persecutes them. In addition, all people are protected from deportation to a state where they face torture. The Federal Council and legal experts regard the principle as part of **peremptory international law**. Under Article 139 of the Federal Constitution, popular initiatives that violate peremptory international law are invalid.

abschnitte.titel: On the high seas and via third countries
abschnitte.text: In 2012 the **European Court of Human Rights** ruled in the case of Hirsi Jamaa v. Italy. Italy had intercepted boat refugees on the high seas and taken them back to Libya. The Court found this to be a violation of the ECHR. The principle also applies indirectly: a country may not take a person to a third country which then pushes them on to the state that persecutes them. This is called **indirect refoulement** or chain deportation.

gewusst: The ban on returning people to danger is so strong that in Switzerland not even a popular initiative can abolish it.
The principle also applies to a country's ships on the high seas, far away from any border.

teile.einleitung: The rainbow flag is a colourful flag with stripes in the colours of the rainbow. It is seen all over the world as a sign of diversity and tolerance.
wichtigste: Today the well-known rainbow flag usually has six stripes.
Red is at the very top, followed by orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
The artist Gilbert Baker designed it in 1978.
It flew for the first time in 1978 at a parade in San Francisco.
The very first flag had eight stripes.
Another rainbow flag with the word “PACE” stands for peace.

abschnitte.text: Today the rainbow flag usually has **six stripes**. The colours follow their order in a rainbow in the sky: **red** at the top, then orange, yellow, **green**, blue and violet at the bottom. So green is between yellow and blue. A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted in raindrops and split into its colours.

The American artist **Gilbert Baker** designed the flag in **1978**. Together with helpers he dyed and sewed the first flags himself. They flew at a parade in **San Francisco** in the USA in 1978. Baker wanted to create a cheerful symbol that stands for many different people.

The very first flag had **eight stripes**, including pink and turquoise. These colours were hard to get as fabric at that time. So some colours were left out, and the flag became easier to make. This is how today's usual flag with six stripes came about.

The rainbow flag stands for **diversity and tolerance**. In particular, it is a symbol of lesbian, gay and other **queer people** and their equal rights. You see it at parades, on buildings and at sports events, including in Swiss cities. There are now also newer versions with additional colours.

There is a second well-known rainbow flag: the **peace flag**. It has the word **“PACE”** on it in large letters. This is Italian and means peace. The peace flag comes from **Italy** and is shown at peace demonstrations. So you can tell the two flags apart by the writing.

gewusst: Gilbert Baker deliberately did not protect his flag legally, so that everyone could use it freely.
Because pink and turquoise were missing, the eight stripes eventually became a flag with six stripes.

teile.einleitung: After the end of the First World War, the victorious powers met in Paris in 1919 to decide on the future of Europe. The Paris Peace Conference produced several peace treaties, including the Treaty of Versailles, and founded the League of Nations.
wichtigste: The conference began in Paris in January 1919.
The most important decisions were made by the “Big Four”: Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau and Orlando.
The defeated countries were excluded from the negotiations.
The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors.
Further treaties settled peace with Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire.
The new League of Nations was based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: In January 1919, representatives of many victorious countries met in Paris. The most important decisions were made by the **“Big Four”**: **Woodrow Wilson** (USA), **David Lloyd George** (Great Britain), **Georges Clemenceau** (France) and **Vittorio Emanuele Orlando** (Italy). Clemenceau chaired the conference. Wilson wanted a just peace, while France wanted above all security from Germany.

Germany and its allies were **not allowed to take part** in the negotiations. They received the finished treaties to accept, which is why people in Germany spoke of a **“dictated peace”**. The **Treaty of Versailles** was signed on **28 June 1919** in the **Hall of Mirrors** of the Palace of Versailles. The German Empire had been proclaimed there in 1871. Germany lost territory and had to pay **reparations**, compensation for war damage.

There was a separate treaty for each defeated country, named after places around Paris. The Treaty of **Saint-Germain-en-Laye** of September 1919 concerned **Austria** and forbade its union with Germany. The Treaty of **Trianon** was concluded with **Hungary** in 1920. Hungary lost more than two thirds of its territory in it. Further treaties applied to Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire.

abschnitte.titel: The League of Nations in Geneva
abschnitte.text: One aim of the conference was the **League of Nations**. This organisation was meant to prevent future wars. **Geneva** was chosen as its seat. Switzerland joined in 1920 after a **popular vote**. However, the **USA** never took part, even though President Wilson had proposed the idea: the **US Senate** rejected the Treaty of Versailles.

gewusst: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles is usually called the “war guilt clause”.
The Treaty of Trianon still shapes how Hungarians remember their history today.

teile.einleitung: The Parliament Building in Budapest is the seat of the Hungarian Parliament. It stands magnificently on the bank of the Danube and is the largest building in Hungary.
wichtigste: The Parliament stands in Budapest right on the Danube.
It was designed by the architect Imre Steindl.
Its model was the Palace of Westminster in London.
The building is 268 metres long and has 691 rooms.
A large dome rises in the middle.
Since 2000 the Holy Crown of Hungary has been kept here.

abschnitte.text: **Budapest** is the capital of **Hungary**. The **Danube** flows right through the city. The **Parliament Building** stands directly on its bank. The Hungarian Parliament works here. Especially in the evening, when it is lit up, it is beautifully reflected in the water. It is one of the city's best-known landmarks.

The building was designed by the architect **Imre Steindl**. He took the British Parliament, the **Palace of Westminster** in London, as his model. That is why the two buildings look somewhat alike. Both are built in the **Gothic Revival style**, with many pointed turrets. Steindl died in 1902. The Parliament was only fully completed in **1904**, so he did not live to see it finished.

The Parliament Building is **268 metres long** and is regarded as the **largest building in Hungary**. It has **691 rooms**, plus many staircases and courtyards. A tall **dome** rises in the middle. Beneath it lies the magnificent **Dome Hall**. To the left and right of it are the two large debating chambers.

Since **2000** the **Holy Crown of Hungary** has been kept in the Dome Hall. It is an important symbol of the country's history. In the past the Hungarian kings were crowned with it. Guards watch over the crown carefully. Visitors can see it on a guided tour of the building.

gewusst: The Budapest Parliament is longer than two football pitches placed end to end.
The Hungarian crown has a crooked cross on its top.

teile.einleitung: The North Atlantic Treaty is NATO's founding treaty. It was signed by twelve countries in Washington on 4 April 1949. Its best-known part is Article 5, the mutual assistance clause.
wichtigste: Twelve countries signed the treaty as founding members.
Article 5 says: an attack on one member counts as an attack on all.
When Article 5 is triggered, this is called invoking collective defence.
Collective defence has so far been invoked only once, after 11 September 2001 (as of 2025).
Article 4 provides for consultations when a member feels threatened.
Article 10 governs the admission of new members.

abschnitte.text: On **4 April 1949** twelve countries signed the **North Atlantic Treaty** in Washington. They were the USA, Canada, Great Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Italy and Portugal. NATO is based on this treaty. It is surprisingly short, with only 14 articles. As a neutral country, Switzerland is not a member.

**Article 5** is the **mutual assistance clause**. An armed attack on one member counts as an attack on all. The other members then help with the defence. But each country decides for itself what help it gives. So it does not necessarily have to send soldiers.

When NATO decides that Article 5 applies, this is called invoking **collective defence**. So far this has happened only once (as of 2025). On the day after the **terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001** in New York and Washington, NATO invoked collective defence. In this way the allies supported the USA. Article 5 refers to **Article 51 of the UN Charter**, which gives countries the right to self-defence.

Under **Article 4**, the members consult one another when one of them sees its security or independence threatened. This is weaker than collective defence, because it is only about talks. Article 4 has already been used several times. In this way the members can think about a dangerous situation together. Afterwards they decide whether further steps are needed.

**Article 10** governs how NATO can grow. The members can **unanimously** invite other European countries to join. These countries must promote the principles of the treaty and contribute to the security of the North Atlantic area. All of NATO's enlargements are based on this article. Over time, twelve founding countries have grown into more than thirty members.

gewusst: The North Atlantic Treaty has only 14 articles and fits on a few pages.
The only time collective defence was invoked in NATO's history, it helped not a small country but the USA.

teile.einleitung: A system of government describes how government and parliament work together in a state and who checks whom. There are parliamentary, presidential and mixed systems. With its Federal Council, Switzerland has a very special system, the directorial system.
wichtigste: In a parliamentary system, parliament can remove the government.
The United States is the classic example of a presidential system.
France has a semi-presidential system with a president and a prime minister.
Switzerland has a directorial system: the Federal Council is elected for a fixed term and cannot be voted out.
In 1748, in “The Spirit of the Laws”, Montesquieu described the separation of powers.
In a consensus democracy like Switzerland, all the major parties share in government.
From 1959 to 2003 the “magic formula” applied in the Federal Council, with 2 FDP, 2 CVP, 2 SP and 1 SVP.

abschnitte.text: In 1748, in “The Spirit of the Laws”, the French thinker **Montesquieu** described how power in the state must be divided. Lawmaking, government and the courts should keep a check on one another. This **separation of powers** is meant to prevent any one person or group from becoming too powerful. Almost all democracies today are based on this idea.

In a **parliamentary system**, parliament elects the government and can also remove it again. Examples are Great Britain and Germany. The British House of Commons is elected by first past the post: in each constituency the person with the most votes wins. In Germany there is the constructive vote of no confidence: the Federal Chancellor can only be brought down if a successor is elected at the same time.

In a **presidential system**, the president is elected by the people and is both head of state and head of government. The classic example is the United States. Parliament, the Congress, cannot simply vote the president out. France has a mixed system: the president is elected directly, but the prime minister depends on parliament; this is called a semi-presidential system.

In Switzerland the country is governed by the **Federal Council**, a collegial government of seven members with equal rights. The Federal Assembly elects it for four years, and after that it cannot be voted out. This system is called the **directorial system**. The President of the Confederation changes every year and is only “first among equals”.

Switzerland is a **consensus democracy**, in which all the major parties are represented in the government. From 1959 to 2003 the magic formula applied, with two seats for the FDP, two for the CVP, two for the SP and one for the SVP. In 2003 the SVP gained a second seat at the expense of the CVP. Because everyone shares in government, the parties have to find compromises.

begriffe.erklaerung: Power in the state is divided between parliament, government and the courts.
A government in which several members with equal rights make decisions together.
A vote in parliament to remove a government.
Cooperation of all the major parties in government.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of very few countries in the world with a seven-member government and no head of government.
Since 1848, members of the Federal Council have only very rarely failed to be re-elected, for example Christoph Blocher in 2007.
Since 2021 the CVP party has been called “The Centre” (Die Mitte).
